en: The Nalacampū (The Tale of Damayantī), First Chapter.
Victorious is the moon-crested Lord, who is like sandalwood paste applied to the breast of the Daughter of the Mountain—a breast that carries the heat of desire;
and thereafter, victorious are the playful expressions of the poets who possess fame, which distill drops of nectar for the virtuous.
Victorious is that certain God of Love, whose companion is Spring, and who is the ancient root of the creeper of the entire cycle of worldly existence.
Following that, may the playful charm of the eyes of young women, directed toward the slope of their outer corners, be victorious.
I salute the stream of Sarasvatī, which flows with a profound inner vibration, a temple of bliss for the wise, and mature with its manifold aesthetic flavors.
Clear, captivating in their luster, and skilled in various forms of wordplay—such words exist in the mouth and such women exist in the home of someone through his merits.
What is the use of that poetry for a poet? What is the use of an arrow for an archer?

Those who do not cause the head to reel when fixed upon another’s heart, who are modest in their placement of words, and who are the causes of a mother’s affection— such poets are like children, full of much chatter.
I bow to the multitude of jewels of well-spoken verses from the wise— a collection that knows the turning of the rosary, that accepts the seat of kusha grass,
that is worthy of salutation by the assembly of the wicked like the goddess Brāhmī, and that possesses a girdle of virtues.
I bow to the multitude of jewels of well-spoken verses from the wise.
Even a low-quality piece of glass, when fallen amidst jewels, is regarded as a precious gem;
but where is the likeness between the nature of the moon and a virtuous person, both born of the Atri lineage,
and that of the night and a wicked person, both born of darkness?
It is certain that no one who possesses a father is truly of noble birth if he is of equal intellect;
for he who does not delight in poetry entirely connected with the Asuras (demons), even if it be flawed, is faultless, and even if harsh, is exceedingly tender.
Salutations to that Vyāsa, the best among those who uphold the earth, who is worthy of praise like Himavat; by whom, the most patient of beings, this delightful Rāmāyaṇa was composed,
and by whom the expansive Bhārata was created, resembling Gaurī.
Whom does the speech of the Bhārata not delight, like a beloved woman whose eyes are the wandering Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna darting to the corners of her ears, and who,
with her bow as her constant companion, assumes a form that bends low?
Just as all people are delighted by a bow rich in its string,
so too have these learned men— their ears and hearts completely filled— been colored by the essences of these poets' poetic narratives and tales, like jars brimming with water.
Where indeed could words such as these find room for those like me whose intellects are bewildered by the distinction between what is said and its meaning? Or rather, the wise are all-enduring;
yet words attain hardness through the particularity of their punning and double meanings.
One should not feel agitation in that regard, because this [work] of the poet is not a single thing;
like a mango fruit, whether tender or otherwise, its flavor may appear different due to the particularity of its composition and style.

There exists a lineage of the great seer named Śāṇḍilya, whose lotus-feet are worthy of worship by the entire host of sages and gods, who has descended into the wheel of worldly existence due to the necessity of his all-pervading activity as the Lord of Ordainers (Brahmā), and who is preeminent in the performance of seasonal rites and sacrificial acts.

And there are heard certain learned Brahmins, pure, truthful in speech, possessing the splendor of Brahmā, whose conduct is worthy of worship, and who are knowers of the Veda—like sandalwood shoots, appropriate for hearing. Nor are there those people of Laṅkā who are "puṇyajanas" (meritorious beings) yet not "puṇyajanas" (thieves); who are "sasūtras" (versed in the Sūtras) yet not "lampaṭas" (lecherous); who are "prasiddhas" (renowned) yet not "lampākas" (people of Lampāka); who provide "kāmavarṣa" (rain of desires) yet are not "laṅghanas" (jumpers) from the path of virtue; who, though in the bloom of youth, are not "lambālakas" (with hanging curls); who are "mahābhāratikas" (versed in the Mahābhārata) yet not "raṅgopajīvins" (stage-players); and who, though they have served the Apsarases, are not "rambhānvitas" (accompanied by plantains).
What need is there for much? For only those of similar nature can speak of the virtues of such as they;
the Earth alone knows the weight of mountains that rests upon her own vastness.

In their lineage, born of Śrīdhara— who possessed pure fame— there was a son named Ēvāditya, whose discernment of the Vedic sciences blossomed through his own intellect; people everywhere [beheld] his ocean of nectar-like glory surging with waves in every direction.

I am born as his son, Trivikrama, a vessel of dullness, by whose various personal virtues he— who even now has his eyes closed as he drinks him in with the cups of his ears— has become the tilaka (the crowning ornament) of the three worlds.

Just as a foolish cripple might wish to act like a swan, so do I, of dull intellect, desire to act like a preeminent poet; yet by me, who attempts this difficult task of composing verses bound by puns and paronomasia, [this is being done].
The ocean began to be crossed by arms;
those with foul faces made their remarks with bloated cheeks,
yet only a true poet truly understands the labor of another poet.
Joined with a multitude of delightful sentiments, possessing the beautiful refuge of Mount Meru,
and like the garland of the Nandana grove, let this narrative— endowed with a noble hero and composed of virtuous episodes and verses— be beheld by those who are well-disposed.
By whom are the Campū and the Hārayaṣṭi not held in the heart?

There is a land named Āryāvarta, which serves as a flight of stairs for ascending to heaven by means of its rolling waves—the Gaṅgā, whose sacred waters flood it; whose banks are adorned by flocks of swans, cakoras, cakravākas, and kāraṇḍavas, turned tawny by the pollen rising from blossoming golden lotuses and blue water-lilies; who acts like a crest-jewel upon the matted locks of Paśupati (Śiva), yet is free from the loss of letters, the alteration of phonemes, or the elision of prefixes and particles found in those who have not studied grammar; who sports with the playful grace of a beautiful forehead-mark upon the expansive surface of the entire earth; who is equal to the celestial realm in being worthy of service; who is captivating to the mind even though devoid of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) found in the compositions of vulgar poets; who is like Bhīma, the ornament of the Bharata lineage; who is the foremost among all objects of sense, like the touch of a beloved’s rounded breasts; whose one region is adorned by the Candrabhāgā river; which is the essence of the entire wheel of worldly existence; the abode of those who performed great deeds in ancient times; a pleasure garden for the plantain grove of amorous dalliance; the home of Dharma; the seat of prosperity; the refuge of spiritual welfare; a mine of jewels in the form of virtuous conduct; and a temple of teachers for the instruction of noble boundaries of conduct.

In this [kingdom], where the instruction of incessant religious duties has pacified all disturbances caused by disease, the subjects live out their full human lifespan and enjoy every happiness of worldly existence. For instance: the application of *kuṣṭha* (leprosy) is seen only in the shops of perfumers; the mention of *sphoṭa* (boils) only among grammarians; *saṃnipāta* (fever/aggregation) only in palmistry; the transition of *graha* (planets/seizures) only in the science of astronomy; the discourse on *bhūta-vikāra* (possession by spirits/disturbances of the elements) only among the Sāṃkhyas; *kṣaya* (decline/waning) only in the lunar dates; *gulma-vṛddhi* (tumors/growth) only in forest lands; *galagraha* (throat-obstruction) only among fish; the appearance of *gaṇḍaka* (goiters/swelling) only in mountain forests; and the binding of *śūla-jham* (sharp pain/axle-pin) only in the temples of Caṇḍikā—not so among the subjects.

Wherein the villages were like battles, adorned by fourfold herds of cattle; the city districts were like mountains everywhere, with their lofty peaks and entire dwellings; the towns were like anklets, embellished by the practice of virtuous conduct; the people were like winds, ever enjoying the fragrance of gifts; the forests were like periods of youth, whose essence lay in pleasant conversation; the groves were like female attendants, concealed by trees; the sugar-cane fields and almshouses were like noble wives, being seats of tranquility; the portions of the tanks were immeasurable, characterized by water and mud like beasts and men; the wells were like the servants of the Lord of Laṅkā when agitated by angry troops of monkeys—having shattered Kumbhakarṇa’s deep slumber; the cows were like rivers, possessing thick banks; and the women of good family were like pairs of suns, free from the defect of excessive heat.

And there were rice fields where pairs of charming cranes stood like *tatpuruṣa* compounds, and which, appearing as if they were prose compositions of the *Kādambarī*, seemed to abound in *bahuvrīhi* formations.
What more need be said?
There is no city where there are neither ponds nor breasts.
And where no woman with swelling breasts is seen,
even the branches of the trees become leafless in the month of Phālguna.

No calamities ever arise in that world, where people—whose minds are delighted by excellent governance and who are intent on initiating a continuous succession of great festivals augmented by every prosperity—constantly mock the inhabitants of heaven. For there, the noble are never ignoble; those who have attained celestial chariots (*vimāna*) never suffer the ruin of their chariots; those who possess many treasures (*vasu*) are not merely adorned with a few; and thus these people hold the dwellers of paradise in derision. How, then, could this realm not surpass heaven?

In that land, in every house there were fair-complexioned women; the people were devoted to Maheśvara; the horses were capable and bay-colored; and at every step there were world-protectors who were dispensers of wealth. There was no king other than the Lord of the Gods (Indra), nor was there any Vināyaka.
Where the connection with movement and the onset of strife were seen only in the trees and not among men;
where talk of camaras and the destruction of extreme cold were heard only in the regions of the Snowy Mountains and not among the subjects.
And yet, though presided over by wise men, it was devoid of policy; though full of wells, it was crowded with pits; though endowed with artisans, it lacked the beauty of form.

In that place, the constellations and lunar mansions committed no transgression against their elders; the scribes did not quarrel over syllables; the owls showed no hostility toward the rising of their friends; the cuckoos did not abandon their offspring; and the summer days did not cause the destruction of the lives of their kinsmen—not so, however, did the people.
What more need be said?
To whom would this most holy region not be dear— a land whose very *yojanas* are filled with people endowed with compassion? In the midst of that realm lies a famous district named Niṣadha.
There, in Niṣadha, is a city worthy of the residence of Puruṣottama; that city,
which constantly brings joy to its noble lord who is ever delighted at heart,
shines as enchanting as Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain.

In that city, the horses of the sun’s chariot, faltering in their midday course as they long to swallow the tips of the young grass-blades nourished by the mass of rays supported by the thousands of cloud-scraping peaks of sapphire palaces, weary themselves in the sky.

And in that city, swarms of innocent bees fall upon the rows of red lac footprints left by the moving housewives upon the courtyards of mansions paved with crystal slabs, mistaking them for young, reddish lotuses floating within the pure water.

In that city, upon the beautiful and transparent walls of dwelling-houses constructed from various gems, beloved women, seeing their own reflections and suspecting them to be other women, were somehow brought back by their lovers. In that city, the roads were adorned with divine temples like heavens; the citizens, always clothed in water-laden garments, were like oceans; the houses, surrounded on all sides by elephants, were like forests; the wells, attended by celestial beings, were like the kings of heaven; and the monasteries, illuminating the region of the neck, were like magnificent pearl necklaces.

In that city, within, nectar-like mansions endowed with many auspicious marks are seen in abundance; and without, four oceans appear with beautifully adorned waves. Within, music halls are observed; and without, there are lotus ponds for the sport of swans. Hindered by much grain, they are reached with some difficulty; within, there are the quarters of noble women; and without, there are agricultural fields. Adorned with various parrots, there are pleasure groves within; and without, there are rows of mango orchards. With the spread of fragrant flowers, marketplaces shine within; and without, there are reservoirs of water. What more need be said?
There, the grounds—both outside and within—are adorned with various gardens that always bring delight to people of diverse ages;

therein, in the temples, deities are seen presiding over those who partake in devotion; in the marketplaces, merchants are seen; in the assemblies of poets, poets are observed intent on their verses; in the gambling dens, gamblers are found; at the palace gates, elephants fond of the passion for the forest roam; and in the courtyards of the courtesans, libertines frequent.

And in that city—which was the crest-jewel of the entire circle of the earth, adorned by the shores of the four oceans; which, through its lovely palaces fashioned with jewels, surpassed the city of the Lord of the Gods—there was imperishability in the indeclinables (*avyaya*), grammatical suffixes (*vyākaraṇa*), and prefixes (*upasarga*), but not in the wealth of the rich. There was the cessation of giving among the circles of temples of rutting elephants, but not among the houses of the generous. There was the breaking of enjoyment in serpents, but not among the people of pleasure. There was the exhaustion of oil in lamp-vessels extinguished at the end of night, but not in the hearts of those who had taken refuge [in the city]. There was the application of false notes in specific melodic strains (*tāna*) of song, but not in legal transactions. There was conflict over accentuation among the students of grammar, but not between master and servant. And there was a difference in position in paintings, but not among virtuous men.
What need is there for much?
In that city, the tips of the crests of the celestial abodes shine as if vying with the prosperity of the city of the gods, bound by the knots of the sacrificial offerings.
Moreover, the Vaijayantī banners, fluttering in the wind in the sky with their excellent foliage, display supreme majesty here.
And furthermore—
That city, Cārvī, which is always prepared for virtuous conduct and frequented by those who delight in bathing,
is not devoid of great prosperity.

In that city lived King Nala, the son of Śrī Vīrasena; he was a royal swan floating upon the vast flood of tears flowing from the blue-lotus eyes of the wives of all his enemies, who had been crushed by the strength of his own two arms. He adorned the world with pillars of fame planted in the forests on the shores of every ocean. Like the expanse of the earth, he was capable of bearing much; like a palace, he possessed a fresh coating of plaster; like the sun, he was the refuge of manifold splendors. To women, he was ever-generous like the world of the Danavas; like Vasiṣṭha, he struck terror into Viśvāmitra; like Janamejaya, he was the son of Parīkṣit; like Paraśurāma, he was radiant with his axe; like Rāghava, he delighted his father with his great belly and unbreakable nature; like Sumeru, he possessed an abundance of gold; like the snowy mountain, he was accompanied by the holy Bhāgīrathī. He was a wish-fulfilling gem to his supplicants, the leader of warriors in battle, a preceptor to those learned in study, a mirror for all sciences, the conduct of the courageous, an instructor of weaponry and scripture, a mighty champion among those who strike deep blows, the foremost among the meritorious, the last of the wise, the final of the generous, the ultimate of masters of cleverness. With the Goddess of Victory appearing as a statue fixed to the pillar-like shafts of his arms, which served as a support for the weight of the boundless earth, he was the king whose beautiful banner of fame became the pinnacle of the temple of the entire world—a king who was a chain for restraining the fickleness of the female elephant of royal fortune, and a forest fire to the sprouts of the multitude of the wicked, named Nala.

His virtues, possessing the luster of the moon, jasmine, and the white water-lily, were a welcome guest to the ears of all the world; yet, distressed by the misery of dwelling confined within the single shell of this one universe, they seemed to petition the lotus-born Lord Viśvasṛj for the construction of many millions of other universes, and thus they continued to inhabit the heavenly realm, ever clinging to his ears.

And during the reign of that king who brought joy to the people and gladdened the earth, there were mixtures of castes in songs, disruptions of various rhythms in musical time, the employment of discordant gestures in dances, blows with sticks and hands in instrumental music, obstructions in the commencement of meritorious works, the use of snares in board-games, the cutting off of hands from flowering *ketakī* trees, the lopping of feet from banyan trees, and the gouging out of eyes for the decoration of bodices; yet these things existed among the instruments of music and not among the subjects.

And he was a protector of the world unlike any other; for instance: he was an unprecedented lord of the gods, a king of righteousness who imposed no fines, a Pracetas who was not inferior, and a giver of wealth who was unsurpassed.

By him—the circle of whose fierce staff-like arms rested upon the Goddess of Victory, whose eyes plundered the pride of women whose faces resembled the petals of blue lotuses on their ears, and who could assume any form at will—both the Earth and his beloved were enjoyed.

She whose forehead-mound captivates the minds of all people, whose locks of hair possess a loveliness that inspires the desire to sing of them, whose nasal region is praiseworthy, whose central region (the waist) is richly endowed with sight and adorned with a row of body-hairs, and whose region of the hips displays the playful charms of the pinnacle of love—
what more need be said?

Adorned by the expansive fullness of her breasts, which are heavily perfumed with the fragrance of black aloe and sandalwood, the incomparable and fresh glory of her youth dances, as it were, within her limbs through its exquisite loveliness.
Furthermore:

He is yet another new incarnation, a certain Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) who is not defiled by the form of a fish; nor did he assume the body of a tortoise while bearing the weight of the entire universe; nor did he support the earth with labor in the form of a boar; nor was he a man-lion who destroyed Hiraṇyakaśipu; nor did he act with meanness as Vāmana during the binding of King Bali; nor did he carry away the splendor of the Lord of Laṅkā as Rāma; nor was he Buddha, nor an incarnation of the Kalki lineage.
What more need be said?
Blessed are those days in which Nala— the crest-jewel of kings, whose fame rested upon the earth bounded by the Lokāloka mountain— came into being;
and blessed likewise are those ancient people who flourished while he ruled.

And furthermore: those whose beauty was tasted by the world with eyes wide open like unfolding petals— those who possess the luster of kunda flowers and have been made into ear-ornaments by all the worlds.
He by whom the walls of every direction have been painted as if with inscribed chalk-marks,
and by whose virtues even our hearts are so adorned that we stand with hair bristling in joy—
he is that preeminent king, a singular treasury of great qualities.

And he whose manner of speech was never useless, like that of Yudhiṣṭhira; whose mind was sinless, like the region of Maru; whose actions were essential, like a kitchen for a master cook; whose generosity possessed millions of virtues, like a bow; whose sovereignty had witnessed the festival of Vṛṣaparvan, like the lineage of Dānava; and whose heart was always free from agitation, like a lotus free from bees.
He who, though delighting in supreme dalliance, was not an adulterer; who, though possessing sons, was not joined with ugliness.
What more need be said?
Even the Himālaya, the lord of mountains, does not attain equality with that [lake] whose waters are ever agitated by swans and whose mind is as restless as its own flowing water.
Moreover—
Born into a royal lineage, he is indeed a partaker of celestial enjoyments;
for even the golden mountain, though possessed of noble form, cannot attain equality with him in any respect.

And that great monarch had a minister named Śrutaśīla, the son of Sālaṅkāyana, who was a pillar of praise for the rows of letters of all the scriptures and treatises; a banyan tree for the sprouts of meritorious deeds; a mine of the jewels of virtuous conduct; a moon for the moonlight of royal policy; a bulbous root for the entire cluster of sprouts of the arts; an ocean for the gems of all human virtues; a tethering post for the dust of the fickle goddess of sovereignty; a helmsman for the ship navigating the vast sea of worldly affairs; one who adorned the lake of the entire world with the lotus-clusters of his fame, white as the froth of the ocean of nectar; one who made all the dependents of other kings feel affection; one who was like his own life, like his vital breath, like his heart, and like a second self from whom only the physical body differed; one who had come down through the lineage of his family; a mirror reflecting both joy and sorrow; naturally devoted, pure, speaking words sanctified by truth, grateful, and a Brahmin.

That brahmin became the king’s friend, counselor, well-wisher, and beloved companion, equal to him in learning, age, and character; he was his assistant, capable of bearing the burden of the entire earth.
Moreover—
Even one devoted to Brahman who steals the wealth of Brahmins, or one joined with women who is mostly separated from them,
or one wearing the garb of a sage whose mind is free from hatred— who has ever seen or heard of such a person?

Then that king, having entrusted the burden of his extensive royal affairs to that minister—who was surrounded by a retinue of attendants, possessed of mature wisdom, a keeper of secret counsel, who treated the pleasures of the female sex as mere straw, who inspired affection for good governance, and who was regarded by the people as a father—was one whose intellect had been purified by all tests of integrity. Remaining in a state of life that was delightful due to the onset of fresh youth, pleasing to the eyes and hearts of beautiful women, possessing the hue of the *priyaṅgu* flower, surpassing the laughter of Madana, eclipsing the beauty and fame of gods and demons, astonishing the minds of all people, a mass of shimmering loveliness that surpassed the waters of all oceans, and a moon gazed upon with longing by its own splendor; he, the very essence of the youth of women, personally and incessantly experienced the full harvest of all worldly pleasures.
For instance— at times, like Garuḍa when poison has not yet arisen, he, though intent on harming his enemies, displayed the playful majesty of Indra;
and at other times, like the Moon-crested Lord [Śiva], he roamed upon mountain slopes shrouded by the *atimuktaka* flowers that serve as the bow for the arrows of Love.
Sometimes, like Acyuta, his body bristling with horripilation from plunging into a cool lotus-pond, he enjoyed the bliss of the state of infinite serpenthood.
Sometimes, like Nīlīnayoni, seated in the assembly of kings, he contemplated the affairs of his subjects.
And sometimes, like a peacock, he experienced joy at the sight of the playful grace of the circle of lovely, swelling breasts.

Sometimes, accompanied by an army like the constellation Aśvinī, he roamed through many forest paths in pursuit of deer. Sometimes, like the son of Añjanā (Hanumān), he engaged in the diversion of dice. And sometimes, like Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, he commanded the foremost of the vanaras, saying, "O Vānaras, let the request of the supplicant Kākutstha—who is as light-footed as a bird—be made fruitful," while uttering the name "Vaidēhī."
At times, like the god of love, he made his own virtues the ear-ornaments for the flowers that served as his arrows.

At other times, like the ocean, he enjoyed the courtesans of the shore—women delightful with high breasts and navels, whose eyes possessed the playful charm of a sidelong glance and who were full of passion.
At other times, like Daśaratha stationed in the city of Ayodhyā, accompanied by Sumitrā, he experienced a moment of joy in beholding Rāma and Bharata as they played.

In this manner, his days passed as he experienced the continuous succession of pleasures for the entire world of living beings. Then, on one occasion, there appeared women who were resplendent with streams of water falling between their rising breasts; whose eyes were as lovely as lotus petals; whose brows were curved like the bow of the gods; who wore girdles of lightning-stones as ornaments; who had released peacocks upon their crests; and who moved with the grace of full-grown female elephants.

The rainy seasons descended as if to behold this king— who was praised for his virtues by the entire world, who shone with a mass of incomparable beauty and charm, and whose five-faced countenance surpassed the collection of the moon’s lovely rays— with their thundering clouds for necks and their rain-showers for eyes.
And therein—
[the sound of] the clouds, like the drum of the sovereignty of the god of love, [arose].
As the peacock of the dancing Kikidivika family performed its sweet mṛdaṅga-like beat,
the earth, bristling with joy as if covered in horripilation under the guise of the opening petals of blue kandala flowers, raised up mushrooms like banners.
Moreover—
listening with their leaf-ears, which act as ear-cups and are expanded by the abundance of fresh nectar, to the sweet thundering of the mass of clouds merging with the orb of the sun;
The mango trees bear a cascade of flower-buds as if out of joy, their banners of swarming bees wandering about the weight of fragrance emanating from the tips of their branches;
then, in due course—
The water was free from lotuses, the surface of the earth was dustless,
and even the forest became filled with bees drawn by the fragrance of the blossoms of various species of creepers.
And furthermore—
The winds blew, slow-moving due to the fresh pollen falling from the clusters of shaken *kadamba* trees, stealing away the frost from the hearts of those who love the joy of passion.

Then, when the splendor of the sun had been eclipsed; when the spray of water was falling from the clouds; when the heat of the wind had subsided; when the elephant-like body of the summer season had entered *nirvāṇa*; when the knot of the pride-grasp of the arrogant had been stolen away; when the parching of the *javāsaka* grass had been produced; when there was enmity toward widowed wives; when the frogs’ joy had increased; when the moon was sealed away; when the lotus-lakes were withered; when the beloveds were under one’s own control; when the age of the wandering *kalahaṃsa* geese had passed; when the luster of the circle of stars had vanished; when the sky was turned dark-blue; when the pollen of the *nīpa* flowers was falling; when the eight quarters of the horizon were turned tawny by the pollen of blossoming *phuṭaja* trees; when it bore the brilliant circle of the rainbow of the gods; when it acted as the rut-fluid for peacocks; when it brought about the emaciation of buffaloes; when the rivers were spreading out; when lightning was flashing; when the wind was carrying slow-moving clouds; when the women of the fields were rejoicing; when the bees were intoxicated by drinking the scent of blooming *ketakī* flowers; when the trees were putting forth new growth; when the sleep of the poor was being stolen away; when cows were being milked with pride; when honeybees were clinging to clusters of *kadamba* trees; when the thundering of clouds, resembling the loud laughter of Madana, was bringing joy; when the beauty of the forest interiors was darkened by ripening *jambū* fruits; when the company of travelers was rendered pure; when the sweet cries of peacocks intoxicated with rut were being heard; when the *kośātakī* vines were blossoming; when *yūthikā* clusters were appearing; when garlands of *navamālikā* were being worn; when *kandala* shoots were emerging; when the rows of *jambū* groves were shining as they ripened; when mendicants were exhausted at the moment of begging; when the affliction of the deer had ceased; when young birds were busy building nests; when thick Indra-cows (rain-clouds) were joined together; when it resembled a house with dripping streams of water; when the ten directions were turning dark; when even by day the cries of flocks of *cakravāka* birds, agitated by the suspicion that it was night, were being heard; when the movement of carts was obstructed; when the splendor of the sun was obscured; when the battle between Arjuna and Duryodhana had come to rest; when the hunger of oxen was diminished; when the arms of Bāṇa, who was sleeping in the Ocean of Milk, were severed; when the currents of the Indus were broken; when forest fires were extinguished; when the hearts of those separated from their lovers were tormented; when the joy of the people was produced; when the shade of the *tāpiccha* trees was unceasing; when horses were being tethered within hidden huts; when groves of *bakula* trees were shining in full bloom; when the boundaries of the villages were furrowed by ploughs; when the God of Love was triumphant; when the life-giver of the world had arrived—the season of clouds—at some time during the day, while it was raining, a forest-guardian of the hunting grounds entered and addressed the King.
"O Lord,
could this be a pair of long, water-laden clouds clinging to the Vindhya mountain, or rather a pair of cranes embracing a couple of crystal pillars?"
"Is this an empty elephant?"— thus creating such a delusion—
a boar with a terrifying face like that of Death, possessing a pair of tusks, arrived from somewhere;
and then he—
Breaking through the moist regions of the earth filled with tubers of the *kasēruka* plant,

shattering mountain peaks resembling the *añjana* mountain, and gently churning the pleasure-lakes— which resemble the ocean— with the playful grace of Mount Mandara, he [the elephant] destroys the bowers of blossoming creepers.
"In the grove of Bhava’s lap, a boar plays as if terrifying the guards.
Upon hearing this, the king thought:
"The edges of the forest are covered with grass as clear and green as clusters of parrot feathers."
Now, those [forests] adorned with swarms of dancing peacocks thick as the moon’s rays are to be visited, wherein the winds blow gently, slightly tossing the waves of the pond water white as milk,
and slowly rolling over the trunks of the ketaka groves in full bloom.
"And now the stallions are rearing up in them; therefore, it is fitting to go out for sport. Having thus resolved, he summoned his commander-in-chief named Bāhuka and commanded him:

"Good sir, let this be carried out quickly! Let the foot-soldiers who have long harbored enmity toward their foes be marshalled; let the horses whose minds are as swift as thought be made to circle about; let the dogs, who surpass the wind in speed, be readied; let the bows, which have stripped away the lives of enemies, be mounted; and let the nooses, by which the leaders of the herds of rearing stallions were once crushed, be taken up."
Then, with his pair of lotus-hands folded like buds touching his crest, the commander-in-chief said, "As the King commands," and having done so with haste,
he himself also—
[prepared], with a fleshless face, narrow in the middle, and small at the ears.
A king should mount a horse that is well-proportioned on its shoulders, immeasurable in girth, smooth in the hair of its chest,
thick at the rear flanks, broad-backed, preeminent in speed,
and endowed with all auspicious qualities.

Having ascended [the mountain] in due order, he was followed by countless hunters—men whose hair was bound with rags from Kārdamika, who carried fragments of sticks in their hands, and who possessed the appearance suited for cruel deeds; they were like the messengers of Yama, bearing nooses in their hands and carrying nets. His joyful neighing was heard from afar by the forest creatures, who raised their necks and pricked up their ears as if their lives had suddenly taken flight. Even from a distance, the forest deities seemed to ward him off out of fear, raising their hands under the guise of the tips of tree branches trembling in the wind, and using the clamor of flocks of birds taking flight as a pretext. He was as if obstructed by the forest breezes, which, opening up clusters of blossoms and carrying showers of nectar-drops, approached him as if offering an *arghya* out of apprehension for the destruction of the woods. He was as if being forbidden by the forest creepers, whose dense masses of filaments and sprouts were fully blossomed, appearing as if their hair stood on end in terror, and who seemed to protest with the faltering cries of wandering bees. Delighted by the sight of the emerging, radiant, and abundant shoots of the *kandala* plant, and though followed by horses, he reached that forest situated in the midst of elephants, accompanied by his elephant.

Then, some leaders of the Gaṇas with upraised axes, some moon-faced ones who had witnessed the prowess of Siṃhikā’s son, some jackal-like guardians of the quarters with nooses in hand, some Valabhadras following the path of Hari, some discus-bearing Madhusūdanās, some fierce followers of the Śiva-āgamas, some world-renowned sacrificers who maintain the sacred fires, some Prabhāsanās whose coral-like lips were stained by crushed collyrium, and some sword-wielding Nistriṃśas who had uprooted the tusks of elephants with their fists—the foot soldiers of that lord of the earth, having thrown the beasts of prey into confusion, hemmed in the forest.

And then, by them, the forest groves and elephants were left mutilated; swords and rhinoceroses were slain in many ways; bow-staves and gaṇḍaka deer were drawn with cries; arrows and śarabha beasts were scattered in every direction; and trees and taṁrakṣa animals were broken.

In an instant, fat boars fell down; elephants sank; startled deer bleated discordantly; rohit deer climbed the rocky mountain out of fear; buffaloes, reeling from the impact of the arrow-shower, hit the earth; tigers with darting eyes took refuge in difficult terrain; and deer, their speed surpassing that of horses, leaped into the sky as if crossing it with extreme haste.
And in that tumult, the gods, filled with sudden wonder, cried out, "What is this? while listening.
A certain tumultuous roar of the hunt arose, which caused the elephants of the quarters to trumpet in terror as their ears flapped, and which, inciting fever in all living beings,
made the belly of the vessel of the universe seem as if it were bursting, filled to the brim.

The king, too, having felled a rutting elephant with a single arrow, was roaming here and there with the effortless ease of slaying lions, deer, rabbits, śambara antelopes, and boars on all sides; he beheld that heroic boar in a certain muddy and impassable region thick with dense clusters of bhadramustā grass—its body facing him, its mane dark as a thicket of very young tamāla blossoms, its ears pricked up and its snout quivering, emitting a continuous, deep, and terrible gurgling roar, its bushy tail tossed aloft, like another mountain scorched by a forest fire.

And having observed his lightness in aiming and discharging arrows, he rained down upon that lord of the Rākṣasas feathered shafts furnished with various kinds of fletching, like Rāghava [Rāma] against the lord of the Rākṣasas.
And in that encounter— was it a horse, clever in leaping about its flanks, or was it perhaps a king?
Is it the restless boar that, with its highly agitated trunk drawing the bow, discharges arrows?
Or is it the one who, being a connoisseur of valor, has warded off the arrows? We do not know which among them is the supreme one to be honored here.
Moreover—
the duel between those two caused the birth of a tremor throughout the circle of the earth and made the mountains shake in some inexplicable way.
In whom even the Lord of Day became a spectator of the wonder of his valor, as he surpassed the speed of a stumbling horse; then,
having somehow conquered the leader of the Prōthi herd, he—
Like one afflicted by fever, the majestic king, weary and with his cheeks moistened by drops of perspiration, sought comfort at the foot of a *sāla* tree,
his playful locks dangling about him.

And there, swaying the flowering trees, causing the circles of peacock crests to quiver, making the clusters of sprouts upon their creeper-like bodies dance, bearing showers of cool spray from the overflowing waters, and opening the buds of the *kuṭaja* flowers, the winds—releasing drops of nectar and shaking the *nīpa* groves—gently gladdened him as he sat there with his lotus-eyes closed in fatigue.

Immediately thereafter, while the attendants ran about in every direction, distracted by the devouring of herds of fierce jackals, boars, deer, lions, and young elephants; while the sun, its rays like a garland of light, stood in the midst of the sky with arms outstretched at intervals as if to restrain the hunters who had brought upon themselves the malady of slaughtering various female deer; while from the eyes of the forest creepers—those beautiful flowers—tears seemed to fall in the form of drops of nectar melted by the midday heat, as if out of a heavy burden of grief for the destruction of the deer; while the warbling of various birds flying up from the groves was heard like the reproaches of the forest deities for the devastation of the woods; while the rows of forest trees seemed to cry out in protest against the injustice under the guise of the piteous cries of the doe whose fawn had been struck down; while a cloud of dust, grey as the feathers of a domestic pigeon, rose up from the surface of the earth dug up by the tips of the hooves of the fleetest horses moving here and there, as if to report the news of the slaughter to the denizens of the sky, and fell again and again upon the ground as if fainting because no protection had been afforded; while the circle of restless bees, agitated by the clusters of fresh *makharī* flowers shaken by the flapping tails of trembling monkeys, hummed sweetly as they moved through the interior of the forest; and when the army had grown weary from its progress and the king, having relieved his fatigue, sat down beneath that very same tree of lush and straight *śāla* wood— [The passage continues with the description of the king’s state and the arrival of the sage.]
Suddenly, from somewhere— his head grey with a garment of bark, carrying a staff upon his shoulder,
a water-pot hanging from his neck, clad in a tattered loincloth, and emaciated.
A certain weary traveler, having bound a tattered rag around his feet and carrying a begging bowl fashioned from betel-nut husks,
arrived; and upon seeing the king, he reflected with astonishment:

His pair of arms is auspicious and endowed with beauty; his head bears a great uṣṇīṣa; his face possesses the splendor of the full moon together with its companion, the ūrṇā-hair; a lotus rests upon the palm of his hand, and on his throat there is a triple line resembling a conch shell.
"His brilliance is likewise like that of the ocean; he is some extraordinary lord of the earth.

Indeed, such are those who are truly venerable and possessed of great majesty. Having thus reflected, she approached him and said, "May there be well-being unto you, who have surpassed the god of love with your own splendor."

The king, his mind filled with wonder and his head slightly bowed, greeted him with a welcome and said: "O pilgrim, from where have you come? Where and how much further must you still travel? Pray, sit down; having rested, tell us some unprecedented news. For those who have traveled through many lands are surely observers of wonders. Nor should even a single doubt be entertained—that this sudden appearance is a lack of acquaintance or that our affection is slight. Even when meeting for the first time, jewels do not abandon their natural brilliance. Therefore, come; let us both enjoy the pleasure of conversation together for a moment. Thus he spoke to him.
He too, saying, "O connoisseur of the taste of hearing unprecedented and wondrous tales, listen if you so desire," sat down beside him who was already comfortably seated and began to speak:
"There exists a region equal to heaven, the foremost among all lands in the world to be venerated, an ornament of the southern quarter, a mine of jewels for both men and women."

In which [place] the regions are never empty of fortunate people who are devoted to the great festival of generosity, and which are filled with a weight of desirable qualities— who would they not make eager, and how could they not be praised?

There, the Blessed One, the wielder of the trident, dwells as a servant upon Śrīśaila—a mountain whose splendor puts Kailāsa to shame, where the multitude of light from the moon-like rays of his toenails is kissed by the cakora-birds that are the circles of radiance from the crest-jewels of Hari and Viriñci, and which steals the beauty of the tilaka-mark on the forehead of the consort of Tripura’s destroyer.

And there, the lands along the banks of the Kāverī possess the loveliness of the celestial realm; their surroundings are graced by pairs of Vidarbha lovers, languid with sleep and exhausted from the pleasures of love, being fanned by the breeze scented by various blossoming forest groves and stirred by the waving leaves of plantain trees used as fans. These regions, rich in the essence of ripening rice fields, enchanting with flocks of cakoras, cakravākas, and kapiñjala birds, and delightful with peacocks amidst the dense, swaying nicula thickets, are filled with lush mango groves.
What more need be said?
May all be well with the glorious Southern Quarter, the repository of all jewels!

For the sake of prosperity that rivals heaven, for the banks of the rivers of the heart, where women— the weapons of Kamadeva— become the abode of happiness and the very ground for the play of amorous enjoyment, they are like young fawns trembling with fear.

There, for the sake of beholding the divine Lord Skanda—who dwells upon Mount Gandhamādana, whose two lotus-feet are made to blossom by the thick saffron paste of the mass of crimson rays from the heads of gods and asuras bowing down before him, and who is the destroyer of Krauñca—I have come from here.
And while returning from that place, having rested at the foot of a certain banyan tree that obstructs the path because I was exhausted by the long journey, listen to the wonder that I beheld.

Mounted upon the shoulders of noble female elephants whose gait was characterized by graceful, playful steps; accompanied primarily by mature female companions; with the sprouts of her hands dancing to the breeze from beautiful fly-whisks falling at her sides; wearing ornaments of blue lotuses upon her ears; adorned with shimmering anklets on her lovely feet; fixing her attention on the rhythmic swaying produced by the sweet songs emerging from the throats of musicians with passionate melodies moving before her; slightly rolling her eyes; and possessing a parasol-circle like the plumage of the peacock of Fortune—this princess, whose eyebrows were as curved as the bow of the god of love, set out from somewhere or other and sought refuge in that very bower of shade beneath the banyan tree.
Beholding her, I reflected with a mind full of wonder:
"Is it the Goddess Lakṣmī herself who has come here from the chest of the Lord Murāri,
or has the Goddess Bhavānī manifested on earth as an incarnation out of anger toward her husband?"
O Father, Creator! What do you not do for me as I gaze upon her, whose pure and moving eyes are like dark blue lotuses? Even so, grant me a thousand eyes in my face.
Her face captures the beauty of the moon; her lotus-rivalling eye-lashes rival the waves of the Yamunā with their graceful undulations;
what else of hers remains to be praised, for she is a treasure-house of auspicious virtues whose very beginning is poetry itself?
Victorious is the beauty of youth, the banner of the flower-arrowed god, which intoxicates young men.
Moreover:
that captivating form, that majesty, that birth, and that age.
That loveliness, that fortune of good luck which causes the world to marvel— that alone is capable of describing each of her particular qualities,
were one to possess two thousand tongues like those of the Lord of Serpents.

Just as you now question me here, she too began to rest there for a moment, earnestly questioning some northern traveler who had met her halfway and was setting out toward the southern direction. I too heard from him the remnants of a conversation concerning the praiseworthy deeds of a certain northern king.
[I beheld] that youth with a smiling face, whose two arms were as long as sacrificial posts.
Blessed were those whose eyes fell under the sway of Kandarpa;
what more need be said?
You are that very Manmathamañjarī, and he is that youth, the bee who is truly your fit mate.
What else could be more praiseworthy for you two than this? Nevertheless, we hope that through the union of these two human jewels— each possessing both fortune and capability—
the labor of the Creator’s craftsmanship in his diverse designs may become truly successful.
I do not know who that fortunate man was by whom she—her garment already bristling with the sprouts of thick horripilation at the mere mention of him—was thus described in such detail before her.

And I, too, having forgotten my discernment through astonishment, did not persist in asking questions such as: "Who is she? Whose is she? Where has she come from? Or where is she going? Rather, with all other activities extinguished by an excess of sudden curiosity born from seeing a form never seen before, I remained there with one-pointed attention—like one whose vision was blocked by an eclipse, like one who is blind, mute, unconscious, reeling from poison, or paralyzed by a spell—even after she had departed, I sat for a long time right there at the foot of that banyan tree with that traveler.
O long-lived one, this is the account of my own experience that I have related.

"In that direction, by her who is the moonlight for the entire world, and in this place, by you—who are the moon to the night-lotuses of the eyes of all people—having been seen, everything worth seeing has been seen by me. My birth has become praiseworthy; my two eyes have achieved their purpose; and the effort of my wandering has become fruitful.
Therefore, what else remains now?
Grant me permission to go to my own realm," he said, and then fell silent.
Having heard this, the king also reflected:

"That realm, a great mine of the jewel of women, is like a traveler; its speech is true and inexhaustible, and its activity is as wondrously fashioned as that of Fate—so why should such a thing not be possible?"

But what wonder is there? When her beauty and majesty are unseen and unheard of, even the mind of one whose heart is exalted by her name alone becomes humbled; for instance: * *kiṃ tv āścaryaṃ adṛṣṭarūpavibhavā vyākaraṇyāmānā satī |* * *kāntety unnatacetaso ’pi kurute nāmnaiva nimnaṃ manaḥ ||* * *tathā hi—* What wonder is there that, when her form and splendor are unseen and her fame is being proclaimed, the very name "Beloved" causes even the mind of one with a lofty spirit to sink low? For it is so.
I have not repeatedly drunk the nectar of her true form with the cupped hands of my eyes, nor have I even made the sprout of her name and lineage an ornament for my ears; yet,
it is a marvel that this one made of magnetic iron forcibly kisses her from afar, just as a magnet attracts iron.
In the same way, although my fortitude has been challenged, this mind of mine runs toward her.

This passion of men for things difficult to obtain is a fever without illness, a state of ill-health without poverty, a reeling without tasting poison, a trembling without fear, a state of dependence without selling oneself, a dullness that does not age, a flaming without fuel, a madness that seizes without contact, a tossing about without the blow of a whirlwind, a muteness without silence, a deafness without loss of hearing, a blindness without loss of sight, a paralysis of the mind whose desires do not falter, and a possession without incantations.

"In every way, salutations to the god of love, who is difficult for both the well-established and the wicked to withstand, and whose activity is of such a nature!"—reflecting thus, he removed the ornaments from all his limbs and gave them to him with compassion.
After staying for some time engaged in various conversations, he then, with great difficulty, sent that traveler away on his journey as he had set out.

The king himself, followed by his hunting attendants who carried equipment including the *śravaṇa*, *citra*, and *kṛttikā* [weapons], and who resembled the *mṛgaśiras*, *hasta*, *śravaṇa*, *citra*, and *kṛttikā* constellations joined together at that time, returned to his own residence.
And from that time forth—
in the waters of the river rippled by the breeze from the charming garden, beneath the trees—

Upon the stone slab, which is covered with fresh lotus petals as numerous as those of a water-lily, the fire of passion— though its power is checked by the corner of the thatched hut of his mind— is perceived to have forcibly attached itself to the heart of even this steadfast man, whose soul is weary,
as evidenced by his limbs being rendered involuntary.
Thus,
as he continues to question travelers on the road about that place,
the monsoon days pass by for him in succession— days that serve as the dwelling of Love’s enemy, while his head bears the imprint of the mark of the two lotus-feet of Hara.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Mark of the Lotus-Foot of Hara," in the *Damayantī-kathā* composed by the illustrious Trivikramabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the second chapter.

Then, at one time, when the rains had almost passed—when the forests were rendered empty of their *kuṭaja* and *kadamba* flower-ear-ornaments by swarms of bees drawn to their falling, thick fragrance; when the cries of peacocks, noisy with rut, were finding rest; when the beauty of the slender lightning-streaks had faded; when the rows of swans (the twice-born) had departed; when the clouds were falling, the semen was spent, and they were like aged women whose youth was gone; when autumn had arrived like a longing young woman, captivating with the laughter of swans sweet with passion, yet no longer offering sexual pleasure; when herds of lions, their throats formidable with manes bristling in rage, were roaring amidst the shadows of blossoming *saptacchada* trees chased by the scent of elephant ichor; when flocks of swans were crying out, charming as they ceased their snapping at the stalks of lotus-fibers in the palace ponds, sounding like auspicious drums for the entry of the autumn season; when clusters of beautiful *bandhūka* flowers bloomed upon the forest grounds like a mass of blood-drops dripping from the wounds inflicted on caravans of travelers by the multitude of Cupid’s arrows; when groups of parrots, free from fear, were spreading like garlands of greeting for the joy of the autumn goddess’s arrival; when the songs of joy from village girls tending the fields of ripened *kalama* rice were sounding like proclamations of victory in the kingdom of the God of Love; when blue lotuses opened like side-glances from the Beauty of Autumn; and when the circles of bees hummed like the war-drums for the departure of the bride of the rainy season; when the lake, adorned with dense rows of blooming lotuses, appeared like the dawn delightful in its cessation of thick darkness, and became the enemy of the sleep of Viṣṇu as he lay upon his ocean-bed—the king heard these three verses, free from vulgarity, being sung by a pair of *kiṃnaras* sporting nearby in the forest.
Blessed are the citizens accompanied by their wives who, in autumn, enjoy the palaces with their shimmering, variegated rice-fields;
and blessed are the farmers who enjoy the rice-stalks, bowed down by the weight of their fruit and beyond measure.
Indeed, seeing the fields in bloom and their wives free from desire,
and beholding the monsoon and autumn seasons which so beautifully fill the sky, what man would not be filled with longing for the company of a woman free from passion?

With these three verses—whose syllables were made to dance by gentle modulations, which were the first dear guests upon the path of his hearing, and which served as an axe hard for the ascetic’s staff of enmity toward the poison-like objects of the senses—he, though averse to the taking of a wife, began to frequent that very garden, which was delightful with the sweet humming of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of the abundant nectar of *mandāra* flowers, while being raised to the lofty peak of the horned god of love (*Śṛṅgāra*).

With his body bristling with thrill as he was being addressed by a forest breeze—first wafting directly toward him, fragrant with swaying sandalwood, causing the blossoming treetops to tremble so that the Kinnarīs, exhausted from the fatigue of lovemaking, were startled and closely embraced by their Kinnara lovers; charming with the outpouring of the sweet nectar of fresh lotuses dancing upon the bosom of the ripples in the pleasure-lotus pond; and possessing the playful grace of the swaying creepers of Nala’s wife, who was captivated by the youth of the King of Niṣadha—he traversed a short distance and observed the various sites for forest recreation pointed out by a forest-keeper skilled in puns and double entendres: “O Lord, in the forest of your enemies’ wives, the *nāraṅga* trees (oranges) possess the beauty of the *nāraṅga* fruit (or the face); the *lobhra* creepers (or pride) serve as ornaments for the *gaṇḍaśaila* (boulders or cheeks); the *candana* leaves (or sandalwood paste) are fashioned into decorative patterns (*patrabhaṅga*); the *nālikera* (coconut) serves as the *tilaka* mark; the dark *añjana* (collyrium or mascara) has not yet entered the path of their vision; the *tamāla* trees (or hair) are exceedingly dark; the redness of the *tāmbūlī* (betel vine or lips) has not been rendered unsteady; and this cluster of *aśoka* trees (or grief) is seen to have put forth new sprouts. And here is a pleasure-mountain well-constructed like Mount Meru. And here is a grove of young *śāla* trees with uncut shoots, like the beard of a Gujarati. And here is a cluster of wells crowded with many kinds of *vakula* trees, like the city of your enemy filled with various *vakula* (cowards). And here is the vicinity of a pond surrounded by *puṃnāga* trees, like the matted locks of Śiva encircled by male attendants (*puṃnāga*). And here is the bank of a pleasure-river where the *aśvattha* trees (or Aśvatthāman) are honored, like the army of the Kurus which paid homage to Aśvatthāman. Thus he beheld the sites for forest diversion as they were described by the keeper.

Having traversed a short distance along this forest path—rough with the petals of *campaka* and *ākuṃara* blossoms crushed by the feet of bees, which were as restless as the beaks of flocks of *cakravāka* birds—he spoke to her once more:
"O Queen, what can be said of this forest that rivals the Nandana garden which delights Indra?

Here, the trees mock the Lord of Laṅkā: they possess many matted locks (*jaṭā*) in the form of their many roots (*jaṭā*), they bear many flowers (*puṣpa*) through the shimmering of their *ekapuṣpa* blossoms, and while causing distress to Rāma, they bring joy to the women (*rāmā*)."

And in this [composition], which is as charming as a rutting peacock and proceeds with the *bhadra-bhujaṅga-prayāta* meter, various meters (*jāti*) such as *vaitālīya*, *mālinī*, *śikhariṇī*, and *puṣpitāgrā* are seen, like those in a treatise on prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*), featuring diverse *krauñca-pada* verses.

Furthermore, in this [work], there are those who have been conquered and overwhelmed by a single Bhīma-Arjuna; those who have provoked a single Nakuḷa and have been tormented by that Nakuḷa; and those who, competing with a single Sahadeva, have encountered many Sahadevas. These Kuru heroes do not hold even the creepers in high regard.
Moreover, let Your Majesty observe this further:

Behold the peacock, dark as a rising cloud, who dances with intense soft and sweet cries above the flowering trees; he, absorbed in his dance, slowly and gently wags his plumage, which is adorned with rows of eye-like spots like a swarm of bees.
Moreover—
And here, having joined blossoming flowers— whose humming bees are like twanging bowstrings—
to his arrows, the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma) remains stationed to conquer the entire world, exerting himself with his bow.

O Hari, even here, the herd of deer belonging to the lioness does not pluck the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass; though they are situated amidst a thicket of jasmine vines dripping with a profusion of honey-drops from flowers, they remain as if painted in a picture, their attention fixed on the sweet songs of the female bees.
O fortunate one, this is that very pleasure-mountain, free from the vice of greed, upon which the kinnarī, accompanied by deer, sings of the essence; it shines with its silver peak,
the leader of all peaks.
Upon hearing a *kiṃnara* singing therein, who would not find delight? And from this [place],
the playful deer produce the perception of water.
Here, this wall surface of polished crystal possesses a brilliant luster; here, the shimmering rays of emeralds produce a longing for the charm of fresh, succulent blades of grass.
And this:
the mountain of one who possesses mountains performs no service for the mountainless; the bee of one who possesses bees performs no service for the beeless.
Moreover—
here, in a cave where the earth is covered with lotus-roots, a herd of boars plays, sporting with their snouts;
here, in the lake, deer stretch out their necks and drink as bees hover over the interior of the lotuses.
Moreover, here, having incessantly heard the swarms of bees [humming] over the buds of split trees,
the lords of the *kiṃnaras* play the lute, producing a sound as pleasing to the ear as that [of the bees].
And from this direction, let Your Majesty proceed along the ground beneath the trees on the bank of the lotus-pond at the pleasure-mountain.
And there—

the autumn breeze blows, shimmering with the fresh blossoming of new flowers, where bees hum as they cling to the filaments; it makes the rows of lotuses dance, variegated by the pollen from the clusters of *saptacchada* flowers that rival the scent of rutting elephants.

The king, however, being thoroughly delighted by her elaborate display of affectionate conversation and her revelation of all the lovely forest regions, said, “Excellent, O Sārasikā! Well-spoken cluster of gems; well done! Accept this reward,” and by bestowing ornaments upon all her limbs, he made her face radiant with joy.

And then, O Bhārata, go to wander in that forest named Sarvatṛṇīvāsa, which serves as an ornament to the earth—a forest where the unseasonal monsoon is heralded by the tumultuous abundance of honey-dripping from the Vakula, Campaka, mango, sandalwood, and Mandāra trees, shaken by the force of wandering, restless bees and birds; where groves of Nimba, Kimvuka, Jambīra, and Jambu trees are stirred by the swaying betel vines; where Karavīra creepers are in bloom and the thickets of Karasāñjana are budding, while parrots and Kapiñjala birds practice their lessons; where peacocks dance beneath the Tamāla trees, dark as the clouds of the rainy season; where circular lotus-pools are adorned by the crests of intoxicated, warbling Kalahaṃsa geese; where birds are made to frolic among Kaṣa, Kōlakuṭma, Nālikera, Lavanga, Pūga, Puṃnāga, and Nāraṅga trees, all swaying gently in the breeze and laden with blossoms; where the ground is dusty with masses of pollen from the clusters of Sarja and Khajūra flowers crushed by the claws and beaks of bees; and which thus acts as a true ornament to the world.

And in that tumult, there suddenly descended from somewhere white-winged *rāsahaṃsas* (crane-like birds), their rows of wings as pale as lotuses, adorning the surface of the earth with a pattern like a cluster of full-blown white lotuses; they filled the interior of the world with a deep and resonant clamor; they displayed the grace of milk-waves leaping high from the Ocean of Milk when churned by Mount Mandara; they were as white as the circle of the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa; they fell like personified fragments of the laughter of the delighted Hara; they emulated masses of white foam falling from the celestial Gaṅgā in the sky when agitated by the lords of the divine Cāraṇas; they bore the semblance of tiny autumn clouds rippled by a gentle breeze; they made the sky appear as if it were echoing with a thousand rising lunar discs; and they possessed the splendor of the massive boulders of the Himālaya mountains tossed about by the fierce winds of universal dissolution.

And during such an occurrence, the king, together with his retinue, remained motionless as he gazed upon the scene; his eyes possessed the beauty of blue lotus petals, motionless due to being forgotten by wonder, while his mind was agitated by a surge of curiosity.

And those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, too, having taken the side of the Pāṇḍus, though twice-born, were as if intoxicated; some, with their beaks opened wide, were devouring the buds of the *sthala-kamala* lotuses near the water’s edge and the tender sprouts of the lotus stalks; some, with their long necks raised high, turned away from the lotus groves and gazed toward the sky; some, with the *kandala* plants shaken by the wind from the flapping of their upraised wings, leaped about playfully; and some, whose own sweet cries of intoxication surpassed the tinkling of anklets, began to run before him as they roamed about.

The king, his retinue entirely preoccupied with the frantic pursuit of catching the birds, his sprout-like lower lip blossoming with the beauty of pure teeth revealed in laughter, seized with ease one of those swans as it moved gracefully with its feet moving in an unceasingly swift dance, its playful female mate laughing at the charm of its slightly raised wings, its neck uplifted.

And he was lifted up by him, whose sprout-like hand possessed the splendor of the interior of a red lotus; for a moment, he shone like a royal swan upon the surface of a pale lotus—the *padyarāga* pearl-oyster—resembling the crest of a ruby peak on the mountain of sunrise, while soft-sounding silver bells tinkled with a low, resonant tone. Having uttered a blessing, he began to praise the King in verses of distinct syllables: "May that Kapālin bring you auspiciousness—he who bears a neck like a swarm of bees clinging to a pale lotus, and who, being obedient to you, carries a skull."
Moreover—

how is it that this body of yours, which is fond of the *sarala* tree, rich in virtues (*guṇa*), adorned with hanging garlands, and marked with various tilakas, like a forest, has not become a refuge for the people of the king?
Moreover: O King, how is it that you— who are composed of excellent *sahakāra*, *karañjaka*, *vīratara*, *aśoka*, *madana*, *apuṃnāga*, and various other trees— are nowhere a *bibhītaka*?
Moreover—

O King, although you possess various forms such as the *bāṇa*, *karavīra*, *damanaka*, *śatapatraka*, *bandhujīvaka*, and *sujāta* trees, how is it that you are not yet a true *viṭapa* (a spreading tree)?

The king, having heard this, was filled with wonder and thought: "Oh, what fortitude he possesses even in the presence of men! How marvelous his beauty, the sweetness of his speech, the abundance of his wisdom, the nobility of his purpose, and the depth of his articulation! Generally, among these species of birds, whose discernment is limited to food, sex, sleep, fear, and wandering, how can such boldness exist? Therefore, this must be some traveler in disguise, moving at will."

"By no means can any living beings be disregarded even by the mind; for creatures wander about, possessing various wonders, their forms shattered by the power of karma, desire, or curses. Reflecting thus, he who knew what was appropriate honored him with words that seemed like blossoms of the *sinduvāra* tree slightly unfurled, yet possessed the radiant luster of jasmine, and asked after his welcome.

He too, with his head bowed in affection, as if honoring the king with a mass of pure radiance in the form of a heap of white flowers, welcomed the monarch by saying, "O Lord, today my welcome is fulfilled, for my mind is gladdened by the sight of you. Thus he paid homage to the king.

In the meantime, a female swan (*haṃsī*), her pupils trembling with agitation and her eyes seemingly floating upon a wave of tears that had suddenly burst forth, displaying a flight toward the branches under the guise of the unfolding of her wing-leaves as she gathered her companion, approached the king from afar and recited two verses in a voice as soft as the chiming of silver bells:
"O King, why is this swan being slain by you— he who practices yoga in solitude, whose only finery is his pearl necklace, and who is worthy of liberation?"
Abiding in the stainless state, yet associated with the entire cycle of worldly existence, how could the Swan ever be slain anywhere— he for whom no other object of attachment exists?
And another [verse]:
"O King, those water-birds who, like sages, desire fish for food, are addicted to wandering about in many ways and are vessels of poison. Therefore, enough with this persistence.
But the king, being gratified by the essence of the verse she had spoken—which was full of double meanings—and by the playful charm of her jesting conversation, addressed her:
"He who indeed always displays partiality in many ways toward the good and the wicked alike—"
That bird, whose habit it is to sport in the fields of *haṃsī* lotuses, is not bound; what more need be said?

Furthermore, hear another cause for its captivity. In my possession there is a heroine among the *mr̥ṇālikā* lilies; though her lotus-face was veiled by resentment, she was forcibly destroyed by this [bird]. Falling upon him, she was mangled by his talons, her petal-like lower lip torn, her forehead-ornament of *alikā* flowers crushed, and her delicate nature stripped away.
What has not been accomplished by this great lake?

Therefore, as long as he plunges into its waters, splashing about in many ways until his very waist, how could I feel satisfied? Furthermore, there is no more grievous sin than when a twice-born man who has consecrated himself for a sacrifice is obstructed.

"O innocent Kalahaṃsikā, you, however, endure humiliation even though you have come to the Mānasa lake; this behavior of yours is quite contrary to your nature. For a bee turns its back on the forest of a noble bamboo and desires a lovely lotus-stalk that is easy to live upon and frequented by swarms of bees. Enough of this! Go, my child, as you please," said the Lord of the Earth.

The female swan, too, with a playful smile, said to the male swan who had begun a quarrel: "O serpent among birds, do you desire the lotus stalk, whose heart is protected by its passion for the interior of the lotus? Or rather, O you of slender body, is such a thing not conceivable in one who serves those devoid of essence?"

He too said: "O bearer of the burden of cleverness, O scholar in the art of deceitful speech, O one heavy with wisdom, O master of dexterity—do not provoke my beloved! You and we are indeed alike, for we are both royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*). We enjoy the splendor of lakes; we take our place in the vessels of rivers. We are not to be praised for our conduct on foot. Therefore, do not be an adversary to those who are our allies.
For she is my heart, my life, my very breath, and my vital force—the entirety of the happiness of worldly existence; for to living beings, a loved person is everything."
“Where can one find a wife who is endowed with beauty, free from vulgarity, full of affection, sweet-spoken, of noble birth, and well-disposed?

Enough, therefore, with this commencement of a false quarrel! I shall soon perform some service for you as well, so that you too may become the hero in this drama of the expansion of love. Thus he spoke to the king.
In the meantime, a voice of enchanting clarity and distinct articulation was heard from the expanse of the sky:
"O King, lotus-petal-eyed one, let the swan be released quickly;
he shall become your messenger for the seduction of Damayantī."

The king, however, with his body causing horripilation as if by the application of *sōṣmabalā* oil, and experiencing a pleasure like the touch of the soft feathers of a young partridge from the name "Damayantī" which had entered deep within his ears, closed his eyes and reflected:
"Even when merely heard, her hips— resplendent with their girdles— are like golden jars filled with the water of bliss that delight the senses."

"Who is this Damayantī? Who is this bird, a marvel to behold? And what is this voice from the sky? All of this must be known in detail. Reflecting thus, he sat down upon a stone slab—cool with a shower of spray from the nectar of mountain flowers—within the shade of a bower of creepers blooming and budding, and addressed that swan.

"O noble one, friendship formed by walking seven steps together, affection arising from a few pleasant words exchanged, courtesy that is independent of self-interest, a natural and excellent tenderness, and a beautiful disposition of friendliness without cause—these are the characteristics of the virtuous. You possess all of these in embodied form; therefore, speak without hesitation. Tell me: who is this Damayantī? Whose daughter is she? What is her appearance like? Where does she dwell? And who are you that desires to do us a favor? What is this divine voice? Thus addressed, he began to speak.
"O Cupid, the vessel of the erotic sentiment, let this sprout of wonderous news be placed upon the ear of that creeper of beauty."

There is the Southern Country (Dakṣiṇāpatha), which serves as an ornament to the vast circle of the earth; which is delightful with its mountains, cities, towns, monasteries, and gardens; whose ground is purified by the lotus feet of the Lord of the Raghus who wandered there accompanied by Sītā; where the spread of the forest fire of sins is warded off by the waters of the Ganges and Godāvarī, whose waves are exceedingly holy; which, like Mount Mandara, underwent revolutions caused by King Bali; which, like Kailāsa, has made its abode the world of Maheśvara; which, like Meru, is beautiful due to its golden nature; which, like the Yadu lineage, has witnessed the incarnation of the Supreme Person (Śrī Kṛṣṇa); which, like the Lunar dynasty, is preeminent in its wise (or: possesses Mercury as its chief); which, like the recitation of the Vedas, is endowed with many sacrifices (or: libations); which has Śiva (Sthāṇu) on every mountain, ancient Puruṣas (Viṣṇu) in every city, lotus-born ones (Brahmās) in every body of water, temples in every step, Varuṇas (water-deities) in every forest, and Nandana groves in every place; which is the bolt barring the way to heaven; which, though full of heat (the Tāpī river), does not cause distress to its people; and which, though situated in the direction blocked by the Vindhya mountains, is the northernmost among regions yet remains the "Southern" country.

In that treatise, in that weapon, in the Veda, in the physician, in the Bharata, in the Bhārata, in ritual, and in art, there dwells eternally the world of Aśoka—foremost, wealthy, blessed, possessed of grain, eloquent in speech, charming in countenance, and tender in heart.

There, the God whose banner is the makara—his passion fixed upon their hips—lay hidden within the limbs of playful women who had already conquered the mind of the Supreme Lord merely by casting sidelong glances out of fear of the flickering flames from the eye on the forehead of the enraged Dhūrjaṭi. He deposited the very essence of erotic love in their high, jar-like breasts; honey in the petals of their lips; a bow in the knitting of their brows; and flower-arrows in their side-long glances.

For them, youth itself was the ornament for the beauty of all their limbs; the loveliness of their high, swelling breasts was the mirror for beholding their lotus-faces; the intense radiance of their eyes was the sandal-paste tilaka for adorning their countenances; the play of their eyebrows was the musk-leaf designs for their graceful charms; their side-long glances were the supreme weapons for conquering young men; their lips, possessing the luster of the bandhūka flower, were the Indra-stone for enchanting the minds of the world’s eyes; and the sweet humming of bees drawn by the fragrance of their lotus-faces was the sound of the lute for their diversion.
What need of more?
I consider those very deer-eyed women to be the abode of liberation and the very place where those who are liberated find their rest, for it is between their breasts that they dwell.

I think that even the venerable Agastya, the one born from a jar, must have been tempted by those very women— who were like jars containing the essence of various amorous dalliances— which is why even today he does not abandon the southern quarter.
Or rather,
who would not find this region dear, filled with women and abounding in every excellence of love?
In which [place], even a youth took delight, having abandoned the triple heaven whose sole desire had been consumed by fire.

Within that [kingdom] was the province of Vidarbha, which served as its ornament. It was free from agitation and rivaled the city of the Lord of the Immortals (Indraprastha). It was encircled by a series of magnificent and heart-stealing gardens growing along the edges of its moats. Its lofty palace towers, white as massive clouds and reaching toward the sky, surpassed the speed of the sun’s chariot-horses with the expanse of their peaks. It was inhabited by Brāhmaṇas who, though performing Agnihotra sacrifices purified by mantras and oblations, were free from anger even when all celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents had been destroyed; who, though reciting the Sūktas, were masters of Nirukta; who, though established on the path of truth, were householders; who, though accompanied by wives, were celibate; who, though devoted to guests, were skilled in receiving them; who, though primarily engaged in the application of conciliation (Sāma), were strong in the rod of punishment (Daṇḍa); who, though following the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, were single-minded in their path. In one part, it was presided over by merchants in the marketplace, resembling the Kurus led by Droṇa; like palaces, they were supported by scales (tulādhārin); like Naiyāyikas, they were experts in inference and the objects to be inferred; like Vaiśeṣikas, they were learned in the specific actions corresponding to substances; like Grammarians, they were intent on the perfection of form; like the Rudras, they wore matted hair bound in many knots. In another part, it was filled with Karṇāṭaka maidservants who were like the initiations of profligates and rogues, enticing people with their misshapen beauty; like the poetic styles of bad poets, they broke the rules of meter and prosody; like night-stalkers (Rākṣasīs), they were passionate for the night; though restless in their hips and faces turned everywhere, they were nonetheless ignoble. Elsewhere, it was crowded with children like a potter's workshop; elsewhere, it shone with prosperity like a forest ruled by elephants. It was adorned with rows of houses that were like the art of painting—beautified by every child growing up within, marked with Svastika signs, and decorated with Sarvatobhadra patterns. It was filled with temples that were like dramas, joined together with banners and emblems; like wicked Kirātas, they were seen performing deceptive rites; like weapons, they possessed sharp edges; they were variegated yet full of splendor, and possessed of proportions yet beyond compare. Though vast, it was rich in halls; though endowed with four quarters, it was free from the feet of the wicked; though frequented by profligates, its paths were pure; though everywhere abounding in crossroads, its nature was stable. On the bank of the river Varadā—which was graced by royal swans shining like rows of fresh lotuses amidst the dancing young Arjuna trees tossed by high waves, and whose beauty was enhanced by the faces of the women of Mahārāṣṭra—stood the delightful city named Kuṇḍina, possessing a beautiful lake.

Not far from it flows the Payoṣṇī river, whose holy waters mock the Gaṅgā—she who, by her very sight, dispels the sins born of bathing in the waters of the Dūritopaplava; [the Payoṣṇī] serves as a ladder for those seeking the path to heaven.

And to its west lies the hermitage of the blessed Bhārgava, born at Bhojakaṭa-kūpa, whose lotus-feet are kissed by the swarms of bees that are the rays from the sapphires in the crowns of the prostrate gods and demons; he who, having brought about the fall of Yayāti through old age, terrified the Vaidarbha region by the grand display of his fierce punishments upon those deserving of punishment.

And where there were virtuous men who were like trees with fallen leaves, but no actual trees; where there were lakes whose lotuses were blooming, but not the minds of people; where there were pleasure-pools adorned with blue water-lilies, but not women; and where there were families of fish overcome by misfortune, but not noble lineages.
To say more:
among all regions, there was the southern region, and within it, the Vaidarbha district.
There too, there was the Varadātīra maṇḍala and the city of Kuṇḍina.
