In that place there was a king named Bhīma, who was capable of destroying the entire host of his enemies; whose toe-nail mirrors were polished by the rubs of the crest-jewels of submissive sovereigns; who whitened the circle of the earth with the nectar of his fame, renowned as being as numerous as the grains of sand on the shores of the four oceans; who had acquired the unassailable glory of victory on the field of battle—which acted like a cage of birds confined within the expanse of his own arms; whose auspicious form was worshipped by the garlands of blue-lotus petals from the eyes of beautiful women intoxicated by the pride of youth; who, like the Sun, was the progenitor of the Nāsatyas (the Aśvins); who, like Indra, was celebrated in heaven; who, like Garuḍa, was a scorner of the arrival of serpents; who, like a cluster of lotuses, was possessed of stalks; who, like a treatise on grammar, was endowed with names; who was the abode of splendors, the foundation of fortitude, the city of manly prowess, and the refuge of blessings, fortunes, and sacred scriptures; and who was a king who felt no fear in the arenas of battle.

For whom the trees of the pleasure groves and the city folk were his constant, sublime abodes; whose wealth of speech was free from harshness toward his heirs; whose assembly members and the land itself were devoid of envy; whose limbs and the pleasure mountains were clusters of blossoming flowers; whose ornaments and the host of his army were invincible; and whose enemies and the heaps of flowers met their utter destruction in the forest of his prowess.

In that city, it was the rutting elephants who possessed the lovely beauty of Kandarpa, not the world of proud women; it was the trees in the pleasure groves whose minds were intent on drinking from the branches, not the women of the inner apartments; it was the women adorned with bracelets whose limbs were decorated with ornaments, not the waylayers. And the pair of his lotus-feet was purified by the people bowing down to him, not by ritual bathing; he generated passion in women, not in rivers.
He who provides new wealth to those dependent on him, not bondage;
he who delights in the virtues of the women of men, not in the women themselves;
and in whose agrahāras dedicated to the venerable ones the story of Nala is heard, not the story of Lopāmudrā.

And during whose reign there occurred the binding of a book that possessed letters, the drawing of a bow endowed with strings, the handling of a parasol produced from a noble bamboo, the uprooting of a particular garden of excellent birth, and the commencement of the extraction of a bulbous root of high lineage; even as the observation of an eclipse of the moon, which is fixed upon the true path and possesses the *punarvasu* asterism. What need of more? The King was the forehead-mark (*tilaka*) of the southern quarter, [the refuge] for the breasts of the lovely women of Karṇāṭaka...
Why should that lion of valor seek anything else—

he upon whose staff-like arms the glory of heroism rests, like a lioness upon the floor of a pavilion, her sprouting fangs drenched with the blood from the frontal globes of the lordly elephants that were his enemies, while he himself is a deer for the pleasure-mountain of his majesty and a bulbous root for the plantain-tree of his prowess?

And that great lord of the earth had a beloved named Priyaṅgumañjarī, who was the foremost among all the ladies of his harem; she was the very essence of the excellence of beauty that put to shame the loveliness of all the celestial nymphs with her own form; she was the sprout of the family of blemishes for the pride of Kāmadeva, who is like a pillar supporting the arrogance of the lordly elephant of passion; she was the deer-trap for the eyes of all people, the banner of the splendor of emerging youth, and the temple of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra); she was the earth for the sprouts of feminine grace, the expanse of the portion of good fortune, and the theater for the dance of amorous movements.

Her luster resembles a lotus in her eyes; the excellence of her form vies with the *rambhā* plant in the expanse of her hips; her hair-braid is as captivating as a flower, while her arched eyebrows are like a circle of bees; the forehead-plate upon which her dark curls shine is like a blue water-lily; and the radiance of her lips imitates coral, as does the pair of her hands and feet.
Her speech is golden, and her anklets captivate the mind at every step.

Upon her neck, which is graced by a flower garland, shines a beautiful necklace of very sweet speech; and together with the creeper-like tresses hanging from her forehead, Tilakamañjarī radiates splendor.
What more need be said?
Her eyes, moving with the playful grace of a charming young doe, are captivated by her own loveliness.
Though the essence of the beauty of her languid and shimmering loveliness was being drunk in by the cupped hands of the eyes of infatuated people, it did not find enough room within her limbs;
for she was even more beautiful as she moved, like waves upon the stage.
In this way, the days pass for these two, whose minds are gladdened by tasting the flavor of all the pleasures of saṃsāra.

And at one time, a certain female monkey appeared within the range of vision as she sported upon the ground beneath the trees on the sacred sandy banks of the Varadā—a ground thick with drops of abundant nectar trickling from clusters of blossoms broken by the heavy pressure of the constant kissing and alighting of swarms of restless young bees, its interior spaces bristling with petals crushed by the play of various winged birds, and its breezes carrying the fragrant scents of the kinsman of Smara (the god of love). She was carrying two young ones: one clinging to her belly and another resting upon her back; her beauty was like the reddish hue of a ripe *indravāruṇī* gourd, and her sprout-like trunk was tossed about as she scratched the itching of her entire body.
Beholding her, a tumultuous surge of grief born of childlessness took up residence in the hearts of those two;

their minds were tormented by the unbearable pain of being cut by the edge of a saw, and they fell into profound despondency regarding their vast kingdom, their people, and even their very lives, thinking: "Of what use is this sovereignty if it is devoid of offspring?
In every way..."

"O Maheśvara, we take refuge in the one whose lotus feet are kissed by the bees that are the rays from the red jewels at the tips of the crowns of all the gods and asuras, and who is dear to Ambikā"—thus they deliberated with one another.

Then, as the horses of the Sun’s chariot were being brought down by Aruṇa, as if to offer them wine (*vāruṇī*) to allay the fatigue of traversing the vast sky; as the shadows of trees ran toward the eastern quarter to console it, as if it were being filled with a mass of darkness out of a burden of grief while the Lord of Day remained attached to the western side; as the herds of cattle, green as the *hārīta* bird, slowly turned back from the depths of the forest; as the face of the western quarter grew red, as if being bathed in a flood of liquid red sandalwood paste offered by the forest-deities of the sunset mountain (*astācala*); as leaf-patterns (*patrabhaṅga*) were being fashioned upon the circular cheeks of courtesans; as the trees began to shed their leaves in fear, as it were; as the lotus buds performed gestures of supplication with folded hands—like prostrations—distressed by separation, as if trying to stop the Lord of Day from departing for the sunset mountain under the pretext of the piteous cries of female *cakravāka* birds about to be separated from their mates; and as the orb of the sun was seen gradually becoming entangled in a web of shimmering rays resembling the filaments of a very young copper-colored lotus within the waves of the western ocean, the mass of darkness rushed far away like a swarm of bees in great agitation. While the faces of the women of the quarters were adorned as if with leaf-patterns made of black agallochum paste; while the interiors of the forests were as if being invaded by the sweet warbling of cuckoos; while the reservoirs of water were darkened as if by the dense, deep-blue luster of blooming blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*); while the forest groves were as if being covered by the foliage of *tāpiccha* clusters; while the rocky surfaces of mountain peaks were as if being blackened by the plumage of dancing peacocks; while the palace walls were as if being painted with designs of collyrium; while the dwellings of travelers were as if being darkened by the smoke of sighs from women separated from their lovers; while the garden-enclosures of the pleasure-houses of amorous men were as if being sprinkled
And then—
Śambhu remained in her heart with his power unimpaired by the darkness of night, while the moon was upon the mountain of sunrise.
She offered her salutations daily to that auspicious moon, who bears a golden luster, delights in the sky,
and eternally wears within himself the beauty of the deer.
"O Lord Soma, whose mount is the bull white with ashes, salutations, salutations!
And thus, before long—
flooding [the world] as if with the surging waters of the churning Ocean of Milk—
That rising of the moon, which enchants the eyes of the world and is born as a friend to the God of Love,
is such that even a crow acts like a swan before a furious flock of owls wandering about, embarking on a battle terrible with accumulated enmity.
Moreover—
this earth, its splendor turned white by the spreading mass of the radiance of beautiful moons dripping with sandalwood paste, somehow shines thus.
The wretched crow, sleepless with the fear of day, crying out as he searches for his beloved even though she stands right before him, wanders like the whirling of a potter’s wheel;
and furthermore—
The foolish elephants, thinking it to be milk, hold jars beneath their trunks; even the beautiful women place blue water-lilies upon their ears, mistaking them for white lotuses;
and the Śavarī woman gathers the jujube fruit, desiring it to be a pearl.
Whose heart does this thick moonlight not agitate? And where women, with the longing for strings of pearls, catch hold of the moonbeams at the window.
In the cow-pen, the cowherd’s wife desires to churn the curds contained in the jar; the garland-makers, longing for jasmine flowers, gather them from the *mālatī* vines;
and who, beholding these white, enchanting moonbeams, would not be deluded?
Moreover—is it particles of camphor trickling from the sky? Or are these drops of sandalwood paste, slow and delightful to the mind? Or perhaps are they streams of flowing nectar?
"Thus, O dear one, these rays of the moon— beautiful as the petals of a blooming jasmine bud— clinging to his body, produce in people a delusion [that he is the moon].
Thus, the moon, which had inspired joy, appeared like a garland of *sinduvāra* flowers.
While the sun was scattering its web of rays across the circle of the quarters,
she, worshipping the pair of lotus-feet of Hara upon her bed of pure kusha grass, then fell asleep.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Dayamantī-kathā*, composed by the illustrious Trivikramabhaṭṭa, which bears the mark of the lotus-feet of Hari; [now begins] the third chapter.

Then, as night—whose line of hair was the down on the neck of the young pigeon-dove—gradually took up the lunar orb like a silver pitcher for the purpose of filling it with water and followed the sandy shore of the western ocean; as swarms of bees, appearing like lines of collyrium, emerged from the eyes of all the lotus-beds in the form of their blossoming buds; as the geese, whose ornaments were the ponds, uttered sweet sounds like anklets while sporting in the thickets of lotus clusters, their fresh lotuses trembling in the breeze stirred by the flapping of the white wings of autumnal clouds; as the flocks of cranes raised a clamor like the auspicious drum for the union of the ruddy geese, and the herds of *sārasa* birds resounded with the pleasant jingling of silver bells; as the wind blew, cool with droplets of dew, scattering the pollen of the blossoms of trees that had just awakened and making the air fragrant; as the wind faltered like the sigh of the world when its life had been bitten by the serpent of darkness, wearying the bosoms of beautiful women exhausted by the amorous play of dawn; and as the sun—the charming green horse—reddened the sky’s breast, which had been rubbed by his hand, dispelling the veil of greenish gloom—she, who had slept soundly, beheld a dream.

It is said that Lord Hara, whose lotus feet are made into crowns by the heads of all gods and demons, whose beautiful praises are composed by Brahmā, who dwells in the lotus, and by Nārāyaṇa; who shines with the fire-like eye on his forehead and the moon; who wears a full-blown blue lotus in his ear and a skull in his hand; who bears the pride of non-violence both in mind and in form; who carries the blazing flames of his eyes and the ashes of the sacrificial pyre; who is resplendent with a shoulder and neck like those of a bull; who possesses arms as graceful as a forest and bears Bhavānī; and who holds the trident that destroys the hosts of all Dānavas and the river Mandākinī—descended from the lunar orb, he spoke: "Daughter Priyaṅgumañjarī, take this cluster of blossoms. Do not fear. At dawn, at my command, a great sage named Damanaka will arrive; he shall bestow his grace upon you. Having spoken thus, he gave her a Pārijāta blossom, which was beautiful with the sweet sound of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of the slow-dripping nectar from its peak.
She too, saying "This is a favor," performed a hymn of praise with her head bowed in prostration even as she was in a dream:
"Homage to you, Śambhu, the remover of the heat of sorrow for the stainless world, who has rendered the onset of the great deceit of darkness futile."
O All-pervading One, endowed with sovereign power, adorned by the Lord of Serpents,
salutations, salutations to You, whose resolve is unfailing, the innermost Self!
In the meantime, [there appeared] the long eyes of her whose luster was as soft as the morning sun, resembling the petals of a blossoming lotus.
The sound of soft, auspicious musical instruments at the end of the night brought about her awakening, marking the cessation of the night's rest.

Gradually, as the eastern quarter was being as if drenched by jars of thick saffron water, and when the delicate web of rays capable of dispelling the stars had begun to prevail; when the orb of the sun—the auspicious jar for the commencement of the world’s awakening—had ascended the plateau of the eastern mountain; when the cluster of white lotuses was performing a grand *tāṇḍava* dance; when the flocks of *kāraṇḍava* ducks, like garlands of heads adorning the ponds, were wandering about; when the sound of the beginning of salutations by throngs of young bards, which gladdened the heart, rested within the hollows of the ears; when lute-players and flute-players were making their lutes and flutes resound with their plectrums; when the singers were singing the *grāmarāga* melodies, skilled in the ornamentation of the throbbing vibrations within the hollows of their throats; and when the dawn had arrived, possessing a luster equal to the clear brilliance of old *japā* flowers or split crystal—at that moment, she arose, became pure, scattered a handful of water as an offering (*argha*) from the interior of a blooming wild lotus, and offered a hymn of praise to the blessed Sun.

Having said this, he summoned the astrologers at that very moment and commanded: "Let the day for the festival of the installation of the heir apparent be declared."

Then they also spoke: "O Lord, please listen. This very day is a faultless one, indeed worthy for the royal consecration. All the planets are in exaltation, the month is auspicious, the lunar day is full, the conjunction is praiseworthy, the day of the week is commendable, the asterism is favorable, and the hour is propitious. Let that which is to be done be performed. When they had finished speaking and stood aside, immediately thereafter [the king said]: "O lady of beautiful hips, listen to this wonder we have heard. This is most fitting, most fitting for kings who are the very abodes of fortitude."
Just as he was praising the commencement of his third year— which is pungent to the eyes of beloved women—
a sharp sound of trumpets suddenly arose in the sky as if in emulation of him.
Moreover—

the rain of flowers released by the gods fell upon the assembly, drenching the ground with a continuous stream of honey from the weight of the swarms of bees that moved about, blinded by the fragrance above and humming as they gathered.

And at that very moment, certain Brahman-sages descended from the vault of the sky—having sanctified the regions of the quarters with the mass of their radiant, Brahma-like luster; holding in their hands earthen bowls filled with water from the shores of all the oceans, along with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and medicinal herbs; and having removed all the impurities of the Kali age by their mere sight.

Having been honored with hospitality by the King—who bowed with joy, humility, and his retinue, his temples turned golden-yellow by the thick pollen falling from his moving blue-lotus ears—they graced appropriate seats.
Having exchanged greetings and inquiries regarding his welfare, they presented their respective waters from their water-pots to the king, who had commenced the consecration of the prince:
"This is the water of the Mandākinī, which has come after he descended into it, its circular waves bent by the peaks of the full breasts of the celestial nymphs."
O King, this water of the Kālindī has its waves made exceedingly fragrant within by the falling flowers of the trees and creepers on its blossoming banks;
and this is the water of the Godāvarī, which has flowed down from the matted locks of the Three-eyed Lord.

This water of the Narmadā, churned at the foothills of the Vindhya range, has its blue lotuses fashioned by the eyes of Mahārāṣṭra women during their ritual bathing, and its half-lotuses scattered by sages swaying upon rafts.
And here is another pair of verses:
This very [ocean] has reached the ultimate limit of meritorious deeds.
There, at the time of rest for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, his feet were washed with milk;
and as he emerged for his pleasure, the faces of the multitude of Varuṇa’s wives momentarily assumed the splendor of a field of newly blossomed, unbroken rice stalks.
At that moment, his body bristling with the sprouts of dense horripilation, as if possessed by some extraordinary emotion, the king shook his head and reflected:

"Surely this must be one of the incarnations of Hari, Hara, or Brahmā descended into our house; for where is this manner of instruction, where is this sudden thought in this youth regarding his consecration, where is the perfection of such a favorable time, and where are these great sages with their hands full of all the requisites for anointment?"

"In every way, let there be homage to the Creator, who accomplishes the impossible, whose activity is thus so wonderful!"—reflecting thus, he rose and took those waters from the sacred fords (*tīrtha*). Having placed them in golden jars, while being cheered by throngs of playful women dancing with the impetuous joy of drums and cymbals struck at that moment, and surrounded by his attendants making auspicious proclamations, he forcibly seated Nala—who was unwilling even as he said, "Father, may you protect the kingdom for a thousand years"—upon the ceremonial throne along with Sālaṅkāyana, and performed the consecration himself.

Having dressed him in auspicious garments and ornaments and seated him upon the throne, he stood before his son with a golden staff in hand and for a moment performed the ritual of consecration. Sālaṅkāyana, out of great affection, held over him a pale white parasol from which a pearl necklace hung down like a stream of nectar, resembling the orb of the moon; meanwhile, the circle of vassal kings displayed their humility, their sprout-like hands occupied with clusters of beautiful fly-whisks made of shimmering gold.
The sages also recited mantras praised in the four Vedas; rising up and taking unbroken grains (akṣata) in their hands, they scattered them over his head and spoke this again:
"Those [mantras] which the Self-born God himself uttered for Skanda upon his victory over Tāraka, and which Vācaspati himself recited at the great festival of the sovereignty of Śacī’s beloved."
Today, we hope for your welfare through those Vedic utterances— like female swans on the lotus-face of Brahmā— which were recited at the time of your marriage to the Earth;
O fair-browed one, hear also of another marvel that occurred on that day.
The quarters became serene, a fragrant breeze blew, and showers of celestial flowers fell from the sky;
even the drums, though not struck, resounded for Nala who had been consecrated, and some invisible being in the atmosphere recited two verses of benediction.
Wearing a garland of serpents and a body clad in yellow garments,
may Hara and Hari both bring you auspiciousness, O lord of kings—
and furthermore:
May Hara, who playfully holds up serpents by coiling them into a circle,
and may the Lord Varāha, grant you exceeding prosperity.

Having thus offered his benediction, when the celestial voice had ceased and the sages—who had received the appropriate honors—had vanished in an instant, the day passed for the king as he considered his purpose fulfilled. He was as one who had attained the bliss of heaven, one who had enjoyed the entirety of the world, one who had tasted the essence of nectar, and one who had experienced supreme bliss. Meanwhile, the city streets were filled with the women of the capital, intoxicated by the dance and vocalizing soft auspicious songs; and from all sides, the chatter of the attendants could be heard: "Let the victory banners be raised! Let the arches be erected! Let the roads be sprinkled with sandalwood water! Let the courtyards be adorned with smooth lines of powdered pearls! Let the squares be made radiant with the glow of flowers! Let the twice-born and the deities be worshipped! Let gifts be distributed! Let auspicious hymns be sung! Let the wealthy be released! And let even the birds be freed from their cages!"

Thus, as some days passed, when the great festival had grown stale and the entire circle of invited vassal lords had departed as they had come, the lord of men addressed Nala—himself the submarine fire to the ocean of his enemies—while his retinue stood guard all around him on behalf of the crown prince.

"Father, let us say something if you do not mind. At present, our dear friend is a source of welfare for us, not a woman. Tresses of matted hair are fit for bearing a burden, not necklaces! Wise men are fit for assistance, not kinsmen. A bed of *kuśa* grass is suitable for lying down, not a fine couch! Excellent, swift-flowing rivers are fit for sport, not horses! And the grace of Śiva is to be prayed for, not palaces!"

Then, O long-lived one, having said, "You have been seen by me; you have not been asked; you have not been embraced; you have been forgiven for the harsh words spoken," he placed [the youth] upon his lap, laid him upon his chest which was drenched by a flood of tears flowing at that moment, and embraced him again and again with vine-like arms bristling with horripilation. With his cheeks moistened by incessant tears flowing as his heart was choked by a weight of inner grief, and his eyes closed in the darkness of a swoon of fainting, he smelled the crown of his head and set out for the forest accompanied by his wife.

When that king had departed, having relinquished his kingdom, the subjects raised piteous cries like female cakravāka birds separated from their mates at the end of night; and as the elderly citizens rose from every house, King Aśoka spoke: “O auspicious one, here is a respectful salutation with joined palms out of paternal affection. You must forgive even these few offenses of Śrutaśīla, who has served you through generations, even though he has committed a transgression, out of compassion for us. Look: do not the rays of the moon cause distress to the ocean, even as they cause the beds of lotuses to close? And do not even the flowers endure being crushed by the weight of bees? Having said this and entrusted his own son to him, he departed. As King Aśoka followed him out of love, Sālaṅkāyana—whose arms were as long as a sāl tree—placed the boy upon his shoulder. Then Nala, his limbs trembling from the heat of the water in a drying lake like a young elephant separated from its herd leader, his chest adorned with a necklace formed by the thick clusters of falling teardrops, cried out, “Alas, father! and opened his eyes no more that day.
With a voice faltering from the forceful outpouring of his intense grief, he recited this verse again and again:
"The eager calling from afar by my father who showed me such respect,
and the embracing with both arms after placing me upon his lap."
"And that betel, half-chewed, was offered from his mouth with such great affection—O stone-like one! Alas, O ungrateful heart, why do you not shatter upon remembering this?

Damayantī thought thus, and determining, "Oh, this noble-souled man is indeed full of affection and has a tender heart; therefore, he must in every way be a worthy recipient of our love," she questioned him once more.
"‘Huṃ haṃsa, tatastaḥ. Then that royal swan, wishing to conclude the story, recited this verse:
‘O you who are more beautiful than the beautiful, and furthermore—’"
Now, being made to forget the sorrow of his father’s absence by his own attendants through various diversions,
he passes the turning of the days.
"Having fixed his attention upon the pair of lotus-feet of Hara"—
thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Damayantī-kathā* composed by the illustrious Trivikramabhaṭṭa, titled *Hara-caraṇa-sarōjāṅkā*.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Then, when King Nala had ceased speaking—having described his lineage with words as clear and distinct as those of Vācaspati himself—the princess Damayantī declared, “I am a seeker of service,” and was thus constrained by the twice-born Śrutānurāga, who had already arranged her upper garment. He embraced her to his heart with a surge of anxiety, saying, “Child, you have been reunited after a long time. She was embraced as if he were addressing her, “Daughter, by some means or other you have finally been seen,” while she was overcome by a state of horripilation that caused a trembling throughout her entire body. He touched her face with his own, which bore a pallor at its forefront, as if saying, “Young girl, let this childhood conduct be abandoned now. And she was made to accept the command of the powerful god of love, as if being instructed by him: “O innocent one, let this state of self-will be relinquished. Nevertheless, for a moment, she remained there, maintaining her great dignity, her true condition unperceived.

Beholding Damayantī—who, with her breath forced into a straight line, betrayed the intensity of the internal torment of love; whose fortitude was suddenly blunted like a stream of water; whose eyes turned inward as if to gaze upon Nala brought there by her own desires within the lotus of her heart; and who was fainting from a sudden fit of love-swoon—the friend named Parihāsaśīlā, who was skilled in reading gestures and intent on jesting, addressed the royal swan: "O noble one, even now our faculty of hearing does not tire of listening to his virtues; our tongue does not reach satiety in the elixir of inquiry; our intellect finds no contentment in discerning his particulars; and our mind never ceases its passion for him. Therefore, why have you brought about this cessation of the narrative—a discordant note like that of a song, a wrong measure like that of a dance, a misstep like that of a performance, and a break that cuts off the extreme flow of sentiment? It is like stopping the stream of water for one who, out of thirst, is just beginning to drink; it is half-satisfaction for one eating, a frustration of desire for one whose passion has not yet been attained. Thus, it is not fitting to stop midway. O benefactor without motive, let the fountain-pavilion of the nectar of his true nature be opened for that mass of merit; and let those like us, long tormented by the summer heat of the bodiless god (Kāma), find relief with their cupped hands of ears outstretched. Thus, casting a side-glance at Damayantī for a moment, she caused the royal swan to converse.
He too said, "O Sundarī, what else remains to be praised of him, who is like a statue installed within a palace that is the heart of every woman?

For when he is heard of, the sound of the flute and lute is not sweet; when seen, the God of Love is not charming; when conversed with, eloquent speech is not essential; when familiarized, nectar is not praiseworthy; when practiced, the moon is not a source of bliss; and when propitiated, the Giver of Wealth is not a fit object of praise.
What more need be said?"

O lotus-faced one, even if there were a thousand eloquent mouths with incomparable attentiveness and long life, it would still be uncertain whether they could or could not perform a full investigation of that lord of the earth’s virtues;
moreover—
In this ocean of saṃsāra, these two jewels—a woman and a man—were born:

you, O lady with eyes like those of a young doe, are the pinnacle of good fortune among women, and Nala is the limit of excellence among men; therefore, you are the worthy consort for that lord of the earth.
This much has been told; what else remains? We shall now depart; may it be well with you.

And furthermore, O moon-faced one: when grammar—which possesses excellent euphonic combinations (*saṃdhi*), declensions (*samāsa*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), and primary and secondary suffixes (*taddhita*); which is rich in case-roles (*kāraka*) and skilled in technical rules (*paribhāṣā*); and which, upon investigation, discerns the relative strength (*balābala*) [of grammatical elements]—is being sent forth by a messenger, there occurs a connection with ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*). Therefore, let some such messenger as that be dispatched to him.

"Even when one considers the *puṇyaśloka*, which is endowed with the perfection of the *vṛhatī* meter, described as *jagatī*, composed of refined heavy syllables, and possessing the grandeur of the *śārdūlavikrīḍita*—and while that very Lord of Mountains is being praised in such a meter, there occurs a break in the metrical rhythm," she said, and then moved away.
As he was departing, she, who was habituated to jesting, spoke to him again.

“O noble lady, since you have spoken with these words that are the very root of affection, he too must be addressed with words worthy of longing. For a clap of the hands is not struck with only one palm; nor is a heated piece of iron joined to another piece of iron unless it is itself heated; nor does a red garment attain beauty when joined with another cloth that is not red—it merely remains a pair of separate pieces.
To Damayantī, who was speaking thus, the playful Nala replied:
“Friend, why do you ask this of me, who am so naturally affectionate toward you without cause?”

He who possesses toward us an impartiality free from expectation, a natural goodness of character, a genuine feeling of affection, an unfeigned quality of helpfulness, a love born of no prior acquaintance, a friendship requiring no practice, and a kindness never seen before.

Thus, why should such a friend without cause be entreated? By whom are the moon, sandalwood, and lotuses ever asked for the sake of helping others? But what can we say of this one, whose heart has been bound by our friendship for a few moments and who now desires to depart so suddenly and so unwillingly? To say "Do not go" is an ill omen; "Go" is cruelty; "Do as you please" is indifference; "You are dear to me until I see you no more" is empty talk; "Who are you, such a jewel among divine birds? is an irrelevant question; "What do you desire? is out of place; "What may I do for you that is pleasing? is mere formal courtesy; and "You have already done us a favor" is a direct flattery.

Therefore, O friend of virtue, we do not understand what you say: that for those like you there is only the final sight, and not the unbearable obstruction of sight caused by the limbs and members of the body being cut away; it would be better for nectar never to have been tasted at all than to suffer the pain of its loss after having drunk it once.

"Therefore, for the sake of seeing you again at Pārthya, this Hāralatā, who acts as the stage-manager for the drama of our remembrance, shall serve merely as a gift from someone dear to you. Having spoken thus and having accepted Nala, she said, "O noble one, you have been heard of by two: by us, the traveler, and by that royal swan; you are served by two: by us with our hearts and by him with his devotion; you are remembered twice: by day and by night; and we have now two possible courses: either you or death. As if doubling her message of greeting, she unfastened from her own throat a pearl necklace that seemed like her own longing incarnate and hung it around his neck.
He too, saying, "O Sundarī, this burden of describing his virtues before you has been taken up by me under the guise of this pearl necklace," flew up into the air along with that flock of birds.

And as it rose up toward the vault of the sky, she cried out from afar under the guise of its fluttering leaf-like wings, as if summoning the guardians of the quarters: "May your eyes become fruitful; behold this unprecedented jewel among women! She fanned the heavens scorched by the fierce rays of the sun, and comforted the quarters whose space was obstructed by the thickets of the directions. With her eyes fixed without blinking for a long time upon that circle of birds, the princess stood gazing upward in wonder.
And she thought:
"O Father Creator, even you do not grant me such a sight."
If only I had wings like a bird, so that I might fly up and see her face;
indeed,
these birds are better off as they fly away.

But she did not think, "He is a mere human, inferior in merit," for she was still gazing upward even after they had departed; with eyes wide with wonder, she remained motionless as if made of wood, and only after a long time was she brought home by her friends who roused her from her trance.

From that time forth, her sighs became straightened, but not her smiles; her speech faltered, but not her grief; lethargy increased, but not sleep; perspiration flowed, but not paralysis; her voice grew faint, but not her passion; her longing was for sandalwood paste, not for movement; she sought the application of its virtues to soothe her fever, not a bath; her necklace brought her pleasure, not her food; and the garden breeze, as it touched her limbs, brought her comfort, but not the people.
And she recited this verse again and again:
"They find no rest anywhere, yet they do not lose their way even upon the paths."

In that place where my beloved resides, my desires—clinging to the cage-like treetops of the lofty mountain—do not falter; how could they weary while rushing with longing along the path, even when it is rugged?
They do not stumble, for he who is dear dwells there.

Those royal swans also, sporting in the lake waters that resembled the orb of the moon, that were like forests possessing five-faced lions (tigers) with their playful expansion, that bore the auspicious form of Śiva, that possessed the great beauty of moonlight, and that perpetually imitated the swelling of the ocean; and traversing mountain valleys, triple-pathed rivers, mountains, cities, villages, hamlets, towns, and regions as if they were the peaks of the Snowy Mountain (Himalaya); after a few days, they arrived at the grove of Niṣadhā and began to sport there at their own will.

Then, having observed one of them among those [lotuses], a royal swan arrived at the lotus-cage of a pleasure-pond; and the lake-guardian, approaching with haste, informed the king who was eager for news of the swans: "O King, Your Majesty asks daily after the swans; today, a certain one does not take a morsel of stalk and casts the inner fibers far away."
O King, even the female swan dwelling in the garden lake— like the wife of your enemy—
is not satisfied with food, nor does she sleep even upon a bed of fresh lotus petals.
"O King, the female swan belonging to your enemy's wife has become free from passion.

As the king was contemplating this pair of Āryā verses with their double meaning, the sprout of his lower lip was whitened by the nectar of a slight smile, and he said, "Lavaṅgikā, it is just as you say; those swans have indeed arrived for her. Otherwise, how could she possibly exist all alone? And so he remained absorbed in that news.

Then the forest-keeperess, whose eyes were as long as the petals of a blue lotus, whose face was like the moon, whose lips possessed the lovely hue of the *bandhūka* flower, who wore a garment of white silk, whose limbs were fair as the stalks of ripened rice, who possessed a radiant smile, and who was followed by a flight of swans—like the personified autumn season herself—entered and said, "O King, here is that offending bird, the cause of your longing, who has somehow arrived. Having spoken thus, she placed the royal swan before the king’s lotus-feet, holding him with both her lotus-hands as if he were a full-blown white lotus, and performed a salutation to the monarch.

The King also said, "Sārasikā, well done! Let your office not remain vacant; go now to your proper place. Having spoken thus, he dismissed her—along with Lavaṅgikā—having gratified her with gifts of satisfaction. Then, having thinned out his attendants, he gazed for a long time with a steady eye at her who had arrived, as if she were the medicine for reviving the dead, the syllables that protect life, a jewel that restores health, a healing herb for consolation, and the very root of delight—a state motionless with joy. Honoring her greatly, he asked her welcome with a charming smile.
He too, experiencing the nectar of the sight of the King, said, "Welcome," and offered this praise:
"O King— the fragrance of whose lotus-like mouth has spread abroad, and whose throat is choked with emotion..."
When you are provoked to anger, your enemies— frightened— pay no heed even to their own ponds or their wives, [ponds] which possess garlands of lotuses dripping with ghee and waves of rising ripples.
Furthermore:
its banks are no longer lush with greenery, its remaining mud has been stripped away, and it is bereft of the splendor of the blooming pollen of white water-lilies.

We have beheld much sorrow here in the forest depths, as well as the world of your youthful enemies and the lake in the month of summer; yet, O treasure-house of affection, you have captivated our minds so that these days have somehow passed for us— days devoid of the perception of pleasure, filled with the onset of torment, and sprouting the shoots of restless longing.

Tell me, then, which direction is to be congratulated, in which you have made your dwelling? Who were those people with fruitful eyes, by whom you were long gazed upon? Who were they who tasted the nectar-essence of your well-spoken words, by whom you were addressed? Who were they who attained the fruit of their very life, with whom you held conversation? O you whose company is so desirable, now that you have gone—like a treatise on logic (tarka-śāstra) that has introduced the highest delusion, or like grammar (vyākaraṇa) that has ceased to function—this mind of ours has become utterly bewildered.
Saying, "Come, come," he himself lifted her up with the palm of his lotus-like hand and stroked her affectionately.

He, for his part, replied, "This is a great favor that Your Majesty shows us such compassion," and recounted everything from the moment of departure—the entire sequence of events concerning the sight and conversation with Damayantī—up until the presentation of the pearl necklace.
Having spoken, he drew the pearl necklace from the tip of her neck by its single thread while she remained in that very position, and said this:

"O Lord of Men, let this pearl necklace— which intoxicates, which serves as the bowstring for the circle of the god of love’s bow, which is the banner of the supreme glory of the fortune of good luck, and which is the family treasure— grasp your neck like her very arm.
Moreover— "
The director of the new drama of the unfolding of love, the personified command of King Manobhava (the God of Love),
and the very cause for his choosing her in a svayaṃvara— may this necklace, Hārāvalī, find a place in your heart.
But the king, having taken it and examined it, fell into deep reflection.

"Whose heart would this extraordinary mass of pearls— not comparable to anything else, pure with qualities as beautiful as bliss— bringing a festival to the eyes and captivating the mind, not take its place?
Thinking thus, he doubled his single string of beads and gazed at her again with longing.

But Haṃsa laughed and made a jest: "This [pearl], though possessing many virtues— given by her, brought by me, delightful by its very nature, and so forth— how is it reduced to having only a single virtue by you?"
The king, too, showing the inner thread in jest, said: "O foremost of birds, do you not see that this [string] possesses but a single quality?
Or rather—who, however virtuous, could possibly enumerate the qualities of this [garland], which clearly possesses the glory of a praiseworthy birth?"

Having said, "She whose pair of breasts naturally expands like two jars rests here at ease," and having drawn his own throat-stalk toward them, he placed her within the center of his heart as if to show Damayantī, who remained inside, saying, "There dwells that former lover of yours."

Having offered a slight, sweet smile and speaking in an exceedingly sweet voice, he said: "O foremost of birds, tell me again: what is she like? What is her form? What is her age? What is the perfection of her beauty? What is her diversion? What is her eloquence? What is her favorite thing? What is her conversation? Thus, as if hearing news of something never before heard, he proceeded with great interest to inquire after her; meanwhile, he remained for many hours, unaware of the passing of time, while the god of love aimed his arrows with restless hands and drew his bow-circlet with incessant, wondrous revolutions, making him his target.

And while the Lord Sun, shining with radiant light, remained stationed in the middle of the sky, and while the sound of kettledrums, resounding with a deep *bhaṃkāra* at the end of the watch, reached the path of his ears, he said: "Friend, rest now on this bank surrounded by Mandāra trees; you are requested to remain in the lotus-pond of the palace garden. You must not leave unless dismissed as before. Having thus restrained the royal swan, he himself arose for his daily rites.
And so it was for that king, whose other activities had all been slackened.
For Damayantī, whose own kinsmen have been left behind, the autumnal days pass by with the swan, diverting themselves with accounts of her conduct; thus,
unaware of the passing of time, the days go on.

Once, when the darkness—possessing the luster of fresh black collyrium—was being pierced by the radiance of the dawning morning, and when the quarter beloved by Śacī was slowly awakened by the warbling of swarms of restless bees rising from lotus buds as it was, as it were, sprinkled with dissolved lac-dye; then a certain bird, followed by a flock of royal swans whose plumage shone with rows of feathers trembling incessantly as they shook their curved beaks, left the shore of the lake and approached the king, who was waking from his necessary duties at the conclusion of his morning prayers while lulled by the sweet sound of Kinnara songs, and spoke these words.

"O Lord, we seek an audience with Your Majesty—a sight that is like sandalwood beyond all comparison, a smearing of camphor powder that is beyond touch, nectar that is beyond drinking, an elixir that is beyond tasting, and honey that is beyond licking. How indeed could even a thousand years of experiencing these bring us complete satisfaction? Yet, the possession of others obstructs the independence of living beings, and that which is difficult to abandon—namely, one's birthplace—is hard to leave, even for those born from the lotus. Your Majesty will surely understand all this with confidence: what kind of people we are and by what service in a previous life we were sent here. Truly, this is no occasion for such an untimely discourse."

"May Your Majesty thus command us to depart. And we must not be forgotten during your conversations with your attendants. We consider that very birth and life alone to be praiseworthy wherein Your Highnesses take notice of us with favor. Therefore, this is our prostration requesting leave to set out. To him who had spoken thus, the protector of the earth finally granted leave to depart.

And when that lord of the flock of swans, whose favors were not to be forgotten, had departed; when the daughter of the king of Vidarbha, having entered the lake of Manasa through the channel of her ears, was causing it to tremble; while the archer Ananga struck at every limb; and while the exceedingly sweet humming of the bees—whose voices were thick with intoxication from tasting the nectar of the Kunda flowers blooming in the nearby forest—reached the path of her hearing; at that moment, as the string of his bow drawn back to his ear began to vibrate with a twang, there arose a heart whose mind was closing in a state of equal delusion born from the root of emerging despondency.
The eyes of that king, whose pleasure was solely in his own position, became fixed and unblinking in thought, and his lower lip was scorched by sighs; for in him,
only the five passions became his enemies, while all other aesthetic sentiments (rasas) remained as they were.

Thereupon, as if experiencing the unbearable agony of a scorpion sting, as if his vital points in the feet were being pierced by thorns, and as if his limbs were repeatedly embraced by the flickering breezes of the fierce summer that bore the glow of heaps of embers, he found not even the slightest comfort anywhere.
For instance:
[he sought] those [spots] cooled by channels of dripping moonstones, whose air was filled with fragrance...

On this night, beautiful with the splendor of the full moon’s rays, do the upper terraces of the palace— not their windows obscured by spreading clouds of incense smoke, nor strewn with scattered flowers— fail to captivate the hearts of even those who are weary? For what is so heart-stealing to those who are agitated?
Moreover:
[The breezes] wearying from the swaying motion of the crests of waves in the lakes of the heart-garden,
and dispelling the drops of perspiration from the Kinnara maidens exhausted by the fatigue of amorous dalliance;
In the evening, breezes as cold as frost fell softly upon his limbs, gently swaying the dense blossoms of the night-lotuses;

from that time forth, he generally took delight only in southerners, he experienced a thrill of horripilation at the mere mention of the Vidarbha country, and even hearing of it produced pleasure in his ears.
What need of more?
That southern quarter became, for his ears, mind, and eyes, as if smeared with the mud of nectar, or as if touched by the sprouts of bliss.

From the day she beheld the swan, Damayantī was no longer found in the nearby bower-vines of the garden—its borders resounding with the clamor of swarms of wandering bees, its beds strewn with freshly plucked flowers and shoots, and its playful birds fluttering about; nor did she sport in the pleasure-lake, where flocks of *caṭula* bees and *cakravāka* ducks warbled amidst the waters filled with the essence of blooming blue lotuses, white lilies, and water-lilies; nor did she touch with her hand even the ornaments of ruby necklaces; nor did she arrange within the partings of her beautiful, curling locks the placement of blossoms that were beginning to bud; nor did she anywhere experience the bliss of sleep upon a couch of high swan-feather pillows, resting her soft cheeks against them. Instead, with her sprout-like hands placed upon her exceedingly pale cheeks, she sent her gaze every moment toward the northern direction, gazing with longing even at the birds in the sky that had come from that land, conversing with the travelers there as if they were her own kin, and offering her heart to the very breeze that had reached her region by removing her upper garment; thus, day after day, she was overcome by the god of love.
For instance:
the dance is a speck of dust in her eyes, the lute is a thorn in her ears,
and the sandalwood paste along with the wafts of camphor are like iron arrows in her breasts.
To her was born a daughter named Lāvaṇyā, whose eyes were as beautiful as lotuses;
for her, the only thing that sustained her life was the news of her beloved.

Thus, as their mutual passion increased through the words of secret messengers sent by each to the other, their limbs moved but their desires bent low; their eyes turned away but not their hearts; their slender bodies grew thin but not their longing; their energy became dull but not their desire; their helplessness expanded but not their sleep; their anxiety grew but not their joy; and their sprout-like lips withered but not their intense passion.
What need is there for much?
Even upon a couch spread with fresh lotus petals, sprinkled with camphor-water,
where their bodies were tossing about and their flower-garlands had fallen away;

What else occurred for those two, who were under the sway of a faint longing, than that state of poetic affliction (*kāvyavasthā*) in which sandalwood, the moon, rows of campaka petals, and the like were treated as fire?

For them— who were muttering prayers in the form of mutual inquiries regarding each other’s virtues, who were engaged in the recitation of their names as if they were repetitive mantras, and whose meditation was focused on the imagined union with one another— they remained in a state of separation rather than union, even as they offered their own hearts as oblations into the funeral pyre of longing, while remaining silent observers of their vows.

Once, beholding Damayantī’s state of youth—which was a snare for the deer-like eyes of young men, a kettle-drum for the flow of rut from the lordly elephant of Love, a mockery of the beauty and form of the celestial and demonic beauties, and the royal capital of the aesthetic sentiment of love—the Lord of Vidarbha became long troubled with the thought, "Who indeed might be a suitable husband for her? He then, together with his ministers, deliberated on the plan to formally commence the rite of a *svayaṃvara*.
Before long, she dispatched principal messengers, bold and accompanied by gifts, on invitations from the kings of the East, West, North, and South.

To a certain messenger who had set out for an invitation from the northern king—a learned and elderly Brahmin—Damayantī, through the mouth of a trusted female attendant, spoke these words of double meaning:
"O father, regarding the invitation to the kings, let it be conducted in such a manner that..."
“Nala’s intellect would not have failed to understand this scripture; what more could be desired than that?
He too, having grasped the meaning of the verse, gave a reply of the same nature:
“By some particular conduct, by some mature playfulness...”
"I shall accomplish this man's purpose by means of a forceful fast;
therefore, O long-lived one, remain at ease," having said this, he departed.
Then, not long after, that Brahmin Lomaśarman returned; having been summoned to a private place by Damayantī, he was addressed by her with playful and joking conversation.
“O learned one, though summoned by the northern king who carries out my father’s commands, not even a single word—let alone a falsehood—has been communicated to me by you.
He replied, “I shall tell you, O you who are skilled in the art of double-entendre; listen,” and having said this, he began to speak with a smile.

Having departed from there, as I wandered about in the manner of inviting the lords of the regions, I became intent on hunting in the southern forest tracts of the mountain named Niṣadha, whose ridges and peaks—reaching to the very clouds—are variegated by millions of summits.
There, [I beheld him] with shoulders as high as the uplifted hump of a proud, fleshy bull;
with hair possessing the luster of the waters of the Yamunā; and with a face like the full moon of the eastern sky.
A certain charming young man was seen by me on the road; when he was gazed upon by my eyes, which had lost their blinking, the fruit of my birth was attained.
Having determined that "this one is from the South," I addressed him with longing.
I too, having made some small conversation, said:
"O noble one, as this form of yours bestows joy upon the eyes of the world, so you are truly free from greed and devoid of attachment."
Thus addressed, he too gave a reply with a slight, charming smile.
Then, a second youth—his limbs adorned by the bloom of early manhood, mounted upon a tall horse, his belt tightly fastened, and wielding a bow and quiver—arrived at that very spot.

Having arrived, and beholding in a region of rocky ground resembling a young blue flame some woman whose breasts possessed the luster of golden jars and upon whose neck lay a garland of flowers, he spoke as follows:
"O Prince, behold—
on the bank of the river of Vidarbha, there is a certain cowherd girl who, having made Nala her chosen husband, is driving out her cattle."
Having heard this, I also said: "O noble one, not only this one, but some other as well.
When I had spoken thus, he, perceiving my intention, looked at me and spoke again with a smile:
"This one and that one—"

"May the daughter of the cowherd enjoy for a long time the fruits that result from the transformation of the milk of a fickle-eyed woman—she whose affection for the Prince of Niṣadha has now somehow departed despite his great efforts. Let other matters rest for a moment. O traveler, tell me: from where are you to be questioned, and how much further must the path still be traversed?"

Then, after I had related my own story, I questioned him: "Who is this crest-jewel upon the heads of all men, and who are you, who have surpassed even the preceptor of Indra by the abundance of your own wisdom? He replied once more: "This, gentle sir, is that Nala, the son of Vīrasena, an expert in all weapons and scriptures, who has torn asunder his enemies; and what else? I too am one named Śrutaśīla, a servant acting under his command. Having said this, he rested.

Nala, too, having engaged in various conversations centered upon you that manifested the sprouts of love, being capable and desiring to fly away at that very moment out of eagerness to attend the invitation to the *svayaṃvara*, gladdened me with his speech, smiles, and glances as if with a rain of nectar; and making me accept, even against my will, the ornaments from his own limbs for the sake of his journey, he dismissed me quite clearly. He himself, due to his addiction to hunting, mounted a noble horse that galloped steadily with great speed, accompanied by hunters.
"Wearing a beautiful necklace around his neck, he went out again to sport at his own will;
O long-lived one, since I observed his passion for asking about that story regarding my master’s son, I am certain that he will return before long. Having said this, the Brahmin went to his own home.

And when he had gone, Damayantī spent several days in a certain state of being, thinking: "What praiseworthy time is that? What blessed day is it? What auspicious hour is it, at which our eye—like a night-lotus at the sight of the moon—shall experience some indescribable joy upon beholding him?"

Then Nala, invited by that brahmin and spurred on by his own inner longing, accompanied by his minister Madana and surrounded by his army and his yearning, set out at that very moment toward the kingdom of Vidarbha.

When Nala set forth—shattering the circle of high mountains with the movement of his fourfold army, deafening the quarters with the clatter of his chariot wheels, and acting as a forest fire to the groves of his formidable enemies—the mounted horses shone with wonder; their hooves struck the earth with such force that the entire surface resounded, they were radiant with the beauty of their lovely golden trappings, and they were yoked in endless succession, each fit for a universal monarch. And the lordly elephants shook the earth, their massive bodies supported only precariously by the heads of serpents burdened by the great weight; their temples were adorned by the swaying of beautiful chowries, while their faces were made resonant by the humming of bees clinging to them; though their heroic agitation was somehow restrained by the ringing of their bells, vermilion flowed from the temples of their throbbing frontal globes, and they drenched the ground with a thick, flowing rut.
What more need be said? At that moment,
when the armies had crossed the boundary between the eastern and western oceans,
the earth remembered Lord Hari in his boar incarnation due to the burden it bore.
Moreover—
here the groves of white lotuses were gathered together by means of white parasols,
while in other places the earth became a blue lotus with upraised stalks through the use of peacock-feather sunshades.
In some places, during his march, the sky became cloudless due to masses of rising dust;
in other places, it was filled with waves by the fluttering cloths of his banners, like a lake with surging ripples.

Having arisen, the powerful dust-clouds—touching the shanks and hips, greedy to dally upon the surface of the chests, reaching up to seize the necks, forcibly clinging to the garments like shameless women, intent on striking with nail-marks, and licking the chins, cheeks, lips, and eyes of the soldiers—became so excessively pervasive that they clung to their heads and, covering the sky, reached a great height even into the nearby forest thickets.

And there, in that tumult, millions of foot soldiers moved about, shouting and brandishing bows and spears; skilled in the analysis of grammatical locuses like followers of Pāṇini, they surged forward, eager to leap and plunder the cities of their enemies.
And in that conflict—awakening the Kinnaras who were sleeping soundly in their mansions on Mount Mandara...
The dense clamor of the army, echoing within the caverns of Mount Meru’s peaks, caused the three worlds to become deafened as it cried out: "Run! Charge! Go! Clear the path once again!"

Thus, leaping over mountains where many common folk were sporting, villages, rivers adorned with many waves, boundaries, roads filled with birds, and footpaths, he passed by cities accompanied by languid women and courtesans; bypassing fields dark with ripening wheat and the hamlets of forest-dwellers (Bhillas), and crossing over widows—the wives of his enemies—and desolate wastes, he showed great respect for his retinue, his kinsmen’s families, and the lakes; and before long, the Sun proceeded toward the Vindhya mountain, whose thousands of rugged peaks were left behind by his horses, and whose central ridges were constantly occupied by hosts of gods, Gandharvas, and Siddhas.
And then—
what are these that fall incessantly from the sky in every direction,
or has the divine Earth herself brought them forth?
Thus being ferried across by the wives of the Śabaras,
the forces suddenly reached the middle of the broad expanse of the Vindhya range; meanwhile,

Śrutaśīla, having cast his eyes upon the forest glades— where the female deer frolicked upon lofty peaks, where the spaces of the sky were entangled with lattices of bamboos as clear as the starry firmament, and which were made charming by the lovely green sprouts shaken by the movement of herds of young, variegated, and dappled elephant calves— beheld the king and spoke these words.
"O King!

[Behold] the trees, moistened by the flow of ichor dripping from the temples of rutting elephants, resounding with the cries of boars as they play and half-chew the falling tubers of the musta-grass."
Whose heart, alas, do these grounds of the Vindhya region not captivate— the grounds where bower-like creepers sway gently in the slow breeze of travelers well-settled within?
And let Your Majesty look further from here:

This is that Narmadā, whose waves serve as a stage upon the broad rocky laps of the Vindhya’s central region, bestowing bliss upon the Śabara women who rest on her banks weary from amorous play; she whose lovely banks are crowded with beautiful women meeting amidst the dense rows of trees.
These riverbanks, where kandalī plants are crushed by the trampling of wild elephants, are frequented by the Siddhas;
moreover, even within this [river],
there is the fragrance of the water trickling from the temples of the rutting elephants.
Bearing rows of blue lotuses that resemble swarms of bees hovering nearby,
the waves— which steal away the sins of the Kali age and perform playful dances— beautify the path of the sky as if it were a flight of stairs to heaven.
On this bank of his [the river],
there are those whose matted locks are loosened by water dripping from their shoulders and rendered somewhat sluggish;
who are covered only by a small mat and a loincloth made of moist, coarse fibers.
Behold these aged ascetics, their bodies reduced to mere skeletons with cold-induced goosebumps, slowly wading out from the water and falling upon the slippery network of moss; and even further—

Behold these Pulinda women sporting freely at their ease upon the banks of the Anjana, which shines with its blossoming lotuses; the waves of their breasts, resembling the frontal globes of elephants,
shimmer there as they cast their eyes within the petals of the flowers, mistaking them for opening blue lotuses.
Even the swarms of bees, though struck by the creepers of her hands, wander about;
let Your Majesty look further from here as well—
[a place] where the groves of blue lotuses bloom with their filaments and whose fragrance spreads afar.
This deluded peacock, wandering on the bank, joyfully beholds the darkness of clouds filled with water that imitates swarms of wandering bees; meanwhile,
the cakravāka bird circles nearby in fear, crying out like a wheel.

And who, O man of excellent intellect, would not take delight for a long time upon beholding this most beautiful riverbank— enduring the weight of ospreys, lined with swans, and filled with joyful peacocks and ruddy geese?
Moreover—

for these sages, whose wealth is tranquility and who are endowed with right conduct, do not resort to the river Nanda, which resounds with the cries of cranes, nor to the ritual bath at Savana performed out of hypocrisy; rather, they dwell there while remembering Bhava, whose glory is incomparable.
Truly, these noble beings have shaken off all evil.
For instance:
even as they dwell for a time among holy sages who are free from calamity, they still bear the mud of the marks of misfortune.
How do the forests near the banks of the Narmadā become defiled? And here—from one place:
in some spots, there are sprouts shining like excellent red chalk (gairika).
In some places, *cakora* birds flutter beneath the spreading creepers of cloves and *lavalī*; elsewhere, young *kandalī* plants shimmer on the banks of mountain streams;
and in other spots, bees are trapped by the honey of blossoming *nicula* flower clusters.
In some places, it possesses mango sprouts surrounded by restless cuckoos,
and in other places, the roots of its *sāla* trees are thick with the herds of deer; in various spots, it is sanctified by the feet of celestial damsels moving about in great numbers.
This pair of forests here brings even the minds of sages to a state of transformation;
may Your Majesty dwell for this day in this place for the purpose of dispelling the exhaustion and fatigue incurred by the army’s journey.
Supporting themselves upon the mass of air with their flower-eyes expanded,
these trees seem indeed to gaze across the expanse of the sky;
moreover, those of whom—
Behold the rows of clouds hanging within the intervals between the trunks and branches, appearing like dangling *valgulī* birds; and of these—
"Clung to the tips of the high branches, I think that surely the moons of the forest-dwellers cause a confusion with flowers at night.
And furthermore:

Having drunk the nectar from the clusters of various fragrant, blossoming flowers fallen at the foot of trees struck by fierce forest fires, these swarms of bees now fly back toward the peaks and branches; appearing difficult to ascend, they shine like ladders constructed for them by someone else.

And here—on the treetops, which serve as cages for circles of langurs huddled there out of fear of the army, the tails of those animals hanging down like sprouts and new shoots emerging from their bodies create the illusion of swinging ropes for the forest deities’ pleasure swings.
And for this reason as well:

here, the rows of birds, flying up and appearing motionless, shine like lines of banners on the celestial chariots of the hosts of planets, which have become snagged upon the tips of the branches at the crests of the treetops.
And here—

In the mango groves, where clusters of blossoms are unfolding and which display the transformations of all seasons, the flocks of cuckoos are seen as if they were masses of water-bearing clouds gathered in advance by the forest deities to counteract the fierce forest fires.

And here, the ucukunda trees—whose crests are white with clusters of blooming white flowers, whose upper surfaces are as bright as plastered lime, resembling the pleasure-palaces of the flower-arrowed god of love, and appearing like chamberlains of the forest deities with their heads turned grey by age—intensely intoxicate the mind.

Therefore, let Your Majesty sport with his army in these forests where the ground is made fragrant by the showers of thick honey-drops falling from blossoming buds; where the groves of Ashoka trees are made to bloom by the kicks of intoxicated Shabara women who have fled from the fires of forest conflagration; where flocks of peacocks are inferred by their cries perched atop Tamala trees that rival the beauty of a mass of fresh rain-clouds; where the woods are filled with the clamor of wild cocks being trained by the beautiful wives of the languid Pulinda king; where the shores of lakes are surrounded by warbling ospreys; and which are made delightful by the cries of moving Chakoras and Sarasa cranes, while the creepers and sprouts are swayed by the gentle breezes from the waves of the Narmada.
The king, too, having observed those various regions pointed out by Śrutaśīla, reflected: "In these places, the deer have been captivated by does warbling with passion;
the bees wander about; and the trees are most beloved by flocks of cuckoos."
Whose heart would these forest regions not cause to tremble with agitation, as their fragrances perfume the very ends of the quarters with the scent of flowers? And here—
The vast piles of sandalwood forests touch the clouds, fragrant with the scent of *saugandhika* lilies;
the riverbanks, where flocks of peacocks dance and *vīruṇa* reeds blossom,
possess sandy shores lined with rows of cranes and *sārasa* cranes warbling with the intoxication of rut.
Why should one not use the waters of the ocean, which are as white as the pollen of lotuses, as a nasal drop?

Thinking, "It is appropriate to establish our camp here today," he gave orders to his encamped army by means of a signal from the corner of his eye. At that very moment, the clamor of the people led by the commander-in-chief rose up loudly as they issued these commands: "Construct stables for the horses on the low-lying grounds dark with lush, long *dūrvā* grass; build temporary sheds on the sandy banks frequented by rivers; pitch cloth tents in the groves of noble forests; tether the rutting elephants—whose temples are scarred by the rubbing of female elephants—in the thickets of *madaka*, *rāḍu*, *kapōla*, *kāṣa*, *sahēru*, *sarala*, *sāla*, *sallakī*, *sarja*, and *arjuna* trees; clear away far off the masses of moss, stone fragments, wooden logs, and thorny bushes; and level the uneven ground. Unable to endure this uproar, and awaiting an opportunity for it to cease, he withdrew to a secluded spot on the bank of that river and held a council of state upon the surface of a sandy beach, white as fine pearls and powdered shells.

Then, not far ahead of him, in the midst of a flock of ruddy geese moving upon a circle of cool moss, a certain young ruddy goose appeared within the range of his vision. With his wings outspread and his neck upraised, overcome by the god of love, he approached from afar and displayed his skill in amorous flattery toward a passionate female goose. Meanwhile, four other royal swans, also desiring that same female goose, intercepted the approaching youth and repeatedly swooping down, they caused him to falter.
Beholding them, the king smiled and addressed Śrutaśīla, who was standing nearby:
"Friend, look at this inconsistency!
Even though these royal swans have attendants of their own kind suitable to their species, how is it that they desire this female ruddy goose, who is attached to another?"
Truly, this is not a ground for them to be bodiless.
Or rather—
do the lotus-eyed celestial women not exist, that the Lord of the Three Heavens should have pursued Ahalyā, the wife of an ascetic?

While the king was speaking thus—“Who, even a scholar, knows what is appropriate or inappropriate when the fire of love is blazing within the thatched hut of the heart?”—suddenly there arose in the sky the sound of singing belonging to the Gāndhāra scale. It was beautiful with the ornament of its vibration in the hollow of a tender throat, possessing a nature of sweet tones interrupted by intense modulations (*mūrchanā*), made lovely by the clarity of the audible notes (*śruti*) manifested through the application of distinct melodic patterns (*tāna*). Simultaneously, there blew a wind carrying a rain of drops from the nectar of the *pārijāta* flowers, which exhaled an unprecedented fragrance as they were being drunk by swarms of hovering bees.

Then, with his face upturned in curiosity, the king beheld a well-dressed man descending from the sky; he stood before a principal personage who was situated within a halo of golden-yellow radiance like a fragment of refined gold, holding a long staff of pure coral, adorned with earrings, and his head decorated with a garland of blossoming *mandāra* buds.
Having descended, he spoke to the monarch, whose eyes were wide with great astonishment:
"O Lord of Niṣadha, rise quickly and prepare the guest-offering (*argha*)."
Do you not see?

This lord of the gods descends, his hand resting upon the shoulder of Ghṛtācī; lending an ear to the song made pleasant for the senses by the Kinnara, he engages in some embrace with Rambhā while the celestial maidens begin the ritual of fanning him.
Moreover—
these lords,

the world-protectors Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera, have arranged their retinues; they are borne upon the shoulders of celestial elephants ignited by the splendor of their own limbs, and long garlands dangle upon their chests.

Upon hearing this, the king rose up in agitation; the hem of his upper garment was caught as he moved, causing his golden bracelets to jingle with a resonant sound. Placing his two bud-like hands joined in reverence upon his head, his entire body bristling with horripilation from the force of the sudden surge of wonder, he stepped forward a few paces toward him along with his attendants.

Then the blessed Purandara descended from the eastern quarter of the sky, accompanied by the world-protectors. His foot-dust served as a crest-jewel for all the gods; his broad chest bore the scars of wounds from Vṛtra’s weapons, appearing like beautiful ornaments of great sapphires marked with the saffron-paste impressions from the jar-like breasts of many celestial nymphs. Upon the tips of his ears rested fresh clusters of Pārijāta blossoms, from which trickled drops of nectar that resembled the cool spray of Tumburu’s song as he sang directly into his ears—verses so sweet they were like nectar itself—and these drops clung to the contours of his cheeks. The joints of his noble shoulders were covered with pure yellow sandalwood paste, bearing the marks of the betel juice transferred from Śacī’s incessant kisses. Like Andhaka, his chest was struck by a string of pearls; like Mount Vindhya, he possessed a thousand eyes; like the lord of serpents, he wore earrings and shone as if emerging from the netherworld. With the gait of an elephant in rut, he seemed like the flow of the river Sarasvatī descended through the curse of Kali and celebrated in song. Scattering gold dust in every direction, he was tawny-hued like the sun, adorned with an unblemished halo of ruby-red radiance. Thus appeared the divine Indra.

Descending with his thousand eyes, which resembled a forest of blooming lotuses, and beholding this [Indra] prostrate at his feet with eight limbs touching the ground, he playfully raised him up with his right hand—the hand whose fingers were calloused from striking the frontal globes of Airāvata, which served as the primary pillar for bestowing widowhood upon the wives of the most stubborn Daityas and Dānavas, and which bore the lines of saffron paste transferred from its contact with the jar-like breasts of Śacī—and touched him on the crown of his head.

Having exchanged greetings and inquiries after his welfare, he ascended a lofty golden throne, which was dense with a mass of shimmering rays from clusters of jewels, brought to him by the King’s own arm.

When the gods, headed by Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera, had sat down on seats appropriate to their rank, the Lord of Niṣadha, having performed the customary rites in due order, sat down with humility upon the very surface of the earth before him and addressed Purandara:
"By good fortune, O Lord of the dwellers of heaven, has this meeting with you come to pass."
I am the vessel for all that is worthy of praise and for all that leads to the highest good;
moreover,
even those sages who, having observed hundreds of ages and performed austerities, long for the pleasure of union with me.

When that bull among kings had uttered these words of humble inquiry— "Come yourself today and command me, what shall I perform for you who have come to show me favor?"— Purandara, his lower lip illuminated by the luster of teeth as white as slightly opened jasmine buds, smiled gently and, turning his neck with playful grace, looked toward the face of Kuvēra. He too said, "O Lord of Niṣadha, hear the reason for our arrival."

“There is a daughter of Bhīma, the lord of Vidarbha, named Damayantī, also known as Kunda-dantī; she surpasses the blue lotus with her beautiful eyes and eclipses the perfection of the celestial nymphs with her own radiance.

It is said that for her, whose body is as fair as the petals of the campaka flower, the great festival of the *svayaṃvara* has now commenced. Having learned this from Nārada, we too have set out for the city of the lord of Vidarbha.

However, the very act of requesting someone by one's own mouth diminishes that person; for even having gone there, what shall we say to Damayantī? "The world-protectors, Indra and the others, request you"—this is a false display of greatness toward those like us. "You are of a form desirable to all; whom would you not excite with longing?"—this is an inappropriate display of flattery toward strangers. "We gods are indeed ageless"—this is a vulgar beginning of self-praise. "Obtain sovereignty over even the three worlds through union with us"—this is a lure of excessive audacity. "Human beings are short-lived; therefore, choose one among us gods"—this is a most wretched request made under the guise of pointing out another's fault.

"Therefore, you are called one skilled in speech regarding place, time, and action. Go on ahead; be the messenger of the gods, O master of words distinguished by every form of cleverness! What else remains here for you to learn? By various means, by various arts, and by various methods of persuasion, let the work of the gods be accomplished. For the noble, birth and life exist primarily for the sake of benefiting others. And because of our power, no one else shall perceive you as you approach the daughter of the Lord of Vidarbha, even while she is in the secret inner apartments. Having spoken thus, he ceased.

Nala, having heard this, reflected upon this peril according to the maxim: "A tiger here, a precipice there; fire on one side, bandits on the other; a venomous serpent here, and a blind well there. "On one hand, the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva), with his bow drawn to his ear, strikes at my vital organs; on the other, there is this command of theirs which cannot be transgressed. Therefore, I do not know what the answer here should be. To engage in the same matter as both you and I would be a refusal of their affectionate request, a breach of modesty, and an opposition to their words. To say 'I am ignorant of the ways of messengers' would be deceitful; to say 'I am incapable of performing a doubtful task' would be a violation of hope, and a transgression of an order destroys the stream of prosperity like the breaking of a dam. It increases misfortune like seeing the face of a demon, and takes away life like approaching a woman in her menses. Having considered these many points, he said: "Surely no objects are difficult to attain for your honors, who are the lords of the entire world. Nor are you unaware of my well-known resolve. Even so, I shall carry out your command. For one who carries out an order, it is not better to merely reflect upon it; rather, the external mandate is the supreme authority. Having spoken thus, he accepted the mission of the gods as a messenger out of devotion and fear.

Having stayed for a moment in the playful exchange of appropriate conversation and having engaged in certain mutual, pleasant discourses on the subject at hand, those gods took their leave and departed as they had come; then the Lord of Niṣadha reflected for a long time:

"This is death without the cessation of breath, a fainting fit without delusion, the wasting away of the limbs without disease, an internal pain without the piercing of a thorn, and a loss of sleep without poverty."

What else remains for me now that she has heard of my affection, other than this which fate has suddenly made me attempt—a vain resolve born of longing and passion, while I have long been nourishing wicked intentions?
What is best to do here now, since going would be useless, returning would be praiseworthy, staying would be pointless, and further effort would be unproductive?
