While Nala was thus overwhelmed with anxiety and his attendants stood nearby paralyzed by fear, Śrutaśīla approached him somewhat closely; covering the lower part of his face with the edge of his upper garment out of affection, he spoke to Nala word by word with gentle conversation appropriate for that moment.

"O King, I know that the burden of this cruel mission weighs upon Your Majesty like fire consuming wood. Who indeed, even if an ordinary person, would voluntarily accept the state of a servant as a messenger for a desired object—especially when it concerns a woman full of passion? Nevertheless, does Your Majesty not know how the mind suffers great torment: like a beggar, despondency brings no satisfaction; like a physician treating poison, dejection causes doubt for the body; and like the Kuru army held back by Bhīma and Arjuna, the mind experiences intense anguish."
Therefore, enough of this agitation which, like the wandering of a madman, causes the eyes to close in distress.

Has Your Majesty not heard how, at the time of the churning of the nectar, from that ocean of milk—which had its caverns of all the quarters deafened by the roar of the Mandara mountain being whirled by the hands of gods and demons; which scattered the sky with a spray of cool, white milk tossed far and wide; which, through its vast extent, produced many jewels such as the Kaustubha; and whose interior was filled with manifold wonders—the Goddess Lakṣmī, the mother of Smara, arose, creating amazement throughout the world, her auspicious marks shining brilliantly, and holding a fresh lotus in her hand, she who for a moment rivaled the beauty of a cluster of blooming lotuses with the circles of faces of the Apsarases emerging [from the sea].

Having drunk the honey of her entire bodily loveliness with the goblets of their blossoming eyes, those who partook of nectar became overwhelmed by the intoxication of passion; losing control over themselves, they vied with one another to engage in combat with the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).

Then, bypassing all of them as they fell one after another, she quickly cast the garland of self-choice upon the neck of the Blessed One, whose arms were like the touchstone for the gold of Mount Mandara’s peaks, even as he was Vaikuṇṭha himself.

In this way, she too—her limbs as fair as a cluster of campaka buds—being full of passion for you, will surely deceive the gods, since previously the moon was deceived by the splendor of the circle of her face, and the God of Love was surpassed by her beauty. And what need is there for a veil when she has once begun to dance? The deeds of those with beautiful brows are as inconceivable as those of Fate.

Does Your Majesty not remember that long ago, having descended from heaven, the essence of the matter was sung by Gandharva singers in a musical assembly before the Lord, concerning this pair of noble ones?
In any undertaking whatsoever, one who is resolute becomes a vessel for prosperity; however, a man whose manliness is weakened by excessive despondency does not succeed,
even when he sets aside obstacles and pursues his goals.
Even Brahmā fears him, whose daring is unsurpassed.

Thus, as many days passed in the course of narrating the manifold legends of the Ancient Puruṣa, at last the sound of the midday conch arose—seeming to confirm this very purpose for the welfare of that king, who had once again established the pillars of his renewed affection. It was like a gateway to the attainment of his desired ends; like a threatening *huṃkāra* to his obstacles; like the syllable *oṃ* to the recollection of his resolve; and like the cry of "Auspicious Day! (*puṇyāha*) to the palace of his heart’s serenity.
But the king, having dismissed his attendants upon hearing that, performed the activities appropriate for the time of midday right there in the middle of the sandy bank.

After some moments had passed, when the orb of the sun was hanging slightly from the middle of the sky, he—desiring to restore his own mind, which had been whirling like a potter’s wheel set in motion by the tip of a staff or a dry leaf struck by a fierce whirlwind due to that confusion regarding Indra’s command—to find diversion in beholding a certain secluded and lovely region of the Narmadā, surrounded by a few trusted attendants who were favorable to his wishes, left the camp settlement as if it were far behind and proceeded toward the eastern direction along a riverbank. This bank was encircled by groves of young *tāla* trees where peacocks sported; it was made resonant by the warbling of flocks of *cakra* birds and *cakravāka* ducks; its young *dūrvā* grass was trampled by the rows of feet of ascetics who had come for their ablutions; and its sandy shores were rippled by the waves of the flowing flood of water.

And there, upon the grounds of various thickets swarming with flocks of restless bees, there moved women who had emerged from the subterranean realm (Pātāla) like female serpents; their slender bodies were as delicate as young sprouts of the *tāla* and *kandalī* trees, darkened by the ichor of elephants; their gait was languid from the weight of their hips, and their slender waist-vines trembled with three-fold undulations. Some had pearl-strings from elephants hanging from their necks like clusters of buds, appearing like nights of the dark fortnight that had assumed physical forms for sport, adorned with shimmering circles of stars. Others, with the circles of their faces whitened by the luster of ivory ear-ornaments fastened to both ears, resembled the deities of the waters of the Yamunā mingled with the waters of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), invited there by the Narmadā. Others, wearing red shoots as lower garments and girdles of streaks of lightning, appeared like the offspring of moving clouds clinging to the shoulders of the Vindhya mountains. Some, with their forms made terrifying by bees clustering on the circles of elephant-ichor, descended from other reservoirs into the great river like the splendor of all blue lotuses and water-lilies. Others, with ear-ornaments fashioned from clusters of red *aśoka* flowers, resembled the wives of the demons of Tripura whose heads were blackened by smoke and agitated by the flames of Śiva’s fire-arrow, now seeking refuge in the water. Some, followed by graceful, fickle deer, were like the presiding deities of the Añjana mountain-plateaus, eager for immersion in the sacred bathing place (tīrtha). Some walked with a playful grace, supported by the hands of old, decrepit Śabara women; they were like statues carved from flashing sapphire stones being carried about by magicians, possessing the luster of black collyrium flowers. Others, with flat noses and rows of jasmine-white teeth, their variegated braided hair bound with bunches of peacock feathers, were intent on entering the path of vision—intoxicated by drinking the honey of *kādamba* flowers, their eyes rolling, having come for an afternoon bath. These were young Kirāta women, absorbed in the delightful game of rhythmic clapping with their loud-sounding palms.

Then, having enjoyed the pleasure of sporting on the shore—the surface of whose sandy banks was white with fine pearls, where flocks of *kalahaṃsa* geese were drawn by the soft tinkling of anklets produced by the slow movement of human feet, and where deer were made to dance by the waves of their gentle songs—a place abounding in the state of passion (*manaṅga-bhāva*), they subsequently descended into a most enchanting lake of chest-deep, clear water. Its waters flowed swiftly with non-cruel aquatic creatures; it was the very life-breath of the multitude of various blooming lotuses; it resounded with the warbling of *jīvañjīvaka* birds and the cries of *kurara* ospreys; and it was adorned with *hāsi* swans that were intoxicated with joy.

Having descended, they sported for a long time: some like the wives of serpent-lords, with their throats smeared by the venom of raised poisons; some like Rākṣasa women, addicted to the sport of plucking red lotuses; some like cowherd girls, holding lotus-eyed infants; some like the arrows of Kārttikeya, having split apart cranes; some like the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, following the path of the Śakuni birds; some like nights, separated from pairs of cakravāka birds; some like female cakora birds, tasting the water as pure as moonbeams with long lotus stalks held in their beaks; some like female elephants, swallowing living creatures from the lakes; some like mechanical dolls, emitting fine streams of water from the openings at the tips of their joined hands and palms; and some like noble ladies, playing in the water that was fragrant with the scent of young lotuses and whose waves leaped up upon striking the mountain peaks of their breasts.
The lord of the earth, his blinking forgotten due to astonishment, gazed for a long time with unblinking eyes and reflected:
"Where there is no noble birth, there the arrangement of beauty cannot initiate a festival for the eyes;
and where there is the splendor of beauty, there a praiseworthy origin is not easily found."

"O Father Dhātṛ, let this process of creation be consumed by fire for you, who have exerted yourself in vain by practicing a hatred toward all these beautiful qualities gathered together in one place;
for it is thus:"

With lotus-stalk tendrils draped over their necks, with fresh, blooming petals of blue lotuses worn as ear-ornaments so that they seem to possess two eyes, and with waves of their bosoms bent by the weight of their breasts—
who are these, like water-deities, whose very ripples are curved by the fullness of their chests?
The wives of the Pulinda king, intent on bathing, do not even turn their minds away [from her];
moreover—
on the surface of the expanse of her breasts, which resemble the frontal globes of an elephant, [the bees] cling...
O Lordly Elephant within the Cave of the Mouth, this wave, having approached from afar and fallen with speed upon this row of pearl-strings captivating the mind, has dissolved; how so?
Or who else would not dissolve upon union with a passionate woman?

But this woman— mistaking the bee for her own beloved’s face, she kissed its lotus-like form while it was rejoicing; yet, her lower lip being bitten by the bee, she softly uttered a sigh of pain (*sītkāra*).
By her as well—
who, by her own will, incessantly splashes this water with both hands raised high and lovely like blooming lotuses—
As if half of her were apportioned to guests arriving at their own will,
and as if water were bestowed for the sake of the pleasure of childhood play—
of her, moreover:
In the region of the root of her ear, this young bee, though struck gently by her sprout-like hand, forcibly kisses her lotus-face as if she were his beloved; and now she too—
Seeing the crocodile, which causes confusion and intoxicates Makarandini, tossing about the lotus-pond made turbid by its own filth, he crossed the river with rapid strides out of great fear;
and these were they:

"This day is languid; even Love is ready. O travelers, why do you not go home?"—as if addressed by the lotus plants with the sounds of bees emerging from the closing blossoms, the great trees slowly descend the bank after bathing.

While the King—his heart agitated simultaneously by a thrill of joy at the sight of the Śabara beauties who were intent on various amorous sports, by the arising of manifold reflections, and by a slight pangs of love born at that moment due to his steady gaze fixed upon the motionless body of an old female elephant submerged in the mud; while he was thus possessed of a state of conflicting emotions—he, Śrutaśīla, having enjoyed for a very long time the pleasure of sporting in the waters of that Narmadā pool which was adorned with clusters of lotuses, reflected as those Śabara princesses graced the white sandy banks upon the shore.

"This youth of the Śabara women is intoxicating; the Lord is imperishable, possessed of fresh vigor and lovely splendor; the bank of the Revā is captivating with its dancing cakoras and peacocks; and the hope of the God of Love is triumphant—I do not know what it all portends—for thus it is:

tathā hi— The forest is filled with the fragrance of the *mallikā* flowers, while the mountain slopes are adorned with the beauty of the *candana* trees; the river flows with the sound of waterfalls, and the sky is graced by the presence of the moon. Indeed, this place is a veritable paradise on earth."
It confounds the one skilled in the arts, mocks the pure, ridicules the wise,
and humbles the steadfast man. In an instant, even the god Makaradhvaja [is overcome]—
and furthermore:

"The demon of passion truly deceives a man at the slightest stumble in the midst of the three folds [of the waist], the triple path [of the navel], and the courtyard of the full breasts of those with tremulous eyes.
Let that be so; for the minds of masters are turned back by conciliation suited to the occasion, not by hostility toward the practice of what is forbidden," he said to the king, reflecting thus.
"O King, this region is indeed delightful;
for here—
soft breezes gladden [the senses], scattering gentle drops of nectar trickling from crushed lotuses."
These are the Kirāta women, O King of Mountains; these are the rivers whose splendor is shattered by your collision;
and these are the breezes—here on the riverbanks, the Pulinda women, whose swelling breasts surpass the frontal globes of elephants.
With their hair-knots loosened and moist with water, they bear an indescribable power of the god of love; let Your Majesty observe them from here—
these women, with eyes closed in the pleasure of hearing the songs of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of lotus nectar.
Even here, the deer dwell upon the sandy banks for the remainder of the day with motionless limbs, deprived of both recreation and food; moreover,
the lotuses serve as sunshades and the lily petals as couches.
Even their longing for the swinging of cradles is fulfilled by the mass of surging waves;
poison-tipped sprouts serve as their food; and the sandy banks, the playgrounds for their playful pastimes, exist in the waters of the Revā—there the blessed young royal swans dwell in happiness.
And here too—

the royal swan, desiring dalliance, delights the female swan with the offering of a playful morsel from the tip of the first sprout of nectar, appearing like a crescent moon after long-composed flatteries; and he makes her's body thrill with horripilation by scratching her with the tip of his beak.
Moreover:
here the cakora bird frequents the buds of the lotuses; here the cakravāka bird, with its circle of trembling bees, is afraid;
here the jīvañjīvaka delights his mate, the mistress of his life; and even the lovely hārītaka tree here bears a transformation [of blossoms].
Thus the Lord of Niṣadha, having his intense desire to see Śabarī’s beauty diverted by Śrutaśīla under the pretext of showing him other regions of great beauty, returned home with full deliberation.
And he thought:

"How indeed can I, born of human stock, obtain that Damayantī from among the world-protectors headed by Purandara, who possess such great power? Moreover, her kinsmen, seeking a divine alliance, will surely prevent her. Thus the king thought repeatedly, letting out long, heavy sighs. "O King, a lotus-like person, once restrained, flows all the more intensely. For one who is deeply attached, neither long-standing aversion arises nor does false resolve diminish. Furthermore, there is another point: even in women who belong to another, a grasp of passion for someone else occurs. Behold! Even this western quarter, though she has accepted Varuṇa as her husband, will become passionate toward me. Comforting him, as it were, with these words, the blessed Sun descended slowly from the expanse of the sky like a flame, his rays clinging to the peaks of lofty trees as if out of fear of falling, and departed toward the western direction.
When the Lord of the life of the western lotus-pond— the passionate one who has extended his hand to the edge of the sky— is united with the western quarter, which is red like a woman in love;
how is it that this same passionate one has now gone to set in that wretched eastern direction, abandoning me whom he repeatedly honored by rising in my presence during the forenoon?
Thus, when the sun, its rays slackened, had departed toward the western quarter,
the eastern direction appeared as if distressed by envy, anger, and despair due to the darkness,
while it was made to cry out with the piteous wailing of pairs of cakravāka birds agitated by their separation.

When the sun, the friend of the day-lotuses, had departed, the quarters of the sky, like women with faces turning dark on all sides as if out of grief for him who was closing his eyes out of compassion for the lotuses,
vomited forth masses of darkness like columns of smoke from the fire of their sighs.
And at such a juncture of the hour, a pair of charming *kinnaras* sporting nearby sang this to announce the time for the king’s twilight rites:
“Is this skull, stained red and held downward,
being marked with the seal of stars by the Kāpālika of Time?”
"Is this the saffron-colored oyster-shell of the twilight-bride rolling about?"— thus creating doubt, the sun’s orb half-submerged in the ocean prevails.

Then, in due course, as the clusters of stars began to appear faintly—like bubbles on the drops of water offered in the twilight *añjali* by the ascetics on the banks of the celestial Ganges; as the celestial abodes sounded their instruments to mark the day’s end; as slender creepers of darkness wandered through the sky like garlands of thick incense-smoke being burnt; as the forest ranges seemed to offer a welcome to the weary travelers seeking shelter with the clamor of flocks of sleeping birds; as the restless bees began to sip nectar from the lotus buds as if to avoid wandering elsewhere; as the twilight lamps were lit—resembling the great mantra-syllables for the onset of passion in the erotic festivities, resonating with the "kuhu-kuhu" calls of water-fowls nestled in the nests of great trees; and as the twilight glow, pale as the plumage of a brood of old potter’s cocks, turned slightly toward the west—the King, having forgotten his twilight rites in his despondency, performed his salutation to the twilight only because of the insistence of his attendants.
And then, in due course—
the lord of the earth, at the conclusion of his evening rites, having performed service to the pair of lotus-feet of Hara,
passed that night in that place, delighting in the pleasure of listening to songs primarily in the fifth note (*pañcama*) played softly on the lute (*vipañcī*).
Thus ends the fifth canto in the *Damayantī-kathā* composed by the illustrious Trivikramabhaṭṭa, titled *Haracaraṇasarojāṅkā*;
[now begins] the sixth canto.

Then, as the sky—thick with darkness—attained a slight purity as if being washed by the waters of the twilight joined in *añjali* by the multitude of twice-born men; as the stars were gathered in like a florist by the breaking dawn, appearing as if they were flowers from the garden of the firmament; and as the sound of the drum of the morning light arose like a "hum" that dispels sleep, a bard recited near the king for the purpose of awakening him:
"While the pale glow of the eastern light has reached the mountain of sunrise and follows the peak of the western mountain, the night departs."
Victorious is that indescribable splendor now in the midst of the sky, like the waters of the Ganges and Yamunā mingled together;
and as the veil of darkness has departed, the dawn of Aruṇa rises toward the western mountain.
May that indescribable [form]— white and tawny,

yet dark as well, appearing between the two directions like Viṣṇu and Brahmā within the splendor of a *tāpiccha* leaf and a ruby, creating the slight illusion of a single emerging Liṅga— protect you all.

Immediately upon rising, he issued these commands: "Bring forth elephants and horses with the speed of the wind! Yoke the wagons! Prepare the tents! Fold up the pavilions! Roll up the curtains! Uproot the stakes! Swiftly carry away the goods to be transported! Load the young camels and colts! Drive out the exhausted oxen! Cross the river! Move forward! Clear a path fit for passage! While this clamor of the people, busy with various preparations for the march, rose up and the instruments of departure sounded, the king arose; and at the conclusion of his necessary ablutions, having purified his body with a sprinkling of the waters of the Narmadā and performed his morning rites, he addressed the blessed Sun as he occupied the peak of the Eastern Mountain and recited this verse:
"Victorious is the kinsman of the lotus, whose rays are as crimson as the *bandhūka* flower; like a coral jar at the dawn of day, he is as if adorned with sprouts.

Having thus worshipped the Teacher of gods and demons, the Lord of Gaurī, with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), he offered a hymn of praise to the Blessed Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of that [Lord Śiva], for the attainment of his desired goal.
Victorious is he who was gazed upon by the clearly manifest side-long glances of Lakṣmī— tremulous with passion as she emerged from the ocean—
and whose golden armlet was rubbed by the friction of Mandara’s whirling at a speed no less than that of Mount Mandara itself.
Victorious is Hari, the first stage-director of the drama of the slaying of the enemies of the gods,
whose chest is resplendent with the luster of the stainless Kaustubha gem, who strikes down the Dānavas with playful ease, and who possesses the dark blue hue of a fresh Tamāla tree.
Victorious is Hari, whose footstool is moistened by droplets of honey scattered from the rows of blossoming flowers fallen from the heads of the bowing gods,
and who recites the hymns of praise upon the lotus-throne emerging from his own belly.
Hari, who performs beautiful hymns of praise with the rows of mouths from his four faces; who has no limit to his attained majesty; who brings an end to the amorous dalliances of the wives of Madhu;
who is the source of the three worlds; and who removes the fear of worldly existence.
Victorious is He whose splendor is increased by the tears from the eyes of the beautiful wives of the asuras, whose radiant form possesses the luster of a peacock’s neck,
and who wears a yellow garment like the petals of a blossoming kanaka-ketaki flower.
Victorious is Hari, the Lord of all the worlds, saluted by the lords of the gods;
he who is the conqueror of all worlds, the uprooter of the banner of Death that is hell,
and the fierce lion to the ten-headed Rāvaṇa who was like an elephant blinded by intoxication.

Victorious is Hari, who is the rising moon to the lotus-face of his beloved whose thighs are like golden cushions; who is the axe to the head of the son of Siṃhikā, the enemy of the lord of the gods; who is the charioteer of the immortals; and who bears upon his shoulders the weight of the splendor of the pride of the god of love.

Hari, whose expansive virtues are inconceivable, who steals away the beauty of the tilaka-mark shining upon the cheek-slabs of all the wives of Keśin and Kaṃsa, and who bears a fresh smear of sandalwood paste upon the surface of his pair of breasts.
Victory to Him who performs peerless heroic deeds, who brings an end to the sorrow of all the world, whose beautiful discus-weapon flashes with the brilliance of a thousand suns,
who has the lord of birds as His vehicle, and who utterly uproots the root of all impurity.
Victorious is Hari, the architect who fashioned the abodes for the entire series of worlds, the wish-fulfilling tree for the people bowed down by pure devotion,
and the crest-jewel of the hosts of gods led by Indra.
Hari is the forest fire that destroys the grove of the lotuses which are the families of his enemies; he is the preeminent royal swan for the minds of all the sages.

Having thus paid homage to the God of gods, he mounted the back of a victorious lordly elephant. With his retinue of many elephants, horses, and attendants running ahead, he crossed the divine Mekalakanyā (Narmadā), who had her great river-sacrifice performed by a family priest before him; she was the witness to the events of thousands of revolving Yugas; whose banks were occupied by Śiva-liṅgas installed by Brahmarṣis engaged in incessant penance; whose secret bowers of creepers on her shores were frequented by many celestial beauties; whose waves were made exceedingly fragrant by the ichor of wild elephants constantly bathing therein; she was like another Gaṅgā, the queen of another ocean-king, the companion of Mārkaṇḍ

Having spent the remainder of the day with various long-standing occupations, and having passed that night as well, she set out once more in her former manner when the Lord of Day, having somewhat purified the quarters of the sky—which were soiled by the stain of darkness born of his own separation—had touched them with rays tawny with saffron-paste, while the stars, shaken by the winds from the flapping wings of the birds rising at dawn, were being swept away like heaps of pale flowers used for decorating the courtyard of the firmament.

Thus, avoiding paths that were overgrown with wild rice, crossing waters echoing with the cries of cranes, traversing harsh mountain peaks that covered the quarters of the sky along with the dust raised by herds of deer, honoring the ascetics in village hamlets nestled within mountain thickets where water was scarce, he once, at a riverbank not very far away—where the waters were colored by the pollen of lotus clusters kissed by flocks of longing *kādamba* swans, and where a weary traveler sat beneath a tree—beheld a certain wayfarer singing this beautiful pair of verses, whose syllables were made resonant by waves of most sweet melody.
Having enjoyed the fruit of your friendship, it produces amorous play for women whose bodies are red with saffron;
and that mass [of hair], adorned with a girdle, takes its place there.

O King, look! Out of fear of you, O one who has surpassed the God of Love with his beauty, people in the forests conceal themselves among the female monkeys, even though saffron— the very enemy of women— is producing passion in them.
"This restless tree-dweller has been driven from the mountain slope; he remembers the female red monkeys.

While the King was thus reflecting—"Aha! This must be some clever young traveler, whose sprouts of wisdom have blossomed through contact with the nectar of extensive scriptural refinement, and who is truly fit for conversation in the art of poetic wit"—the traveler rose up in haste, stood before him, and with a respectful salutation recited this verse: "The Creator is not tainted by his own knowledge, and Govinda holds the mace."
O God, to whom can Śambhu, Śalinī, and Viṣādī be compared?

The king, having heard that, his mind simultaneously flooded with the sentiments of astonishment at the planet’s obstruction, joy, and wonder, first honored him with a wide-eyed gaze, then with a charming smile, and finally by bestowing ornaments upon all his limbs; then he asked affectionately: “O traveler, tell me—what river is this, which, rising high like a surging wave, seems to lift to heaven the swans on its banks who, holding rosaries and chanting the Vedic sacrifice, scatter soft lotus-fiber bracelets from their upturned beaks as if they were ascetics? And who are you, adorning the base of a young tree, accompanied by the serene Sarasvatī?”

He too said, "Is this some unknown great river of the King’s, resembling a bamboo stalk from the *kūlaka* reed-beds and filled with bees, unsuitable for landing a boat? Having spoken thus, he began to tell a story: "This is the river Tāpī, the daughter of Bhānu and wife of Saṃvaraṇa, the destroyer of sins, whose son was Kuru, after whom they call the land Kurukṣetra."
At the time of her immersion in the water, the waves are constantly ground by the friction against the dense, elevated, and rough slopes of the breasts of men;
for a moment, they appear as if possessed of faces with rolling eyes resembling wandering bees.
The Mahārāṣṭrikas mistake it for a forest of blooming lotuses;
moreover,
if even once the row of her lotuses is made to dance by the wind—
The people dwelling on the riverbanks drink water that is as cooling as frost, fanned by swaying leaf-fans,
and scented by the flowers of the trees; yet they long for nectar— what is there that the world does not desire?
May Your Majesty also know me as the messenger named Puṣkarākṣa;
for indeed—
standing at the window facing the path of your arrival...
I have been sent here by that long-eyed lady, the sovereign of the Niṣadhas, to obtain special news;
for you are the pleasure-mountain of her, whose mind is as charming as that of a young cuckoo.
"And tomorrow, on the morrow, you will find stationed on the banks of the Payoṣṇī—not very far from here, weary from the road—her trusted messenger, a pair of playful Kinnaras sent by her.
And this birch-bark leaf, containing characters written with her own sprout-like hand, must be delivered to her. Having said this, she placed the letter-leaf before him.
The king also, having had her brought forward by his attendants, himself untied the letter with his hand—whose forearm was bristling with dense sprouts of horripilation—and read it with respect:
“O Nala, you are not fire (analas) toward me; therefore, O Prince of Niṣadha, this is not the conduct of those like you.
Likewise, it is not right for women to seize the mind—which is already sealed by the mind—of one such as Nala.”
Moreover—

it is said that fate indeed falls upon the weak; for by that very reason, it is not so with the powerful, since the mind-born god, though he has drawn his bow, does not prevail over those who are strong.
Moreover—
when indeed will the grounds of the Kuṇḍina garden become adorned by your feet, which resemble full-blown land-lotuses?

Thus, his heart drenched by the flood of the nectar-like essence of the affectionate and well-spoken words written in that letter, the king—pondering, "O Fate, grant me a pair of wings like those of a bird so that I may fly and behold her"—embraced that messenger of his beloved with a thrill of horripilation as if he were the man himself; he drank him in with eyes parched by longing, bathed him as it were with the nectar-essence of his sweet smile, and addressed him again and again with great respect.

"O Puṣkarākṣa, that princess is victorious in every respect, whose youth and speech are both tender and adorned with many ornaments, embraced by a noble and radiant luster, and whose attendants are as humble, eloquent, discerning, and clever-minded as yourself. Therefore, tell me—she whose fame is to be celebrated, how does she fare? How does she dwell? What diversion does she pursue? With what occupation does she pass her days, O daughter of my lord? Thus addressed, Nala spoke again, causing the sprout of his passion to blossom: [The rest of the passage follows: "...She is like a lotus-stalk, a vessel for the water of the ocean of beauty; she is like a moon, a source of delight to the eyes of the world; she is like a spring, the abode of the fragrance of youth; she is like a night, the consort of the moon of her own face; she is like a river, the flow of the stream of grace; she is like a garden, the dwelling place of the flower of charm; she is like a lute, the repository of the melody of speech; she is like a painting, the canvas for the colors of loveliness; she is like a poem, the essence of the sentiment of love; she is like a dream, the vision of celestial bliss; she is like a pearl, the fruit of the ocean of merit; she is like a star, the radiance of the sky of her lineage; she is like a song, the embodiment of the joy of the heart; she is like a dance, the movement of the grace of the gods; she is like a sacrifice, the fulfillment of all desires; she is like a festival, the occasion for the celebration of the world; she is like a jewel, the treasure of the earth; she is like a goddess, the manifestation of divine power; she is like a sage, the possessor of inner tranquility; she is like a hero, the conqueror of the senses; she is like a poet, the creator of the world of poetry; she is like a philosopher, the knower of the truth of existence;
