and touches with his dust-covered trunk the moving, slightly curved line of her temple;
or rather, in the consideration of conduct preceded by discernment, these [beings] differ only slightly from humans.

For it is thus heard: in ancient times, indeed, as the Grandfather (Brahmā) lay within the hollow of the lotus-navel of Nārāyaṇa, chanting the Vedic lore and singing the Sāman hymns known as Bṛhat, Rathantara, Vikīrṇa, and Bhāsas, there arose from the flow of those Sāman-stobhas eight great lords of the elephants of the quarters, beginning with Airāvata, Supratīka, Kumuda, Vāmana, Añjana, and so forth.
From them were born the elephants belonging to the Bhadra, Mandra, Mṛga, and Saṃkīrṇa breeds, who roam the mountains, the rivers, and both terrains alike.
And this is well known: "elephants are born from Sāmajā.
However, some relate it otherwise:

it is said that Airāvata was born from the Ocean of Milk when it was churned by Mount Mandara, which was being held in the trunks of all the gods and demons; he was the source of wonder for the world, born together with Lakṣmī, the Moon, Surabhī, the celestial tree, Dhanvantari, the Kaustubha gem, and Uccaiḥśravas, possessing the luster of the moonbeams. And this daughter of his is the one who adorns all the forests.
Therefore, he shall be of noble breed;
for thus it is:
his trunk is lofty, his teeth are tawny, and the joints of his shoulders are well-proportioned.
This noble lord of elephants, whose jewel-like nails possess a glossy copper luster, whose long and rounded trunk is like a lotus stalk,
and whose ichor rivals the fragrance of the seven-leaved *saptacchada* tree,
roams along the banks of mountain rivers amidst dense forests.

"Let this interruption of the pleasure of sport for a loving couple not be for their ultimate good," he said; and with his heart stolen away, his hair standing on end at the dalliance of the wild deer sporting at will, trembling at the breezes from the flowering groves, entertained by the cries of *pheṭṭikila* birds fluttering among the trees on the banks of the falling waterfalls, and by the excellent sayings of the attendants moving nearby—both simultaneously and individually—he crossed the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, which were both low and high, uneven with rocks and yet not uneven with rocks, filled with beasts of prey and yet devoid of beasts of prey, possessing trees and yet treeless. Then, reflecting upon the various descriptions of forest regions offered by Puṣkarākṣa—who pointed out: "O King, behold here the swamps thick with venomous serpents and dense thickets; here the forests where the king's commands are enforced and the throngs of hunters and Pulindas; here the many happy pairs of Śabaras and the jewel-mining sites; here the most delicious fruits and the bamboo groves; here the riverbanks where the earth is perfumed by the ichor of elephants and the flowers; and here the forest lands scorched by fire yet blessed with great power and the circles of sages"—he gradually traversed the succession of mountain peaks and, with his enemies subdued, descended upon the Sahya mountain.
Turning his face again toward the slopes of the southern ridges of the Vindhya range, which were lovely and lush, he gazed at them and addressed Puṣkarākṣa:
"My good man, these trees on the slopes of the Vindhya are indeed difficult to leave behind.
For instance—"

The dwellings of the flower-armed god (Kāma), where the Śabara women hold their secret trysts, where travelers are obstructed by the humming of female bees clustering around the fragrance of blossoms— these delightful abodes,
like dear kinsmen, have long since departed from my sight.
Why do these trees of the Vindhya mountain not burn his heart?
Moreover—
in those [trees] whose flowers are bent low by the weight of wandering bees and which exude the fragrance of trickling honey...

May those trees rejoice, may they bear fruit, and may they attain supreme exaltation— those trees whose fruits satisfy the multitudes of travelers who, having rested in their shade as if in homes, quench their thirst with the water of their falling cascades.
Moreover:
Where trees do not bear fruit, nor lakes with blooming lotuses, nor virtuous people— let that land go to its destruction, for it is equal to a cremation ground.
Therefore, tell us: when shall we behold again this path through the Vindhya forest, with its *lakucha* trees of variegated leaves, as faultlessly as we did Damayantī?
For it is thus:
[it possesses] the beauty of a slender waist bent by the weight of full, swelling, firm breasts, like a *mallalavī* creeper.
I am filled with longing, my voice faltering and trembling, for that beloved forest path on the mountain slopes; moreover— having beheld the beauty of peak after peak and the ridges of the mountains.

"O friend, when shall we wander here with you in every *sāla* grove, like those weary of the world? Tell me, how far away still is that Vidarbha country, where the city of Kuṇḍina is adorned by her—a pearl-like sphere released from within the shell-casket of the universe? When the Lord of Niṣadha had spoken thus, following his words with various conversations, Puṣkarākṣa also replied:
"O King, have we not indeed arrived?"
For this is that very land called Varadātata, the great Maharashtra of heroic men;
there flows the river Vidarbha, which is the Southern Sarasvatī.

Here the subjects are like those of the island of Siṃhala in their lack of fear of taxes; they are equal to a generous person in their great compassion; and they are similar to a water-jar buried in the earth for the deposit of a wretched man in their adherence to modest prosperity.

Here the lotus groves and the circle of kings and nobles alike possess abundant nectar; here the cities and the heart of the world both possess much splendor; here the blades of the sword and the viewing of the ten types of dramatic performance both possess vigor; here the minds of the people and the strength of the protector of the subjects both possess great compassion; and here the villages, towns, and cities and the sheepfold both possess many Brahmins.
And this land of the Brahmin agrahāra, situated in the constellation of Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttara-phalgunī as if it were a path through the sky, is supplied with breezes;
and from here—
[one sees] these peaks resembling mountains rising high in the midst of the village, belonging to the Bhāruyas.
With their arms placed upon one another's shoulders, gathered together out of curiosity,
their gazes motionless due to the intensity of their observation, and their bodies held in restraint as they gaze upon you, these women of the common folk bear the grace of a painted tableau.
Moreover:
O King, just as you move in this place, so too do the faces of the village women,
with their tremulous eyes, move like lotuses stirred by the wind.
Moreover—

upon their high, swelling breasts, from which the garments have slipped due to the heaving of their chests and which are panting intensely from their impetuousness, the strings of guñjā berries are rolling about.
Among these female deer in their state of heat, you appear like a transference of the entire universe;
yet Hari, having assumed forms of irresistible charm, seems as if he would not embrace the cowherd girls.
Oh, how truly wonderful it is! The youthful beauty of these young women intoxicates the minds of youths, even though their adornment is so utterly indifferent to such finery.
For instance: garlands of *karṇikāra* buds upon the head, fragrant pastes and sandalwood, strings of pearls around the neck, and bracelets made of glass and lac.
With turmeric on their limbs, intensely thick collyrium in their eyes,
and such a tasteless attire— nevertheless, vulgar women captivate the heart.

The vegetable gardens are filled with various sprouting shoots: rough *karkaṭikā* gourds, large *kāliṅga* cucumbers, and *kr̥ṣmāṇḍa* melons adorning the pavilions; well-rounded round gourds; *hastikarṇa*, *punarnavā*, and thick-rooted *piṇḍitapalāṇḍu* onions; the ground is covered with *vāstūka* greens; *jīvantikā* herbs have been restored to life; rows of mustard and *rājikā* seeds shine forth; and various vegetables have sprouted from the banks of the flowing river and the water-channels, including *sārivā* and *arisēcana*.
And here—

These gardens—the abodes of the flower-armed god—are filled with blooming *mucukunda* trees, joyful *sinduvāra* trees dripping with beautiful nectar, groves of *ketakī* that serve as the meeting places for common folk, lovely *āmrātaka* trees, *kaṅkola* fruits budding forth, *kuraṇṭaka* flowers in bud, creepers of *vallī* putting forth shoots, *mallikā* jasmine shining in full bloom, well-formed *jāti* flowers, variegated *śatapattra* lilies, and thickets of pale, clustered *aguru* and *karavīra* vines; they display the blossoms of every season.
And here, not far to the south, let Your Majesty cast your gaze.

These very things are seen before us: the fully ripened grains of rice, the sweet and long stalks of sugarcane, the circles of cows with plump limbs grazing on the green grassy plots at the edge of the embankments, and the lakes whose waters shine like the sky free from clouds.
The lands of the grain-fields, with their diverse flocks of birds perching on the tips of the stalks,
and moreover— this city of Kuṇḍina, which reflects the beauty of heaven, and this river Vidarbhā;
This is that very Varadā, and this is that confluence of these two holy waters;
let the army encamp on its bank, which steals away the pride of swans,
where the trees are capable of enduring the sport of being rubbed against the temples of intoxicated lordly elephants.

While the lotus-eyed Lord was thus extending his playful sport under the pretext of revealing various sights worthy of being seen, the Lord of Niṣadha, his heart swelling with joy at the thought, "We have reached the city of Kuṇḍina," spoke these words with supreme satisfaction, preceded by the granting of rewards.

"O noble one, for us whose minds have been captivated by your words—which are woven with tenderness, sweetness, honeyed confidence, and full of graceful puns—it seems as though we have felt no fatigue; it seems as though we have not perceived the distinction between the level and the uneven ground; it seems as though not even a drop of sweat has been produced. Although the great road, which was like a pleasure grove, remains with only half a *gavyūti* left to traverse, it has already passed away. Furthermore, this region of the forest near the confluence of rivers is perfectly suited for the encampment of an army. For here let the soldiers dwell; here too there is grass sufficient for the horses to graze upon, who are restless from their exertion."
Indeed, let the lordly elephants here satisfy their itching temples by devouring the shoots within this grove of trees;
for these grounds on the lap of the confluence of rivers are worthy of being our seat, owing to their extreme loveliness.
To explain further:

“Whom do the beauties of these sandbanks not thrill?—sandbanks where the waters have receded, rippling over the shores; where peacocks dance within bowers of *nicula* reeds; and which are frequented by ospreys and swans.

Having spoken thus, he commanded his general: “My good man, encamp the army in such a way that there is no mutual conflict, that the sacred fords and shrines remain undisturbed, that the nearby gardens are not plundered, that the sacred trees are not cut down, and that the lotus groves are not destroyed.”
He too, acting according to what was instructed, spoke thus:

"O hosts of troops, frequent the patches of durva grass near the ponds, where the plumage of old parrots is worn away; there, amidst the flowering creepers swaying gently in the fragrant breeze, you shall find honey."
Moreover—

O lotus grove, do not, out of pride, destroy that forest bower on the bank which serves as a pleasure-ground for the God of Love and a drinking-hall for the bees; for there, following their dalliance in you, the royal swans remain engaged in various amorous diversions.
Moreover:
Let the soldiers not make their camp in the abode of the gods, nor commit plunder at the confluence of the hermitages on the river;
for here lies the hope of the King of Niṣadha—he who, wherever he may be, brings about the exhaustion and the destruction of that certain, formidable tree-king in yonder world.

While Bāhuka was thus commanding his numerous forces in many ways, there suddenly arose a camp encampment, as delightful as a moving city of the Gandharvas, adorned with swinging banners and fluttering silk pennants on its lofty pavilions and mechanical watch-towers. With its green arched gateways, it seemed composed of flocks of soaring parrots; with its tents pitched upon beds of red chalk, it seemed made of blossoming *kiṃśuka* flowers; and with its white silken canopies, it seemed filled with dancing clusters of great white lotuses. As the dust clouds from the vast army gradually overspread all the quarters of the horizon—like messengers dispatched from the capital of Vidarbha to announce the arrival of the Lord of Niṣadha—the deep thunder of fresh rain-clouds, harsh to the ears of rival kings, resounded along with the shrill blast of conchs and the clanging of battle-axes for the march. While the rows of bards and panegyrists, accompanied by joyful throngs of gods and men, loudly chanted the name of Nala as a "thorn" to the ears of the entire circle of assembled monarchs who had come to the *svayaṃvara*, the King sat comfortably upon a couch of choice Vaidūrya stone with soft, smooth coverings supported by pillars of refined gold. When the attendants were well-settled and Kuṇḍina was not far away, the voice of the police officer rose up loudly.
"Let the royal highways be sprinkled with showers of sandalwood water trickling from the mouths of jars;
let the pillars be adorned with fluttering banners and the archways decorated with clusters of flowers;
and let full vases filled with grain be placed in every city house within the courtyards."
King Nala of Niṣadha drew svastikas with white mustard seeds;
moreover,
this one has arrived— bearing beautiful girdles, sandalwood paste, and pearl necklaces released from the pair of her jar-like breasts.

Let the women go forth, performing wondrous deeds, carrying vessels filled with *dūrvā* grass, parched grain, and white mustard seeds mixed with flowers; adorned with ear-ornaments, holding swan-feather fans, umbrellas, and garments, they chant songs that are melodious with the sound of musical instruments.
Moreover:

May the women of the city finally have their purpose fulfilled; let the Lord who restrains our eyes come within the range of your vision—he who has surely descended from the heavenly realm, the very embodiment of Love (Anaṅga), having obtained grace through the pair of lotus-feet of Śiva.

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Damayantī-kathā*, titled *Haracaraṇasarojāṅkā*, composed by Śrī Trivikrama Bhaṭṭa. The seventh chapter begins: While the King sat in his assembly hall, hearing the clamor of the city’s circle of matrons being driven before him by the staff-bearer—who raised his voice in a loud, undisturbed tone—the aged chamberlain entered. He was dressed in full regalia, his chest struck by the thick golden chains hanging from his neck as he bowed low in prostration. With humility, he spoke: [End of Seventh Chapter]

"Your Majesty, the Brāhmaṇas and the matrons of Kuṇḍinapura, wearing festive attire and bearing golden vessels filled with flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice, stand before you reciting sacred texts. They wait for the opportunity to enter the gate in their desire for a sight of Your Majesty.
And they say this: 'The Lord of Vidarbha also approaches to see Your Majesty;

he is heard to be near, like one possessed by love, and at the outskirts of Vidarbha there is a tumultuous clamor from crowds of bards chanting auspicious songs, accompanied by the sound of conch shells.'"

When he had stood there after saying, "Therefore, let Your Majesty command what is to be done," Nala commanded the doorkeeper: "O Bhadrabhūti, quickly admit the retinue of the Lord of Vidarbha; you yourself follow half the way.
He too, having replied, "As Your Majesty commands," did exactly as instructed.

Immediately thereafter, not long after that, King Bhīma was seen not far from the courtyard, his ear-lotuses dancing in the breeze from the clusters of beautiful, waving chowries; appearing as if leaping along the path upon his restless horse with the rhythmic movements of his graceful galloping, bounding, and leaping; obscuring the expanse of the sky with peacock-feather umbrellas whose golden finials shone like flashes of lightning amidst a mass of clouds suddenly bursting forth; followed on all sides by foot-soldiers moving swiftly, their necks marked by the calluses of wielding weapons, their hard forearms adorned with swinging iron bracelets, their heads formidable with matted locks tied upward, wearing lower garments of red cloth, and carrying sharpened spears in their hands; while his ears were delighted by the sound of flutes being played by musicians, accompanied by the gentle resonance of drums and the soft clanging of cymbals. Thus, the king, whose body was fair as the *karṇikāra* flower, became visible.

Then, leaning upon the sprout-like hand of his fly-whisk bearer, the Lord of Niṣadha rose with ease and advanced a few steps toward him, surrounded by a circle of vassal kings who had risen first in a state of agitation; their chests heaved as they moved forward, they held garlands of flowers, and they were enveloped in the cloud of fragrant camphor, saffron, and musk spreading from them, as well as the dust of aromatic powders falling in haste.
He, for his part, dismounted from the back of his horse even from afar, stepping down onto the shoulder of a man who was hastening toward him carrying a betel-box.

Thus, with their faces lit by smiles as their eyes met, their heads slightly bowed at the same moment, and their arms extended simultaneously, they embraced each other impetuously. Under the guise of the stream of pearls falling from the necklaces shattered by the force of the embrace, they seemed to pour forth a flood of droplets from the first nectar of love overflowing within them. And in such a union, there spread among the spectators a great festival for the eyes and a tumultuous roar of joy, like the meeting of the two guardians of the southern and northern quarters, Dharmarāja and Dhanada.

Thereafter, they both occupied two high golden thrones brought forward by a running usher, which were made beautiful by supports in the form of pillars charming with the figures of Kāṇṭikā women in various triple-bent poses; which shone with strings of pearls released from the mouths of makaras carved in rubies that were expanding; and which were adorned with the faces of auspicious wild beasts fashioned by unprecedented craftsmanship.
When their exchange of pleasant conversation regarding mutual welfare came to an end, the Lord of Vidarbha spoke to the Lord of Niṣadha.

"Today our family lineage has become virtuous; today the southern direction has been blessed; today we have become guests who have attained a meeting obtainable only through merit; today we consider our goals fulfilled, and our own birth and life as truly praiseworthy."
Since you have come to our home through the great rise of our own merit,
from this moment on—
until the end of the Veda— may the songs of the sage reach the ears of the gods as guests.
I shall become a worthy vessel for your fame, which possesses the beauty of the full moon;
moreover, even this wandering through the cycle of worldly existence has become fruitful for me, who was never satiated up to my throat by the nectar of the bliss of your company.

Having spoken thus, he, free from pride, personally presented to the guest a hospitality that was inclined toward affection, upright in virtue, favorable to his family lineage, worthy of the rise of his fortune, appropriate to the time and place, equal to a continuous festival of honor, consistent with his physical excellence, and fitting for his conduct; and he offered elephants that could restrain even irresistible enemy elephants, horses swift as the wind, immeasurable rubies that created the illusion of a circle of Indra’s bow produced by the mass of shimmering rays, necklaces that imitated a cluster of stars renowned in one place, garments of radiant luster, and beautiful women who were the very pinnacle of loveliness.
Even at their first meeting, his heart was uplifted by the impetuous onset of immeasurable affection; then, with words faltering from the bursting forth of excessive joy, he spoke this:

"From the mountain peak marked by the name of Kapi (Hanuman) as far as the ocean, and from the vicinity of the Vindhya range down to the boundaries of the eastern and western seas, let the entire region be adorned with your seal."
Today we have become subject to you who have come to our house;
please accept us—what else remains [to give] besides our lives and our wealth?

In this way, he augmented his love, manifested his eloquence, illuminated his nobility, displayed his respect, and revealed his every feeling. Nala, too, reflecting that "this high-souled one is of straightforward nature and pure heart," said: "Enough, enough with offering all our very selves! To us, the mere sight of you is a gain far superior even to obtaining the entire earth filled with gold from the oceans. For no happiness of gain exceeds the happiness of seeing one's beloved. Nor do we regard your wealth as another's property, nor do we feel it is not our own even in your person. Furthermore, O noble sir, what has been done or what fitting word of affection has been spoken by you, who gladdens our hearts with such songs containing the nectar of well-spoken and pleasant truths? Thus speaking, he honored him greatly.
And during such an occasion, the bard recited this introductory verse:
"May the long-lived kings, from the coastal forests at the limits of the eastern, western, southern, and northern quarters, place [the command] upon their crowns like a garland."
"May the days of you two pass in mutual affection and happiness, you who possess a splendor extending from the Brahma-egg down to the stalk of the plantain tree.

Thus, with the playful conversation of the learned that was not inconsistent with the opening remarks, with the friendly offering of betel leaf surrounded by camphor— which resembled pieces of frozen snow— and with the jesting circles of their satisfied attendants, they remained for a long time, contemplating the talk of the loquacious folk, some of it ever-new, some ancient, some yet to be produced, and some as it truly is.
Immediately thereafter, as the sun-garlanded one followed the middle region of the sky, Nala, with humility, dismissed the Lord of Vidarbha, saying, "May you adorn your own home.

When he had departed, Nala sat for a moment, as it were, with his trusted people and attendants, engaging in conversations inclined toward the King of Vidarbha’s virtues, exclaiming: "Oh, what affection! Oh, what supreme generosity! Oh, what skill in worldly conduct! Oh, what cleverness in the power of speech! Oh, what humility this King of Vidarbha possesses! And he thought:
"Although the accomplishment of one's purpose becomes as if it were already in one's hand through favorable circumstances,
we nevertheless do not trust the Creator, whose crooked ways are as fickle as a serpent trembling with fear;
for instance— "
The kings of Aṅga, Kaṅka, Kaliṅga, Vaṅga, and Magadha— all these rulers—
as well as the guardians of the quarters beginning with Indra, have assembled seeking the maiden;
we do not know how the union will come about here, since that matter must be resolved at this very moment.
For destiny, resembling a magical illusion, is made wondrous through various turns of fate;
or rather,
what concern can a man have there, where human effort prevails?
And since it is beyond the scope of speech and mind, what further deliberation can there be here regarding its injunction?

While the king was thus engaged in various shifting deliberations, and after the subordinate vassals—who were distinguished by the strength of their arms—had been dismissed; while the attendants were scattered about on all sides, and a short time had passed in the course of a gathering of people whose conversation was charming with playful jests; then there entered, preceded by the warder who had been alerted first, many women sent by Damayantī. They were beautiful in form, adorned with abundant and exquisite ornaments. Some held betel nuts and areca fruits in their hands; some carried baskets of betel leaves hanging from their waists; some held in their hands small bundles of fine silk cloths; some were carrying vessels filled with saffron-scented musk and fragrant sandalwood paste; some held trays filled with avakā, nālikera, jambīra, and bījapūraka fruits; and others, bringing countless varieties of sugar-candies and precious auspicious garlands and jewelry, entered with curiosity, led by hunchbacks and dwarfs.

Having entered and beholding the king, who surpassed the beauty of the God of Love, they were filled with wonder and thought: "Well done, O Mistress! Well done! You have fixed your intent upon a worthy object; you have conceived a passion for a suitable one; you have found desire for a fit recipient. You shall reap the fruit of your birth, you shall obtain the fortune inherent to womankind, and you shall experience the pleasures of youth. You shall honor the great festival of the fruits of worldly existence. Oh, how venerable is that mother, a veritable womb of the ocean of jewels of men, from whom this great central gem has arisen amidst the pearl necklace of all the world's heroes! Thus reflecting, with their pearl ornaments swaying as their heads bowed slightly, and with the lotuses of their faces smiling, they gracefully prostrated before the protector of the earth, saying, "O Lord, here is our salutation; some other lady there also bows."
Addressing one another with joyful cries, they spoke thus:
"Ha! Haṃsī! Cakorī! Moon-faced one! Moon-bright one!
Sandalwood-scented one! Campaka! Graceful one! Clove-tree! Gaurī! Kalikā! Kakkolikā! Mālatī!"
May you attain this fruit of birth and life: may your eyes find rest in the king, who is a treasury of the splendor of beauty and a distiller of the nectar of good fortune.
Moreover—

"O beautiful Kundā, O delighter of the moon! O Hālā, by good fortune we celebrate today; for he, the lord of her life whose body is more beautiful than the god of love, has now arrived at the pleasure grove of those trees, for the sake of that slender-limbed lady."
Their leaves wither from the winds of her long sighs, harsh as fire;
moreover,
upon merely hearing of him, the Goddess, whose intoxication was restrained by her youthfulness, became like one possessed by the god of love.

The days are being spent taking refuge in the shade of trees on the banks of the palace ponds; now has arrived that very Nala of Niṣadha, whose eyes are like the petals of the red lotus, and who serves as the tree of rest for the fluttering wings of the wandering eyes of all women.

Having thus addressed one another, they approached his presence; the king, however, with eyes whose pupils were shimmering like waves of affection and which cast long, respectful glances, gazed upon them with longing—like small caskets filled with a mass of contentment, like sprouts of bliss, like statues fashioned from nectar, or like blossoming mango clusters in the springtime—and seeing that they had been sent by Damayantī, he addressed them with agitation: "Come here, come here! Is it well with your ladyships? Pray, sit down; accept this betel; announce the message of your mistress. Thus he spoke to them with great haste.

Saying, "This is a great favor," they sat down and spoke directly to the king: "O King of Kings, the lotus-eyed lady inquires after your welfare: 'Has some fatigue arisen from the heat of the sun upon your person? Or has any distressing exhaustion occurred among your attendants from the toil of traversing uneven paths? Your Majesty has delayed on the road for many days. Furthermore, this beloved gift for the lord of her life has been sent; this was said; this is the message from her beloved; and this is the playful display of her manifest modesty. Thus they addressed the king.

He too, acting as the minister of Love, remained for what seemed like a very long time in the playful diversion of conversation with those women who were protected by their modesty yet made manifest by the erotic sentiment; whose words were like sprays of nectar, blossoming with the rays of innocent smiles; speaking in some ways with simplicity and in others with the curves of bashful affection; asking this and that, sending this and that message; repeating what was said and responding to every jest with a laugh, every well-spoken word with a retort, every endearing thing with a reciprocal endearment—thus he kept them inflamed with passion through the granting of his favor.

"Ah! How truly noble is the character of this lord of men—his conduct is free from vulgarity, his magnanimity is unassailable, his speech is without guile, his giving is without wretchedness, his smile is without pride, and his profundity is beyond the reach of doubt. Thus reflecting, they spent the time with various appropriate diversions, enjoyed the pleasure of conversation, and recounted some account of Damayantī’s playful pastimes. Then, having been granted permission, they departed as they had come, saying: "May Your Majesty command us to depart; the Queen, desiring to drink the nectar of your news, remains waiting in haste for our return."

When they had departed, he summoned a dwarf named Parvataka—who was bold in wisdom, foremost in speech, skilled in the arts, proficient in statecraft, and quick-witted in assembly—and having made him a gift, he sent him off toward Damayantī along with a pair of Kinnaras led by Puṣkarākṣa; these were gratified by his respectful presentation of honors such as excellent garments and ornaments, the chief of which was a brilliant necklace of pearls as large as hard *karkandhū* fruits.

And when midday was being announced by the sound of the conch shells being blown at the start of the daily rites, mingled with the booming resonance of the midday kettledrums, and by the tinkling of the jeweled anklets on the feet of the courtesans emerging from their dwellings, he rose to perform his midday rituals.

Gradually, when the entire body of servants had departed, the dance halls fell silent as if out of the grief of separation from the female attendants who had left after the performance ended; the administrative offices appeared as if asleep due to their stillness; and all the pavilions seemed to have fainted from the midday lethargy because of their emptiness. The royal courtyard shone as if strewn with blooming red lotuses by the rows of vermilion footprints left by the courtesans who had attended the king. Then, as the conchs and trumpets resounded loudly signaling the time for the meal, as the tasters ran about, as the guest-halls were being cleared, as the Brahmins for the first-portion offering were being prepared, as the pure cows fit for the cattle-grazing were being led inside, as the wooden planks atop the pillars for the crows' offerings were being washed, as morsels of food were being distributed outside to the poor, the helpless, and the beggars, as the dining altars were being smeared with cow-dung, as the peacocks were being driven away, and as the deities presiding over the kingdom were being presented with sacrificial offerings—the great kitchen wind blew, enchanting with the fragrance of various cooked foods and carrying the scent of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation. When the King, having completed his sequence of bathing and other rites, was occupying his dining hall, the clamor of the cooks erupted outside.

"Let there be ghee in abundance; let there be rice cooked with *śāli* grains, resembling the unblemished buds of the *kundaka* jasmine; let there be *śikhariṇī* sweetmeat, enchanting with the fragrance of incense, and various savory vegetables; and let diverse foods—abounding in drinks, hard foods, mouthfuls, and things to be licked—be enjoyed."

"O soldiers! Behold, this food sent by the daughter of King Bhīma—alas, these people from the North, West, and East, being devoid of fish and meat, do not even know how to eat their favorite roasted flour (saktu).
Indeed, the practice of eating meat is rare among the Southerners."
Therefore, O Nishadhas, let this be accepted! Having allayed your hunger with liberal portions of excellent food and abundant ghee,
drink slowly the juice of sugarcane prepared with the four aromatic spices (caturjātaka).

Having tasted a little of the sauce, which was desirable due to its abundance of ingredients and its savory flavor, he then ate rice from the Śāli paddy together with a liquid preparation of smooth and thick curd.
The King, however, having said, "O doorkeeper, let it be determined what this clamor outside is," sat down to eat, surrounded by his attendants appropriate for the occasion.
Having gone and returned with speed, that doorkeeper made this representation:

"O Lord, the cooks sent by Damayantī are feeding the army personnel—from the Brāhmaṇas down to the outcasts and cowherds, and including the elephants, horses, and mounts, as well as the vassals and appointed officials—with various kinds of delicious and specially prepared foods."

Mountains of cooked food were seen on all sides; heaps of boiled rice, mounds of soup, streams of clarified butter, rivers of honey, piles of sugar, currents of curd and milk, hills of vegetables, reservoirs of syrups, channels of fruit juices, and peaks of astringent, sour, salty, bitter, and sweet condiments.
Thus the army was fed to its heart's content without stint.
Moreover—
At the end of the meal, his hands are smeared with ghee and used for rubbing; then sandalwood paste is applied, followed by the ritual offering of betel leaves as white as pieces of ginger;
thereafter, two garments as soft as a single lotus fiber are bestowed upon him one by one.

"Something quite inconceivable has been done by the Queen for you: she has provided hospitality for your army, and this *rasavatī* (delicious food) has been prepared for Your Majesty, adorned with special dishes seasoned by the fragrance of her own sprout-like hands, and sent sealed with her own seal," she said, and then ceased speaking.

The King, however, with his head slightly nodding, said with a smile: "Oh, how captivating is her playful charm, characterized by conduct that is unsurpassed, noble, profound, and dignified; and what an extraordinary method of cooking this is, possessing such a desirable fragrance!"

For instance, reflecting thus—"This is sour yet possesses a non-sour flavor; this is slightly astringent yet has been rendered sweet; this is of a single taste yet has been made manifold; this, through its extreme refinement, surpasses even nectar"—he tasted with indifference those various culinary specialties sent by her, thinking: "The daughter of the King of Vidarbha is truly possessed of the essence of flavor.
And he thought:
It is said that among physicians there are six flavors, or eight, or even nine;
yet by her, whose eyes were like lotus petals, everything was rendered of a single flavor.
For instance:

Though our eyes were sealed by sleep, we perceived her as if standing before our minds, as if suspended right in front of our gaze; she seemed to speak, to obstruct us, and to smile slightly with a charming grace— she who had manifested herself in every form.
We see [them] outside and within, by night and by day, on the roads and in the houses.

Thus reflecting, as if still unsatiated with the various delicacies cooked by his own hand that had been served, and remaining dissatisfied even with talk of them, he rinsed his mouth. With the sprout-like palms of his hands whitened by the fragrance of sandalwood and aloe-wood, he took betel leaf prepared with cloves and cardamom and emitting the rising scent of camphor. Having rested for a moment in the afternoon recreation pavilion—which was enchanting with heaps of various scattered flowers, its walls sprinkled with *yakṣakardama* paste, hung with long golden lotuses, fragrant with the smoke of incense, and adorned with lines of powdered camphor—he, whose heart was overcome by longing and who was curious to gaze at the distant horizons, ascended the upper terrace of a cloud-kissing palace built on the riverbank. There, with two peacock-feather umbrellas held aloft, he wandered gracefully and languidly from side to side. He beheld the female elephants on the banks, their trunks extended toward the flowering creepers as they emerged from their play in the river dust; he listened to the cracking sounds of lotus-stalks being broken by the herds of young elephants, white as the tusks of those same calves, amidst the clusters of bees moving restlessly over the blossoming lotus groves where some had just risen from sleep among the sparse leaves. His face-moonlight was drunk in by the women of Kuṇḍinapura who had come for their evening bath—their eyes, fixed with wonder, motionless like the petals of blue lotuses—as they gazed upon him. He was watched even by the presiding deity of the waters of the confluence, who seemed to have wide-open eyes in the guise of the little fish leaping far away, and who displayed the knitting of her eyebrows in the form of the waves. For a moment he rested his eyes upon the pleasure-lotus ponds where swarms of bees incessantly kissed the blossoms; for a moment upon the rows of mango trees in full bloom that lined the outskirts like the riding paths for the horses of Love; for a moment upon the garden avenues of the palaces, lovely with creepers charming with opening flowers; for a moment upon the rows of Bhīma’s inner-apartment mansions, resplendent with the fluttering edges of flying banners; and for a moment upon the city streets, beautiful with the painted patterns of scattered flowers. Thus, his gaze resting upon these sights, he remained there for a long time.
And he thought:
"Neither in the garden, nor on the banks of the river, nor in a lovely palace,
nor even in pleasure-pools where bees hum within the hearts of blooming lotuses."
My gaze, now unsteady like a leaf shattered and whirled by a whirlwind,
does not rest even though I am weary, like a doe frightened by a greedy hunter;
moreover—
It is not accessible to mantras, nor does it fall within the domain of medicines;
yet, despite hundreds of prescribed pacifying rites, it does not perish,
causing some incomparable fracture in a limb due to the force of delusion.
This madness of love bewilders my vision and makes me reel;
moreover, what else is so wondrous?—
the five arrows of the flower-bowed god, his bow, and even its string and barb are made of the ikṣulatā creeper!

"The three worlds must be conquered daily, and yet the bodiless god of love (Anaṅga) must also be conquered"— by the occurrence of such a succession of wonders, he causes the mind to marvel; the activity of Fate, which is utterly barren of reason, is most worthy of praise.

Thus, while the heart of the King of Niṣadha was agitated by manifold reflections, his gaze resting upon the streets of the city of Kuṇḍina, and while he had lent his body to the breeze from the lotus groves—whose waves were exceedingly gentle and which gently swayed the petals of the *mallikā* jasmine—he entered, announced by the doorkeeper. He was clad in two garments as white as the slough of a serpent; his forearms were filled up to the elbows with jingling jeweled bracelets; and his body was pale like a mass of sandalwood paste, appearing like a mountain never seen before.

Having entered and offered a greeting of manifest affection, he was addressed by the Lord with a smile of wonder and a grunt of acknowledgment; then, with a slight nod of his brows as a sign, he began to make his request.

"Your Majesty, listen. Having departed from here, I traversed several paths that surpassed even heaven in their excellence; beholding various palaces that were beautiful with diverse artistic carvings and which brought delight to the mind; with my heart captivated here and there by the glances of playful, smiling women on the shore, languid with passion, whose eyes were slightly narrowed in coquetry; [I reached] a royal palace surrounded by a circle of gardens delightful with the sweet warbling of flocks of male cuckoos in the bowers of mango groves, which were fresh and dripping with swarms of honeybees; where the horses of the king’s favorites, being well-fed and nourished, neighed with joy in their stables and mansions situated near the edge; where auspicious banners were fixed upon lofty peaks; where deer and birds frolicked in the pleasure-grounds within the courtyards; where young princes took their delight in the inner chambers, their limbs anointed with unbroken sandalwood paste; and whose courtyards were adorned with rows of beautiful painted designs, charming like waves fashioned from exceedingly fine pearls—I entered the royal residence."

There, the waters of the pleasure-pools were exceedingly captivating with their garlands of fine lotuses, as were the herds of elephants; the pairs of cranes in the swaying gardens were full of vigor, as was the assembly of poet-servants; there were hanging golden saffron-threads, as was the singing; there was the comfort of hundreds of thousands of lamps untroubled by fire, as was the dramatic spectacle.
What more need be said?
It was a mass of well-established splendor, the source of Fortune, and the abode of jewels.
Upon him all float like dyes upon the surface of the ocean.

And there, having entered the inner apartments—which were like Pātāla crowded with moving maidservants and possessed of endless chambers—I beheld Damayantī seated at a window facing this way, on the seventh floor of a palace whose white-washed walls resembled the lofty peaks of the Himalayas, where a row of banners shone like a troop of seven suns. The courtyard was surrounded by virtuous trees laden with an abundance of various flowers, and its ponds were bordered by moving cakravāka birds; the upper rooms (candraśālās) were graced by them. Like an actor, she appeared upon many stages; like Arjuna, she was accompanied by Subhadrā; like the narrative of the Kuru lineage, she possessed walls variegated with beautiful paintings. She was conversing with those hunchbacked and dwarf maidens who had come from that place, engaging them in the diversion of discussing news of you. With her incessantly flickering glances, she seemed to offer a garland of blue lotuses to the very quarter of the sky presided over by you. Her jar-like breasts were marked with musk-leaf patterns that mimicked the scars of Cupid’s arrows, visible through the transparency of her upper garment. Upon her forehead, which possessed the splendor of a crescent moon on the eighth day, she bore three lines of tilaka made from saffron, musk, and sandalwood paste—like a mark of self-recognition in the likeness of her own complexion, joyfully made by the God of Love, now subject to the three cities, crying out in exultation, "This is mine! This is mine! This is mine! Her face was adorned with a curling lock of hair reaching her ear, reddened as if it were the sprout of a conduit for drinking the nectar of news about you. Because her reflection was cast upon the nearby jeweled wall-mirrors, she seemed to create many replicas of herself, as if to share the burden of the torment caused by the longing for union with you. She was being attended by friends of equal age and dress, skilled in the diversions of music and other arts, like Sarasvatī served by the presiding deities of all the sciences. She was being waited upon by female fly-whisk bearers, charming with their blooming floral ornaments, like the goddesses of the forest attending the embodied beauty of Spring. She was being worshipped by female attendants with ointments and flowers in their hands, like Bhavānī by the women of the many lords of heaven. She scattered a stream of light from the jewels in her ornaments falling here and there, like a mass of cooling rays from the moon. Reflected in every limb of her body, she seemed to be embraced by illusory gods and demons appearing on the nearby painted walls. To the impassioned lover afflicted by the god of love, she offered her reflection out of compassion, like a moon that has set behind a mirror of ruby. I beheld Damayantī, who was like a hall of arms for Manmatha in his conquest of the world, a meeting-place for all the qualities of beauty, the presiding deity of good fortune, a marketplace for loveliness, the final line of the Creator's masterpiece, and a single jewel-sprout of the mountain of endless worldly existence.
Beholding that needle of nectar for the eyes, my gaze dilated with excessive joy, wonder, and curiosity, and I thought:
"For this is the royal capital of the King of Love, the auspicious balcony for the birds of dalliance."
Whose mind is not captivated by this young girl, who is like a theater for the sentiment of love?
Yet,
cursed fate does not ordain that any person shall be beautiful in every quality.
Was the fawn-eyed woman created by the Creator as if out of fear of such exceptions?
And what more can be said—
that other [world] is but a fragment of the atoms of merit that constitute her loveliness.
And he must surely be some other, highly skillful Creator, by whom this marvelous work was fashioned; for the specific quality of the cause is inferred from the excellence of the effect.

As I was reflecting thus, she too, having observed me with a flurry of glances most fitting for one with lotus-eyes—her neck slightly turned and her ear-lotuses trembling—spoke after first asking a greeting: “Oh! After so long a time, today there has been a beautiful dawn; the mass of darkness that once seemed solidified has vanished from Kuṇḍina as if by light. The forest region near the confluence of the rivers has become like a festival of blossoming spring occurring without warning. At last, this southern quarter has become auspicious and marked with excellence; the Sahya mountain seems awakened, and these people have been restored to life as if by a stream of nectar. Having said this, she addressed me with a voice sweet and charming with a smile: “Parvataka, is Nala—the forest fire to the creepers of his enemies—well?”
I too, having bowed as was appropriate, immediately sat upon a seat brought by my friends and accepted those ornaments and gifts sent by Your Majesty.

When they had been received with such respect, and when I was highly honored, and while the discourse concerning the enumeration of your virtues was underway, after a brief interval had passed in the playful sport of friendly conversation, Puṣkarākṣa also spoke:
"O Queen, I shall inform you if you grant me immunity."

Thus have we heard: "Indeed, all the world-protectors, led by the Lord of the Nākis (Brahmā) and Purandara (Indra), desiring you and with the forest-fire of passion clinging to the interior of their hearts, entreated you as you approached, saying: 'For those of great soul are indeed devoted to the dharma of the vow of helping others; therefore, O noble one, for our sake, Damayantī should be chosen by you, regardless of your own purpose.
So, O Queen, the Lord of Niṣadha has arrived on the mission of a divine messenger. Or let the Queen question Parvataka."
Having heard these words spoken by Puṣkarākṣa, she cast a sidelong glance at me, her face smiling with a faint, bashful smile mixed with a touch of dejection.

When those words of Puṣkarākṣa had been confirmed by me as well, she remained for a moment with her vow of silence undertaken, as if experiencing the pain of a sudden blow from hard wood; with her eyes closed, as if so that the lute’s melody might attain its sweetness; with her smile withheld, as if so that her ear-lotuses might receive their full splendor; with her pride cast aside, as if so that the campaka garland hanging from her neck might obtain its beauty; and with her face upturned, as if so that this playful lotus might attain auspicious fortune. She remained thus for a moment.
And during that commotion,
this palace became as if its grace had dissolved, its love-play suddenly shattered by another, and as if swooned, fainted, or sealed shut like a pearl.
The king said, "Parvataka, what happened next? Parvataka replied, "Your Majesty, please listen.
Hereafter—"

Casting upon me a languid glance, shimmering with a smile that possesses the luster of a cluster of radiant teeth like slightly opened jasmine buds, she slightly cast her lotus-hand— resembling a bee— toward her lower lip, which had come to her mind as a bandhūka flower.

Then, beholding her standing there—her head slightly tilted as it shook again and again, her earrings swaying; the flow of her playful words silenced by her attendants; her graceful smiles forgotten by sudden astonishment; her long eyes languid like lotus petals struck by intense frost; the radiance of her moon-like face dimmed by the uneven despondency arising from her hot and heavy sighs—the circle of her friends looked on with sorrow and said, "O Queen, [your palace] has been overturned by the succession of the winds of your sighs."

"The Lord Sun takes refuge in the western mountain as if seeking its hand for support; and this splendor of the day, O King, as if ashamed upon hearing of this solicitation by the world-protectors regarding you, whose heart is fixed on the fortunate Nala, covers her ears and retreats to a distance; these lotuses close their petals like eyes, while their inner nectar is being drunk by bees that remain motionless within; and the waters of the lakes, the companions of the day’s grace, seem to share in the sorrow and grow turbid; and these quarters of the sky grow dark as if out of shame, thinking, 'How can our lords desire a mortal maiden? Therefore, let this Parvataka be sent away. Thus addressed, she—with her speech interrupted by the onset of anxiety—somehow or other raised her face with a slight smile, and extending her palm which resembled a blossoming sprout of the *aśoka* tree, dismissed me at the conclusion of a gift of honor that was impossible to forget.

And having been dismissed by her at that time—she who was observing a vow of silence brought on by the onset of manifesting despondency—I was neither spoken to again, nor looked upon, nor questioned, nor given any message; rather, having gazed at me with a glance whose pupils trembled at the corners of her moving eyes, she sent me away with a mere gesture of her upturned lotus-like hands. Thinking, "Alas! I have come here with feet that are sluggish, faltering, and stumbling, as if they were turned backward.
Having heard this account of her acceptance of the mission as a messenger of the gods, Damayantī fell into a state of extreme despondency. Furthermore, she thought:
"I believe that the forest of trees, its luster withered and devoid of blossoms, [is like one whose sleep has been stolen away]."
With the sky resounded by the cries of flocks of birds swooping down,
and the pairs of cakravāka birds crying out near the river as if afflicted by separation,
even this world became a source of poison to the Queen as she despaired.
When Parvataka had spoken thus and remained silent, the reciter, who read at the appropriate moment, recited this very matter suited to the occasion:
"O mortal, how is it that the nectar-eaters abandon celestial nymphs— slender-limbed women with smiling faces and eyes overwhelmed by passion— and instead desire a maiden devoted to another?"
The lord of the day (the sun), unable to speak further due to shame, sank low as if from exhaustion;
the sun, as if red with anger, entered the western ocean, the abode of Varuṇa.

Hearing this, the king descended from the terrace of the palace roof and performed his evening rites at the confluence of the rivers, where the sandy banks were occupied by Brahmins chanting prayers who had sat down to conclude their twilight worship with the ritual of the *līlāpadma* (the playful lotus).

Then, as the glow of twilight shimmered in the western direction, a mass of darkness unfolded like the Yamunā river—resembling a troop of untimely vetālas rushing about, smeared with blood and eager for flesh—flooding the vault of the sky as if with thousands of streams out of sheer joy, while the Gaṅgā flowed forth through its three channels.
Immediately thereafter, the eastern quarter, pregnant with the moon, assumed the pale whiteness of the petals of the ketakī flower.
And the moonlight, tawny like a mass of pollen from the flowers and tender sprouts of the trees on the rising mountain shaken by the fiercely blowing wind, shone forth.

Then, in due course, the Lord of Stars descended into the range of vision, resembling a royal swan rising from the sandy banks of the eastern ocean toward the celestial Mandākinī; like a young lion emerging from the deep caverns of the cave on the Mountain of Sunrise, pursuing the herd of elephants that is darkness; like a crystal full pitcher prepared by someone for the auspiciousness of the sea-monster Makara as he stands ready for his expedition to conquer the world; like a ball of sandalwood cherished in the embrace of the hand of the Eastern Quarter for her adornment; like a cluster of Śaṅkhikā flowers placed upon the ear of the Beauty of the Sky; like the solitary frontal globe of the lordly elephant roaming the forest of the East that has become manifest; like a bulbous root uprooted by the huntress Night after she had climbed over the creeper of day’s end; like a heap of white flowers, parched rice, and Guñjā berries arranged by the wives of the Siddhas at the crossroads of the Mountain of Sunrise; like a boulder fallen from the peak of Kailāsa; like a pearl in the parting of the hair of the Eastern Quarter; like a white parasol of Purandara, the sovereign of the East; like a play-ball of pearls for the youthful Time; and resembling a mass of milk-foam.
And thereafter—
having caused the blooming of the night-lotuses and illuminating the quarters of the sky, consecrate Madana as the youth to the position of crown prince.
Bathing the world of living beings with its waves of nectar, the moon slowly and gently entered the sky.

Immediately thereafter, the world became as if flooded by an ocean of milk that had overstepped its bounds; as if its courtyards were sprinkled by copious showers of sandalwood water; as if its walls of the quarters were smeared with thick masses of lime-paste; as if filled by a rising rain of camphor powder; as if it had entered the interior of a great palace made of crystal gems; and as if it were floating upon a vast raft of the Himalayas melted into liquid. Thus was the world.
And then—by the mountains, the trees acted as Kailāsa; by the mud, it acted as a white umbrella; in the ocean, it acted as curd; and by the waters, it acted as milk.
And when the moon had risen, the creepers acted like strings of pearl necklaces, the *śrīphala* fruits acted like conch shells,
and the regions of the land acted like the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa.
All birds were swans, all elephants were Airāvatās,
and all mountain peaks became heaps of silver by the rays of the moon;
moreover—
The earth was made by the moonlight as if smeared with nectar-paste, as if covered with crystals,
and as if anointed with melted snow;
moreover—
The tops of the palaces are discerned by clusters of lamps; the pale banners by a gentle fluttering of their wings; the swans by the sound of their sleepy calls;
and the night-lotuses by the humming of bees and the rising fragrance.
When the rising of the moon had occurred— resembling the swelling waters of the churning Ocean of Milk—
and when such a magnificent lunar spectacle had unfolded, the Lord of Niṣadha, overcome by an intense longing, reflected:
"From this direction, the moon radiates dense rays that are not harsh."
Here blows the breeze from the groves of blooming night-lotuses; here too resounds the cry of the geese, languid with sleep;
unbearable is this entire array of the power of the Mind-born God.
Moreover—
from this side, the irresistible god whose banner is the makara hurls his arrows;
from that side, we too are distressed by the command of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
This is indeed a most perilous situation, as it has been said by some people here: "From this side there is the fear of a venomous snake, and from that side the great tiger."

"Now, what is to be done here? For how can the command of the World-Guardians, whose words are never in vain, be disregarded even in jest?"—thinking thus, he departed alone on foot from his own residence. After a short time, during which the spreading nets of moonbeams pointed out the path to him as if they were attendants, he reached King Bhīma’s palace, magnificent with its expansive turrets that resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa. There, invisible to the palace guards due to the boon granted by Indra, he entered the maiden's inner apartments.

Having entered, he ascended the roof of the palace where Damayantī resided; there, he was as if being welcomed by a breeze that had come from afar toward him, its course curved by the continuous smoke of burning black aloe-wood incense, and which seemed to be streaming from the joints of the palace walls moistened with thick yakṣa-paste. After walking a short distance, he was as if summoned by the humming of songs from a musical circle of female friends saying, "The lady is this way, this way! and so he climbed onto the palace roof.

Having ascended, he remained unobserved as it were, and beheld Damayantī, who was being entertained by the soft, low-intoned songs of her friends led by the Kinnarī, which followed the resonance of flutes and lutes; she who, with a pearl resembling a star nestled amidst the creepers of her curls and the dark collyrium-stained lashes of her lotus-eyes, made even the earth appear like the sky filled with the full-orbed moon, as if in joyful rivalry with it; she whose throat was embraced by a necklace that seemed like a row of the Seven Sages and the planets of Smara, swaying upon the high circles of her breasts; her face adorned by a playful leaf-creeper clinging to her ear—like a second flower-cluster sent as a messenger by Spring—and acting as a flattering envoy; her beautiful shoulders graced by clear musk-paste leaf-designs that resembled serpents come for the protection of the nectar of her loveliness; surrounded on the ground nearby by scattered heaps of pale flowers, as if encircled by stars descended from heaven out of curiosity to behold her beauty; wearing a white silk scarf that had become a garment, its ripples gathered at the knot as if longing for the pleasure of touching the circle of her thighs, resembling the Milky Ocean itself; her left foot adorned by a silver anklet that clung to it like the serpent Śeṣa, having approached to be chosen by her at the *svayaṃvara*; appearing as if fashioned by various artistic brushes, her limbs painted with colors of liquid nectar, constructed of the very sprouts of bliss, carved from the stone of the jewel of enchantment, hewn from the timber of erotic passion, created from the atoms of subjugation, and molded from the clay of Love; she who was, to the eyes, a statue of diamond-glaze, to the heart, a magnet-stick of attraction, to passion, a life-giving herb, and to Love, a banner of victory; experiencing the pleasure of the touch of nectar-like moonlight on the terrace of the palace, which was smeared with thick sandalwood water, where the sound of bees mingling with sweet fragrances could be inferred from the scattered heaps of white flowers, and which was slippery with a smooth coating of white plaster; she who sat upon a crystal couch of pure rays, yet remained sleepless.
And having beheld it, he reflected: "Oh, how well-placed is the devotion of the world-protectors! Who would not long for this, which is a treasury of all happiness? And I think—"
Gazing at her alone with wide-open eyes, this sky has become filled with planets;
and this moon, touching her very self with rays as white as sandalwood, bears upon its heart—in the guise of a dark spot—the scar of a wound caused by the burning fire of passion.
And even this breeze from the nearby garden, having offered her the fragrance of flowers, falls obliquely like one afflicted by love, slowly stealing away the edge of her upper garment.
The world of men has been utterly conquered, since such an inconceivable, beyond the range of contemplation, incomparable, wonderful, and priceless jewel of a woman has appeared here.

Ah, Prajāpati! You have reached the perfection of your artistry. O Saṃsāra, you have a true protector. O Madana, you are the host of a great festival. O Eye, you have achieved your purpose. O Heart, your desire is fulfilled. O Fatigue from traveling afar, you have borne fruit.
O you who are like a blossoming creeper that attracts the bee-like minds of all young men, you whose lotus-eyes surpass the lotuses themselves—live long!
For instance:
O slender one, we do not know what kind of mark there is upon your eyes, which resemble lotuses and possess the movement of flickering eyebrows.
Moreover:
When the nectar of the *pañcama* melody issues from the mouths of the *kiṃnaras* and reaches her ear,
the glance of that deer-eyed woman— both languidly turning and trembling— steals away [her composure].

Reflecting thus in many ways, he approached with soft, playful steps and entered the midst of the circle of her friends, who were gathered for a musical assembly and were filled with wonder, their eyes wide open as they asked, "Who is this? and were overcome with agitation.

And when he had entered, the people remained gazing at him for a long time, their eyes—dilated by sudden amazement, whirling with fear, upturned by curiosity, turned away by modesty, meeting in glances with joy, agitated by the intent of love, unblinking from the essence of longing to see, half-closed from the friction of their mutual stares, and closed together in amorous play; meanwhile, they shifted slightly in their seats, their hearts trembled, their fortitude fled, perspiration trickled down their bodies, their limbs bristled with thrill, and they became as frail as the god of love, all while looking at one another’s faces and fixing their gaze upon him.

Damayantī also, hearing the words of the hunchbacked and dwarf maidens who had risen in agitation and were singing with voices faltering from excess of joy—"O Queen, we congratulate you! We congratulate you! Some lord of life has arrived right here!"—abandoned her song and, with her face slightly turned in playful charm, looked toward him and rose from the surface of her bed amidst the soft clapping of their palms and the resulting clamor.

"Ah, how can there be entry into this inner apartment of maidens—guarded by many walls and sentries, difficult for even birds to enter, and especially so at night? Thus she thought, having looked again and again at Nala with eyes motionless from being struck by a surge of wonder and slightly moved. "Blessed is some fortunate woman who has committed no offense, around whose neck you shall roll like a pearl necklace, with your arms outstretched."
"O Father, even you are blessed by this creation; O Mother Earth, you too reap the fruit of your labor.
What more can be said? For he who has been created by you is now your husband.

While she was thinking thus, at that very moment—her lotus-eyes darting back and forth through a succession of various emotions such as intention, curiosity, joy, and fear—she lowered her face with modesty and fell into a state of confusion regarding what ought to be done.

Nala also said to a *kinnarī* who was standing nearby and with whom he had been previously acquainted, "O bird-catchers, is such the conduct of your mistress that she does not even engage in the customary exchange of greetings with a guest?
She, having first offered a respectful salutation with agitation, replied:
"Indeed, has your welcome not already been asked by the sound of bracelets on her slightly trembling hands?"

O Lord, she who bowed with her lotus-face adorned by the auspicious marks of Śrī and Lakṣmī pressed her lotus-eyes to Your feet; she, standing at the threshold with her pair of breasts like auspicious jars, granted You entry into her heart.
O Master, has this friend not performed what is most fitting for a guest?
"Therefore, let my lord ascend this shimmering gem-studded couch offered by her as she rose in haste.
